lawyer: Mr. Mohammadullah, with Mr. Waliur Reza Chowdhury  ------  For the Petitioners.
parties:
Kamrul Ahsan and others  ------  Petitioners
 Versus 
A N M Ziauddin and others  ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
2. Opposite Party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted the suit against the petitioners and others for a decree of declaration that the waqf estate of which the plaintiff is the mutawalli has got title in the suit land measuring about 1.34 acres fully described in the schedule to the plaint. The petitioners have appeared in the suit and filed a joint written statement denying the plaint case. Then, on 14.02.2002 the petitioners made an application under Order VI Rule 11 of the Code for rejection of the plaint mainly on the ground that the suit as framed was barred by provision of Section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 (Ordinance No. 1 of 1962), in brief, the Ordinance. On 20.05.2002 the application was heard and rejected by the impugned order on the view that jurisdiction vests in Civil Court only to decide question of title and correctness of the record of rights pre-pared and published in respect of the suit land. 

 5. In the plaint, amongst other, it is averred that Khan Saheb Maulavi Abdul Khaleque created a waqf in the name of Ama Miah Waqf by a registered deed of waqf being No. 1878 dated 10 Falgoon, 1323 BS. Under the terms of the Waqf, property could be acquired out of the fund of the Waqf but transfer of any land of the Waqf was prohibited. In 1917, the Waqf was enrolled being No. 1526 in the office of the Bengal Waqf Commissioner. Out of the fund of the waqf, the suit land was purchased. When the Defendant No. 1 to 4 and 9 to 13 started talking for sale of the suit land, the present mutawalli enquired about the matter and found that the suit land was not recorded in S A record of rights in the name of the waqf. In order to remove the cloud cast by the wrong record, the mutawalli was constrained to institute the suit for a declaration that the waqf has got title in the suit land. 

 6. The issues involved in such suit are whether or not the waqf has got title in the suit land and whether or not the record of rights in respect of the suit land as pre-pared and published is correct. The issues are essentially civil in nature. Under Section 9 of the Code all suits of civil nature will lie in civil courts unless the same is specially barred by specific provision of law. It is now well settled by a long line of authorities that jurisdiction of a civil court cannot readily be read to have stood ousted. 

 8. Firstly, under the. Ordinance the waqf Administrator is given specified powers for the management and administration of the waqfs only. No power of a civil court is given to the Waqf Administrator to decide any civil dispute, namely, question as to title of a property, correctness of a record of rights, validity of a transfer of a waqf property etc. In the case of Syed Masud All and others v Md. Asmatullah, (1980) 32 DLR (AD) 32, the Appellate Division has interpreted the power of the Administrator under Section 50 of the Ordinance as hereunder,

lawyer:
N.K. Saha, Senior Advocate instructed by Mahmuda Begum, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Petitioner (in all the cases)
Khalilur Rahman, Advocate instructed by Zahirul Islam, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Respondents
parties:
Bhawal Raj Court of Words Estate ------- Petitioner (In both the cases)
Vs.
Rasheda Begum and Ors. ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
3. The common case of all the writ-petitioners, as it appears from the judgment sought to be reviewed, was that the respective case land involved in the respective writ petition originally belonged to Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate; the writ-petitioners were the successors-in-interest of the tenants under the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate. In the C.S. Khatian, the respective case land stood recorded in the name of Bhawal Raj Court Wards Estate. After the acquisition of the land of the Zaminders on cessation of the Zamindary system, the rent receiving interest of the Mouza under which the respective case land belonged, was acquired by the Government under section 3(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act, 1950) vide notification No. 2773 L.R. dated 26.02.1952 and the said notification of acquisition was published in the Dhaka Gazette on 24.03.1952, whereby it was notified that all rent receiving interest vested in the Government with effect from 14.04.1952 and the schedule given in the said Gazette notification includes the Mouza under which the case lands are situated. Thereafter, by notification No. 3126 L.R. dated 27.02.1956 published in the Dhaka Gazette on 29.02.1956, the Government acquired the lands of the Bhawal Raj Courts of Ward Estate, in respect of which, the rent receiving interest was acquired earlier on declaration of the compensation assessment Roll under section 43(2) read with section 46C and 46E(3) of the Act, 1950 and thereby, the respective case land of the respective writ-petitioner(s) vested in the Government with effect from the date of publication of the said notifications and since then the tenants under the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate became the tenants under the Government in respect of such vested lands. Accordingly, during the S.A. survey operation; the names(s) of the respective writ-petitioner(s) and or his/their predecessors-in-interest was/were correctly recorded without any objection from any quarter. During the revisional survey operation, the name(s) of the respective writ-petitioner(s) and or his/their predecessors-in-interest was/were correctly recorded without objection. The respective writ-petitioner(s) directly or through his/their predecessors-in-interest has/have been owning and possessing his/their respective case land as tenants on payment of rents initially to the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and subsequently, after cessation of Zamindary system to the revenue authority of the Government openly and publicly without any objection. During the recent Mahanagor survey operation, the revenue authority found the respective writ-petitioner(s) in possession of his/their respective case land and accordingly the draft record of rights was prepared in his/their respective names(s) in accordance with law, i.e. under rule 29 of the Rules, 1955. The petitioner, Bhawal Raj Court Wards Estate, filed objection under rule 30 of the Rules, 1995 for removing the name(s) of the writ-petitioner(s) as appearing against his/their respective possession in respect of his/their respective case land in the draft record of rights challenging their tenancy; the revenue authority after full-fledged hearing rejected the objection of the petitioner. Against the said order of the revenue authority, the petitioner preferred separate appeal under rule 31 of the Rules, 1955 unsuccessfully and thereby, the draft record of rights was published in the respective name(s) of the writ-petitioner(s) under rule 33 thereof. The petitioner, Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate, filed an application before the Settlement Officer mentioning rule 42A of the Rules, 1995 for correction of the published draft record of rights and on the basis of the said application, fresh hearing was taken and the name(s) of the writ-petitioner(s) was/were substituted by the name of Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate as tenants in respect of the respective case land in the respective khatian on the basis of the C.S. Khatian, disbelieving the intermediary the transfers made during the period till the promulgation of the Act, 1950 and disregarding the acquisition of the rent receiving interest and vesting of the case land in the Government through gazette notification dated 26.02.1952 and 27.02.1956 mentioned above and the fact of payment of rents and taxes to the Government by the respective writ-petitioner(s) in respect of his/their respective case land as tenant(s). Though the name(s) of the respective writ-petitioner(s) was/ were ordered to be substituted by the name of the petitioner, the writ-petitioner(s) was/were ordered to be shown as "illegal possessors through force" and thus the possession of the writ-petitioners in the case lands is admitted. As stated hereinbefore, this order passed in the respective appeal was challenged in the respective writ petition to have been passed without lawful authority and was of no legal effect. 

 9. A perusal of the judgment shows that the point’s takes in the reasons have been dealt with by this Court elaborately while dismissing the petitions affirming those of the High Court Division. Moreso, in the reasons, in fact, the findings of the High Court Division have been sought to be reconsidered. In none of the reasons, the petitioner has been able to point out any mistake or error apparent in the judgment sought to be reviewed within the meaning of rule 1 of Order XLVII of the Code of Civil Procedure. However, from the judgment, it appears that the main question involved in all the writ petitions was whether the application filed by Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate petitioners herein to the settlement officer, Dhaka Land Records and Land Survey Directorate, Tejgaon under rule 42A of the Rules, 1955 to hear the appeals filed under rule 31 thereof afresh was maintainable in law or not. The High Court Division decided the question in the negative and this Court concurred with the view taken by the High Court Division. This Division considering the application filed before the Settlement Officer under rule 42A of the Rules, 1955, the connected facts, particularly, the gazette notifications dated 24.03.1952 and 29.02.1956 as to the acquisition and vesting of rent receiving interest of the lands of Bhawal Raj Court of Wards including the land involved in the respective writ petition upon the Government, the S.A. and the R.S. khatian and payment of rents by the respective, writ-petitioner(s) to the Government, concluded that "Thus we are of the view that the leave petitioner had no locus-standi to challenge the draft Mahanagor survey khatian as prepared in the names of the respective writ-petitioners, at least after publication of the gazette not Notifications dated 24.03.1952 and 29.02.1956."

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 901 of 2018 with CP 1466 of 2022.
lawyer:
AM Aminuddin, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Helal Amin, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioners. (in CP 901/2018) 
Probir Neogi, Senior Advocate, instructed by MadhumalotiChowdhury Barua, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioners. (In CP 1466/2022) 
Abdul WadudB huiya, Senior Advocate with Md Nurul Amin, Senior Advocate and M. Qumrul Hoque Siddique, Advocate, instructed by Bivash Chandra Biswas, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondent No.1- 5. (In CP 901/18) 
 None Represented—Respondent Nos.6-11. (In CP 901/18) 
None Represented—Respondents. (In CP 1466/22)
parties:
Abdur Rashid (Md) and others --------- Petitioners 1 [In CP 901/18]
Syed Sohrawardi and another ------- Petitioners [In CP 1466/22]
VS
ABM Yousuf Abdullah and others ----------- Respondents [In both the cases)
full_judgment:
11. From the impugned notice dated 28-9-2014 as quoted above, it appears that at the instance of Zonal Settlement Officer, Dhaka, Charge Officer and Investigating Officer, issued the aforesaid letter for further hearing and communicated the said letter for holding inquiry on 14-10-2014. The writ petitioner respondents challenged the same without appearing before the concerned office. It further appears from the materials on record that on the basis of the application dated 21-7-2014 Zonal Settlement Officer issued a notice for holding inquiry under the provision of Rule 42A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 to ascertain as to whether any fraud has been committed in making entry of draft record-of-rights or not. The contents of the said notice were as follows: 

 12. Thereafter, by the impugned notice dated 28-9-2014, it was directed to the parties to appear before the Zonal Settlement Officer on 14-10-2014. Rule 41, 42A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 authorized the Revenue Officer to hold enquiry to ascertain as to whether any fraud has been committed in making entry in record-of-right or not and such application should be filed before final publication of the record-of-rights. The said provision run as follows: 

 "42A.--Correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights- 

 The Revenue Officer, with the additional designation of 'Settlement Officer' shall, on receipt of an application or on receipt of an official report for the correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-rights before final publication thereof, after consulting relevant records and making such other enquiries as he deems necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to appeal. At the same time, the Revenue-Officer shall make the correct entry after giving the parties concerned a hearing and recording his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference." 

 13. Admittedly, record-of-right in the instant case, has not yet been published finally. Since petitioner Abdur Rashid brought specific allegations that the writ petitioners procured the order by practising fraud, the Revenue Officer with the additional designation of Settlement Officer can examine as to whether such order has been procured by practising fraud or not. 

 14. The instant case, it appears that the Zonal Settlement Officer simply issued a notice directing the parties to appear before him with their respective papers. The writ petitioners, without appearing before the said Officer, directly filed the instant writ petition and obtained Rule which was finally made absolute. Since the law authorizes the Revenue officer with additional designation of settlement officer to hold inquiry to ascertain as to whether any fraud had been committed in procuring entry for preparation of the record-of-rights before final publication or not, we are of the view, that the said Office acted in its jurisdiction as conferred under the Rule 42A of the State Acquisition Rules, 1955 rightly, the High Court Division erred in law in interfering with the matter at the stage when the writ petitioners have ample opportunity to appear before the Zonal Settlement Officer and to produce documents to justify their claims.
case_type_name: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal

lawyer:
Md Humayun Kabir Bulbul, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners. 
Nurun Nahar, Advocate ----- For the Opposite-Parties;
parties:
Esahaq  Ali Mallik and another ----- Plaintiff-appellant-Petitioners
VS.
Mobarak Sheikh and ors ----- Defendant-respondent Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
2. Material facts of the case, briefly, are that the petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 14 of 1998 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Kachua, Bagerhat praying for declaration of their title in the suit land and perpetual injunction upon the defendants not to dispossess the plaintiffs thereto on the averments that the suit land under Kachua Police Station of Bhasha Mouza of CS Khatian No. 32 and SA Khatian No. 244, Dag No. 56 land measuring 0.47 acres was originally belonged to Asiruddin Mallik, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, that after the death of Asiruddin Mallik his wife Saju Begum, son Jabbar Mallik and 4 daughters namely Faku Bibi, Maju Bibi, Saju Bibi and Moina Bibi inherited the said land and subsequently, on demise of Jabbar Mallik and Saju Begum (wife of late Asiruddin), the said 4 daughters of Late Asiruddin Mallik remained as successor, that the plaintiffs (two full brother) having purchased the suit land from the daughters of Asiruddin Mallik vide two registered kabala deeds dated 13-1-87 and 1-4-87 and became for owner and possessor the same, that the defendants have no right, title and possession in the suit land but the SA record was published mistakenly in the name of some defendants and thereupon, the defendants claimed the suit land and also threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs; that the plaintiffs were not aware about the wrong SA record and due to this the plaintiffs did not face any difficulty but very recently the defendants have claimed the suit land disclosing that the SA record was published in their name and hence that suit. 

 3. The defendant Nos. 1-4 and 7-13 entered appearance in the suit and filed written statement denying all the materials allegations of the plaint contending interalia, that Asiruddin Mallik, the predecessors of the plaintiffs on 20th Jaistha, 1339 BS by an unregistered deed sold the suit land to one Babor Ali, the predecessors of the defendants and after the death of the said Babor Ali, the defendants as his legal heirs inherited the suit land and thereupon, the SA record has been published correctly in their name including the names of their predecessor and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 5. At the trial both the parties led evidences both oral and documentary to prove their respective cases. The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the materials on record dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 12-3-1991 on the ground that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the suit land. 

 7. Mr Md Humayun Kabir Bulbul, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners submits that both the Courts below committed an error of law in passing the impugned judgments in failing to appreciate the case of the respective parties in its true perspective, resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice as such, the same are liable to be set aside. He next in the course of argument after placing the materials on record submits that the judgments of two Courts below are based on total non-consideration of the materials evidence on record and the findings of the Courts below are shockingly perverse to the extent that the plain-tiffs could not prove their possession in the suit landinspite of sufficient corroborative evidence to indicate that the plaintiffs are in possession over the suit property. Drawing my attention to the judgment of the trial Court below Mr Humayun Kabir submits that from a reading of the judgment of the trial Court there is no reason to believe that the plaintiffs cloud not prove their case but in the end the trial Court abruptly arrived at a finding that' the plaintiffs could not prove their possession in the suit land which is perverse being contrary to law, evidence and materials on record. 

 8. Mr Humayun Kabir, further submits that PW 2 proved 2 registered kabala deeds, rent receipts but the Courts below committed wrong in discarding the same without assigning any reason whatsoever which occasioned a failure of justice. The learned Advocate then referring to the evidence of PWs submits that both the Courts below did not at all consider the evidence of PWs namely, PW 1, PW 2, PW 3 and PW 4 in its true perspective since all them testified in one voice that the plaintiffs are in possession over the suit land and PW 2, proved the registered kabala deeds dated 13-1-87 and 1-4-87 as Exhibit Nos. 3 and 3(Ka). Drawing my attention to the evidence of DWs namely DW and DW 2 Mr Humayun Kabir points out that the DWs are not only made inconsistent statement with regard to their so-called unregistered kabala deed they also could not produce any document in support of their so-called unregistered deed before the trial Court but in spite of that the Courts below most illegally relying on the evidence of DWs dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs could not prove their possession over the suit land. Mr Humayun Kabir, relying on the decision reported in 19 DLR 9 and 59 DLR 207 submits that the defendants claimed their right, title over the suit and on the basis of SA record which appears to be prepared wrongly in their name at the early period of the than Pakistan but such record of rights does neither create nor destroy the right, title and possession as acquired by the plaintiff-petitioners on the basis of two registered kabala deeds dated 13-1-87 and 1-4-87 as Exhibit Nos. 3 and 3(Ka). He further adds that the SA record is not a conclusive evidence which is mere a record of physical possession at the time when it is prepared. 

 9. Mr Humayun Kabir, also points out that both the Courts below gave importance to the in-consistence oral evidence of DWs over the documentary evidences, thus committed an error, resulting in the error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate finally contends that since there being a total non-consideration of the material evidence on record both oral and documentary it is incumbent of this Court sitting under provisional jurisdiction to consider the same in order to arrive at a proper finding on the basis of the materials on record. 

 11. Mrs Nurun Nahar, further submits that at the trial the defendant-opposite parties in order to prove their right, title and possession exhibited 9(nine) Dakhilas and admittedly, the SR record was prepared in their name as well as in the name of their predecessor and, as such, there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgments of 2 (two) Courts below. The learned Advocate finally submits that in this case the plaintiff-petitioners could not produce the bia-deeds and that on this score also the plaintiff-petitioner miserably failed to prove their right, title in the suit land. Mrs Nahar, the learned Advocate to strengthen her submission has relied on the decisions reported in 10 MLR (AD) 100, 6 MLR 6, 35 DLR (AD) 216 and 37 DLR (AD) 202. 

 13. It is found that in this case plaintiffs examined in all 4(four) witnesses namely PW 1, PW 2, PW 3 and PW 4 and the defendants examined 2(two). witnesses namely DW 1 and DW 2. On perusal of the materials on record, it appears that the trial Court found after discussion of the evidence on record that the plaintiffs had adduced evidence only one witness namely PW 4 to prove their possession in the suit land, who in a half-hearted manner narrated about the possession of the plaintiffs. The Court of appeal below in its turn also affirmed the decision of the trial Court. 

 14. Now, let me discuss the evidence of PWs in order to resolve the issue whether the impugned judgments of two Courts below are based on correct and proper appreciation of the evidence and materials on record on the point of possession. On going through the materials on record, it appears that plaintiff No. 1, Esahaq Ali Mallik himself was examined as PW 1, who stated that after the death of Asiruddin Mallik his heirs namely Maju Bibi (wife), 4 (four) daughters namely Faku, Maju, Saju and Moyna and one son Jabbar inherited the suit land and Faku, Maju and Saju Bibi transferred 0.36 acres of land to the plaintiffs by a registered deed and Moyna Bibi also transferred her portion of land by executing another registered kabala deed. This witness also stated that after execution of the deeds they handed over the possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs. This witness also stated that : 

 15. It is also found that the plaintiffs in order to prove their right, title in the suit land exhibited two registered deeds namely Exhibit 3 and 3(Ka) and CS Khatian recorded in the name of late Asiruddin Mallik, the predecessor of the plaintiff-petitioners and also exhibited rent receipt vide Exhibit 1. 

 20. There is another aspect of the case which needs to be addressed as it involves and important question of law. It is contended that the SA record has been published correctly in name of some defendants including their predecessor. 

 21. In the case of Abdul Jabbar vs Abdul Aziz reported in 19 DLR 9, it has been held that : "It is not certainly conclusive evidence of the state of things appearing in the record of right, or in other words, it is not conclusive evidence of correctness of the entries in the record of rights." 

 22. In the case of Dhaka City Corporation vs Shamsur Rahman reported in 59 DLR 207, wherein it has been held that : "Such view of the trial Court was reversed rightly by the appellate Court. Because, the decision of the trial Court is based on no authority. Earlier, wrong record of rights could be corrected by a mere application under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. In such proceeding, the aggrieved party was never required to establish title to get an order for correction of the record of rights. Reason is not far away to find. Record of rights does neither create nor destroy title. It is mere a record of physical possession at the time when it is prepared." 

 23. From a reading of the above quoted decision, it transpires that the SA record is not a conclusive evidence to prove the right, title and possession in the suit land. It is mere a record of physical possession at the time where it is prepared. 

 Let a copy of the judgment along with lower Court's record be sent down at once.

lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam with AHM Mushfiqur Rahman, Advocates  ----- For the Petitioner. 
Md Ismail with Shihabuddin Mahmood, Advocates  ----- For the Opposite Party No.1, 4 and 6.
parties:
SM Nasirul Haque ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Omar Faruque Chowdhury and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
7. Opposite party, No. 1 opposed the prayer for preemption by filing a written objection. Main objection is that during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 number of plots was created out of said CS Khatian No. 139 under various khatians on the basis of possession of the persons. As the land measuring 0.63 acre was recorded in a new SA plot No.92 appertaining to first SA Khatian No.76 then 73 in the names of the parents of the preemptor, so, the land of opposite party No. 2 including the transferred land was recorded in separate SA plot No. 54 appertaining to SA khatian No. 48/1. The opposite party No. 2, vendor and others exclusively possessed their respective lands on payment of rents since the record of rights was finally published in 1964. Similarly, all other owners of the rest land of original CS plot No. 139 now exclusively possess their respective land either on the basis of SA record of rights or by subsequent mutations. The preemptor was not a co-sharer in the holding of opposite party No. 2 and, as such, his application was liable to be dismissed. 

 13. Opposing the Rule, Mr. Md Ismail, learned Counsel for the purchaser, opposite party No. 1 submits that the land measuring 3.49 as was recorded as CS plot in 1917-18 in the Cadastral survey was split up in numerous plots under various khatians during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in 1964 and the persons including the preemptor have been exclusively possessing their respective land according to such record of rights. The parents of the preemptor were in exclusive possession in their 0.63 acre of land which was recorded as SA plot No. 92 under SA khatian No. 73 Exhibit 'Ka' while opposite party No. 2 was in exclusive possession in plot No. 54 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 4811. The preemptor is therefore not a co-sharer in the land transferred by the kabala Exhibit No. 8. He accordingly, submits that the learned Additional District Judge did not commit any error in affirming the order of the trial Court in disallowing preemption. He also submits that everyone of purchasers of land of said CS plot No. 139 including the parents of the preemptor got their names mutated and in view of provisions of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the parents of the preemptor ceased to be co-sharer in said land. In support, he cites the decisions in the case of Haladar Dutta vs Abdul Rob Chowdhury, 36 DLR 193 and Md Khairullah vs Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 338. 

 15. We have perused the record, and heard the learned counsels at length. We shall first consider the cases as cited by them. 

 "A plain consideration of nature of the transaction in the circumstances of this case could, in our opinion, lead to but one conclusion. The vendee of a co-sharer who owns an undivided khata in common with another is clothed with the same rights as the vendor has in the property, no more and no less. If the vendor was in exclusive possession of a certain portion of the joint land and transfers its possession to his vendee, so long as there is no partition between the co-sharers, the vendee must be regarded as stepping into the shoes of his transferor qua his ownership rights in the joint property, to the extent of the area purchased by him, provided that the area in question does not exceed the share which the transferor owns in the whole property. Alienation of specific plots transferred to the vendee would only entitle the latter to retain possession of them till such time as an actual partition by metes and bounds takes place between the co-sharers. It is difficult to see in these circumstances why the vendee of specific plots acquired from a co-owner, in an undivided khata, does not become a co-sharer in the khata. It may be pointed out that the mutations in favour of the appellant, which are on the record, described the sale transactions in his favour as hissadari sales of the joint khata in suit. 

 17. SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 230 arose out of an application under section 24 of the Act, 1949. The case land appertained to a permanent tenure recorded in CS Khatian No. 214 in the names of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani. Akshoy instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 for partition and by the decree passed, Akshoy got one-third share while Rangubala got the rest two-third. One Nafisa Khatun purchased the entire share of Akshoy by a registered sale deed dated 19-07-52 while Rangubala settled her share of two-third for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 with Ayesha Khatun, respondent No. 2. Then, Nafisa Khatun sold her share to respondent No. 1 by a registered deed of sale dated 18-04-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered deed of sale dated 10- 09-73. Against this sale, respondent No.1 filed the application for preemption, which was allowed by the trial Court. Against the order, appellant's appeal and revision failed. But the Appellate Division set aside the order and dismissed the application for preemption. But, we find, on different reasons. 

 "the passing of the final decree in a partition suit finally determines the rights of the co-sharers in land. Hence, the application for the preemptor-respondents on the basis of co- sharer ship is not maintainable." 

 23. Ratio decidendi in the above decisions is that a decree of the Court in a partition suit brings separation and division in the joint possession and enjoyment of land. But such decree does not ipso facto result in the splitting of holding along with the jama till such subdivision of the holding and distribution of the rents takes place in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act or the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the case may be. Such division of the land may also be brought about by an amicable partition among the co-sharers in such land. But the main submission of Mr. Islam is that the total area of land in a plot as was plotted in the cadastral survey in 1917-18 must to be taken as an undivided unit. If such land was recorded in the names of more than one person, all such persons and/or their successors-in-interest must be held to be co-sharers in such plot till the land is partitioned by a decree of the Court or by amicable partition among such co-sharers. Even any sub-division of such CS plot and/or the holding to which such plot appertained in subsequent survey, say, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 will not result in the termination of co-sharer ship in such land and thereby, taking away the right of preemption under section 24 of the Act, 1949. The argument appears to be unique in the sense that it was never argued since the Act came into force in 1949. We are unable to accept such interpretation of the law. 

 24. Firstly, we do not find any reason or authority to agree with Mr Islam that the word 'land' as used in the expression 'co-sharer in the land' in section 24(1) of the Act, 1949 should always mean the quantum of land in one plot only. As the word 'co-sharer' always implies the existence of more than one person jointly owning, similarly, such joint ownership may be in respect of land of one plot or several plots. It is now well settled rule of interpretation as to number that in every Act, unless the contrary intention appears, the words in the singular shall include the plural, the words in the plural shall include singular. The land is always recorded under a holding for the purpose of revenue record and payment of rents. This holding may be joint of several persons, or exclusive in the name of one person. It may also may be noted that the holding of any land, agricultural or non-agricultural, could only be sub-divided and rents distributed in accordance with the procedure under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. But the proposition of Mr Islam that such sub-division of the holding and distribution of rents will not affect the land appertaining to such holding is equally misconceived. 

 25. Secondly, who are the co-sharers in the expression, 'co-sharer in the land'? To find the answer, we need not go far just to refer to the holding, more popularly known as khatian, comprising of such land. The concept of 'co-sharer' cannot be conceived independent of any holding or tenancy. If the holding is recorded in the name of more than one person, then, each of such person or his successor-in-interest is the co-sharer to each other in such land. Such a co-sharer will deem to continue as such co-owner in both holding as well as in land so long the holding will continue to be joint. Contrary to such proposition as argued by Mr Islam that sub-division of such holding will not affect the land in any way appear to be fallacious. Because, after sub-division of the holding and creation of new plots in subsequent survey, or by mutation by the acts of parties, the previous co- owners in the holding and/or the land cannot be deemed to still continue as such co-owners. 

 26. Coming to the facts of this case, we find, on 30-04-53 and 30-07-54 parents of the preemptor purchased 0.63 acre of land. After the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 their purchased land was recorded as plot No. 92 appertaining to first khatian No. 76 and then, No. 73, Exhibit 'Ka', Accordingly, they possessed since then, and after them, the preemptor has been in possession and enjoying the land on payment of rents in the separate jama. His possession and enjoyment are absolutely independent and exclusive of others. Similarly, the land transferred by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1 vide sale deed No. 1677 dated 30-06-91 was recorded as SA plot No. 54 appertaining SA khatian No.48/1. In the partition suit, the father of the preemptor as defendant No. 3 along with defendant No. 2 and defendant Nos. 4 to 6 prayed for saham and the preliminary decree dated 15-12-54 has allotted a saham to each of those defendants on the basis of their purchase. Mr Islam told that effecting partition by Advocate Commissioners failed four times. Mr Ismail submitted that chance of any final decree is far remote for the present successors of the original plaintiff have lost all their interest in such a decree. Be that as it may, the final decree that may ultimately be passed will just formalise independent and exclusive possession of present owners. The submission of Mr Islam that even after so many transactions and transfers since the final publication of CS record of rights, and the long and exclusive possession and enjoyment by the present occupiers on the basis of SA record of rights and/or mutation have not yet terminated the original co- sharer ship in CS plot No.139 as recorded in 1917-18 cannot be accepted. 

 28. Lastly, it is now well settled by the decision of our Appellate Division that all lands situate within a municipal area must be deemed to be non-agricultural land for the purpose of preemption. We cannot think of the disastrous consequence of the view as Mr Islam submits that the quantum of land as recorded in one plot in the name of more than one person during the cadastral survey in 1917-18 must be deemed to be an independent unit and in the joint ownership of those persons as recorded then till partition by metes and bound-to declare all such land still joint for the purpose of preemption. Such view will definitely go against the public policy as well. 

 Send down the records.

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Zahidul Bari, Advocate. ...For the Petitioners 
Mr. Md. Abdus Salam Mondal, Advocate. ...For the Opp-Party Nos. 1 & 2
parties:
Md. Abdur Rahman Mondal &Ors.  ------ Petitioners. 
Versus
 Sreemoti Renu Bala Barman and Ors.  ------ Opposite - Parties.
full_judgment:
2. Opposite party No. I and 2 as plaintiffs instituted the suit for a preliminary decree of partition for 4. 38 acres out of the suit land measuring about 7.62 acres appertaining to C. S. Khatian No. 86 fully described in the schedule to the plaint. Plaint case in short is that one Rupchand Mondal was owner in possession of the entire suit land and the C. S. record of rights was prepared and finally published in his name. Rupchand died leaving a son, Debicharan Mondal, wife Kaichu Barmani ans two daughters, plaintiffs. In his life time, Debicharan Nondal transferred 3. 24 acres out of the suit land to one Kona Mondal. Then, Debicharan died leaving mother Kaichu Barmani and two sisters the plaintiffs. Kona Mondal transferred said 3.24 acres Of land to Hasen Ali Mondal and defendant NO. 8 and 24 to 26. After death of Kaichu Barmani the plaintiffs inherited said 4. 38 acres of land left by Debicharan. While Hasen All Mondal and aforesaid defendant No. 8 and 24 to 26 possessed their purchased 3.24 acres of land. The suit land was never partitioned by metes and bounds. On Agrahayan 5, 1401 B. S. the defendants declined to partition the suit land amicable. Hence, the plaintiffs were constrained to institute the suit. 

 8. Mr. Md. Abdus Salam Mondal, learned Advocate for the plaintiffs opposite party No. l and 2 on the other hand submits that when the original title documents of Asiran Nessa, Am isa Khatun and Abdul Mannan were concurrently found by the courts below as collusive, forged, fraudulent and void. The defendants cannot resist the plaintiffs from getting the decree for partition when they are proved to be daughters and sisters of the original rightful owner Rupchand and Debicharan respectively. He further submits that record of rights in respect of the suit land was prepared even after Bangladesh in the name of Debicharan and others including those who purchased from Debicharan and as such, the contesting defendants cannot claim any land was exclusively recorded in their names or they possessed exclusively any land. When they claim to have entered into possession through attorney, they cannot claim now adverse possession against the principals. He further submits that both the courts below have concurrently found that the plaintiffs are daughters left by original owner Rupchand and sisters Debicharan and accordingly in the absence of any other heirs they were rightly found to have inherited. the rest of the suit land He also cites the case of Lai Meah. Vs. Haji Md. Ibrahim Meah and ors (1976) 28 DLR (AD) 61 to submits that the record of rights is not a document of title. 

 9. We have perused the record and heard the learned Advocates at length. As stated above, the suit land measuring 7.62 acres originally belonged to Rupchand Mondal and C. S. record of rights was so prepared in his name. According to the plaintiffs Rupchand died leaving a wife Kaichu Bramani and son Debicharan and two daughters, the plaintiff, which the contesting defendants denied and claimed that the plaintiffs were not daughters of Rupchand. It is also not disputed that during the lifetime. Debicharan transferred 3.24 acres of land. He died leaving a mother and the plaintiffs according to the plaint case but only the mother as per the defence case. As daughters and / or sisters, plaintiffs claimed rest of the entire suit land measuring 4.38 acres. It appears that the trial court found the deeds on which the fate of the defendants rests Exhibit. 'C' and 'F' are collusive, without consideration and void. Then, it found the plaintiffs have right, title and possession in the suit land as heirs. The suit also does not suffer from any defect of parties. Even after deciding all the issues in favour of the plaintiffs trial court held, in the absence of bringing entire land of C. S. Khatian 86 into hotchpot suit for partition is not maintainable. Trial Court accordingly dismissed the suit. Appellate Court affirmed the findings of the trial Court and reversed the conclusion of the trial court regarding hotchpot on the view that entire land of C. S. Khatian 86 was clearly sught for partition. We have also perused the C. S. Khatian and find that the appellate Court has rightly reversed the conclusion of the trial court. First, no issue was raised in the suit nor Mr. Md. Zahidul Bari . did advance any submission thereon. 

 10. We are facing with only two questions as raised by Mr. Bari as to whether the court of appeal below is well founded in holding that the plaintiffs are co-sharers in the suit land and whether they can obtain a decree against the contesting defendants. It is the positive case of the plaintiffs that they are the daughters of Rupchand and sisters of Debicharan. We find their case as testified by P. W. I is corroborated by P. Ws. 3 and 4 P. W. 3 Gulzer Hossain aged about 80 years testified that Rupchand died leaving a on Debicharan and two daughters Subhadra and Renubala and wife Kaichu Barmani and they are living in the suit land. They possessed 131/2 bigha of land. Similarly, P.W.4 Surendranath Barman Aged 55 years testified that Rupchand died leaving a son Debicharan and two daughters who are widow sisters of Debicharan and living in the suit land. On the other hand defendant No. 1 a man of 45 years deposed to have possessed their land for more than 30 years while D. W. 2 and 3 just asserted plaintiffs are no relation of Debicharan. On such evidence the court of appeal below affirmed the finding of the trial court that the plaintiffs are sisters of Debicharan and daughters of Rupchand. We find no other heir was left by either Rupchand or Debicharan from the record. Such finding arrived on due consideration of the evidence on record is binding under section 115 of the Code. 

 12. Lastly, let us see Whether the possession of the contesting defendants could be that of an adverse possession. Appellate Court has affirmed the finding that the plaintiffs have possession of the suit land. We have also perused the record and found that the decision does not suffer from any infirmity' or illegality. Though Mr. Zahidul Bari failed to point out any material evidence either not read or misread in coming such finding on possession. When the plaintiffs are fond to be in possession, even if in a portion of the suit land they are entitled to maintain their suit even for simple partition against the co-sharers namely who acquired the land from Bebicharan and their successors. On the other hand, the contesting defendants claimed to have entered into the land by way of successive purchase. It is on record defendant No. 23 Asiran Nessa got the land from her husband Faraz Ali Mondal who transferred as an attorney of Debicharan. Similarly, Nur Ali Mondal transferred '/2 of the rest of the land to his wife and son Abdul Manan, Defendant failed to produce their so-called power of attorney of Faraz Ali Mondal and Nur Ali Mondal. The Courts below have found the deeds of transfer by Faraz Ali Mondal and Nur Ali Mondal to their respect wives dated 25.4.1959 collusive, without consideration and void. So the possession of Asiran Nessa, defendant No. 23 cannot be deemed to be adverse to the plaintiffs since the possession of an attorney would be at best of a Manager on behalf of the principal. Similarly, the possession of other defendants having entered lawfully cannot convert into hostitle or adverse. We could not find any material on record which will suggest that the defendant possessed any land exclusively and adversely against the plaintiffs. In the absence of the animus, mere possession on payment of rent does not turn such possession into adverse or hostitle. 

 15. Send down the records at once.

lawyer:
PC Guha, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Syed Ziaul Karim, Advocate—For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Moinab Bibi and others ------ Petitioners
VS. 
Abdur Rashid Mridha and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiffs-petitioners instituted Title Suit No. 52 of 1986 in the court of the Assistant Judge, Batagi, District Barguna for declaration of title in respect of "Ka" schedule land for a further declaration that the deed obtained in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 as described in the schedule "Ga" in respect of the "Kha" schedule land is illegal, fraudulent and null and void and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs case is, that the suit land originally belonged to Lalu Forazi and from him the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs got the property and thereafter he was in enjoyment of the said property on payment of the rent to the Government for well over 12 years but the SA and RS Khatian has been wrongly recorded in the name of defendant No. 3 along with the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and, as such, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs Erfan Farazi filed Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 in the court of the then Munsif, 3rd Court Patuakhali for correction of the record of right and the said suit was decreed ex parte on 27-1-1956 in favour of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs. The further case of the plaintiff-petitioners is that the defendant opposite party No. 3 had no right, title and interest in the suit land and the deed in question by which she had transferred the suit land to the defendant opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 did not create any right, title and interest in favour of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and they are also not in possession of the suit land. 

 4. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiffs preferred appeal before the learned District Judge, which was an appeal before the learned District Judge, which was registered as Title Appeal No. 89 of 1987 and the said appeal on transfer was heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge who by the impugned judgment and decreed date 20-2-1991 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the trial Court and being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the appellate Court below the plaintiff petitioners obtained the instant Rule. 

 5. Mr. PC Guha, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-petitioners, submitted only two points. His first point of attack against the impugned judgment is that admittedly the plaintiffs-predecessor filed Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 against the vendor of the defendant opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 for correction of record of right and that suit was decreed ex parte on 27-1-1956 but neither the vendor of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 nor the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 ever took any steps to challenge the legality and propriety of the aforesaid decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 and in that view of the matter both the courts below found that the plaintiffs have failed to prove that the aforesaid decree was not obtained by the predecessor of the plaintiffs properly and without suppressing the process of the court. The second grievance of Mr. Guha is that both the courts concurrently found that the plaintiffs petitioners are not in possession of the suit land but neither of the court below did at all discuss the evidence adduced of the plaintiffs-petitioners before the trial Court in support of their case on possession and that there is overwhelming evidence from the side of the plaintiff-petitioners through which they have successfully proved their possession in the suit land and the appellate Court below without, adverting to those evidence on record and without re-assessing the same afresh as is required by Order 41 rule 31 of the Code in a slipshod manner affirmed the findings of the trial Court and, in that view of the matter, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside. 

 6. Mr. Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, on the other hand, submits that both the courts below on proper assessment of the materials and evidence on record rightly arrived at concurrent finding that the plaintiff petitioners have failed to prove their case and both the courts below concurrently found that the defendant opposite party No. 3 namely, the vendor of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 had valid right, title, interest and possession in respect of the suit land before the transfer made by her in 1986 to the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 after their purchase are in possession of the same and these findings of facts of both the court below are based on materials and evidence on record and, as such, there is no scope for this court to interfere with the concurrent findings of facts based on materials on record. The learned Advocate finally submits that it is true that an ex parte decree dated 27-1-1956 was obtained by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs petitioners but it is crystal clear from the evidence and material on record that the decree was never acted upon and both the SA and RS Khatian in respect of the suit land stands in the name of the vendor of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and in that view of the matter both the defendant opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 did not challenge the legality and validity of the ex parte decree dated 27-1-1956 passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 and the same will not stand in their way. 

 7. On perusal of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment of the trial Court it appears that both the courts concurrently found that the suit land originally belonged to one Lalu Farazi, the father of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and the defendant-opposite party No. 3 and after his death the said property devolved upon one Soleman Bibi wife of Lalu Farazi and to Erfan Farazi and Amena Khatun, son and daughter respectively of said Lalu Farazi and, as such, it is established beyond any shadow of doubt that Amena Khatun inherited the suit property as heir of Lalu Farazi. Both the courts below also concurrently found that both SA and RS Khatian in respect of the suit land stand in the name of the defendant opposite party No. 3 and both the courts below on scrutiny of evidence both oral and documentary arrived at a concurrent finding that the defendant opposite party No. 3 after inheriting the suit property as described in the schedule "Ga" to the plaint was in continuous possession. After her inheritance and while she was so seized with the suit property, she transferred the same to the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 through deed No. 231 dated 29-1-86 and after their purchase the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 are in possession of the same and, in that view of the matter, both the courts below concurrently observed that the suit as framed for a declaration simpliciter is not maintainable. It further appears from a perusal of the judgment of the courts below that they have rightly noticed the fact that the ex parte decree was obtained on 27-1-58 in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 against the defendant opposite party No. 3 but after the passing of the aforesaid decree till the transfer of the suit property made by the defendant-opposite party No. 3 in favour of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 the plaintiffs or their predecessor-in-interest had never taken any steps whatsoever to correct the record of rights in pursuance of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 and taking this aspect of the case into consideration both the courts concurrently found that the plaintiff-petitioners have failed to show that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 was validly obtained by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-petitioners. 

 8. On a perusal of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment of the trial Court it is crystal clear that the predecessor-interest of the plaintiff-petitioners obtained the decree in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 but neither the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs nor the plaintiffs did take any steps to correct the record of rights. It is not clear who paid rent in respect of the suit land for these long 30 years, yet it has been frankly admitted by Mr. Guha in reply to a question posed to him by the court that rents have been paid by the plaintiffs in respect of the suit in the name of the defendant-opposite party No. 3 beside, there is no denial of the fact that both the SA and RS khatian in respect of the "Ka" schedule property stand in the name of the defendant opposite party No. 3. These two factors that rent had been paid for the suit land by the plaintiffs in the name of the defendant-opposite party No. 3 and that suit land stands recorded in the name of the defendant opposite party No. 3 show that the defendant opposite party No. 3 was in possession of the suit land prior to the transfer made by her in 1986 and in that view of the matter, I am of the view that both the courts below rightly observed that in the instant case the plaintiff-petitioners have miserably failed to show that the decree in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 was validly obtained by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-petitioners and also failed to show that the decree had been acted upon. The omission on the part of the plaintiff-petitioners to prove that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 had been acted upon and that the concerned record of rights had been corrected stare at the face of the plaintiff-petitioner and taking this aspect of the case into consideration it appears to me that the courts below rightly arrived at a finding that the ex parte decree dated 27-1-1956 passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 will not stand in the way of the defendant-petitioners to acquire their valid title in respect of suit land. Besides, on a perusal of the records it appears that the plaintiff petitioners have miserably failed to show that they are in possession of the suit land through his father who was the owner of the suit property. Rather it appears from the evidence of the PWs themselves that they had admitted that defendant-opposite party No. 3 got the suit property through inheritance from her father late Lalu Forazi and it is also found from the evidence of PW 4 that the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 are in possession of the suit land since their purchase. It further appears that the evidence of PWs 2 and 3 is not worthy of credence and no reliance could be put on them on the point of possession as they have admitted in their cross examination that they do not know the suit land. It further appears that though PW 1 in his examination-in-chief did not specifically assert that their vendor opposite party No. 3 was is in continuous and uninterrupted possession of the suit land for more than 12 years prior to the date of transfer made on 19-1-1986 yet it appears from the evidence of DW 2 that he has testified to the effect that the defendant-opposite party No. 3, after getting the suit property through inheritance was in possession of the same and using the usufruct thereof through bargader and it further appears from the evidence of PW 3 that even Erfan Farazi the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs, was also for some time bargader of the defendant-opposite party No. 1 prior to the sale of the same to the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 In that view of the matter it appears that the appellate Court below rightly observed that the plaintiffs-petitioners have failed to prove their possession in respect of the suit land and that the defendant-opposite party No. 1 and 2 successfully proved that they are in possession of the suit land since their purchase and their vendor defendant No. 3 was in possession of the suit land prior to the transfer made by her and since there are materials and evidence on record to arrive at such a finding mere non discussion of the evidence by the appellate Court below is not fatal. In this connection it may further be mentioned that the trial Court elaborately discussed the evidence of both the parties in great detail and on proper assessment of the same arrived at a positive finding on the point of possession by referring to the evidence adduced by PWs 1, 2, 3 and 4 vis-a-vis the evidence of the DWs 1-3 that the plaintiff petitioners have failed to prove their possession in the suit land and the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 have been successful in proving their possession in the suit land. It is true that Order 41 rule 31 imposes a duty upon the appellate Court to re-assess the evidence afresh to arrive at a finding, in respect of each and every issue framed in the suit but it is now well settled that in case of affirmance if the appellate Court below failed to discuss the evidence in detail that would not stand in the way of the successful party if it is found that the trial Court has discussed the evidence in detail and there are, in fact, materials on record to arrive at such findings. I have already found that there are sufficient evidence on record for the Courts below to disbelieve the plaintiffs'' case and in view of the settled principles of law that the burden lies on the plaintiff to prove his case and he must succeed on his own strength only and not at the weakness of the adversary, the courts below took the correct view that since the plaintiff-petitioners have failed to prove their case they are not entitled to get any relief as prayed for. 

 9. The suit has been filed for the paramount declaration that the deed No. 231 dated 29-1-1986 of the Betagi Sub-Registry Office is fraudulent, null and void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs inasmuch as the vendor of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 had no right, title and interest and possession in the suit land but it has been found on the admission of PW 1 himself that the defendant-opposite party No. 3 had right, title and interest in the suit land and both the courts below on scrutiny of the evidence both oral and documentary found that defendants are in possession of the suit land and the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit land. It is now well settled that record of rights are documents of possession and in the instant case both SA and RS khatian stand in the name of defendant-opposite party No. 3. This documentary evidence coupled with the oral evidence of both the parties conclusively prove that defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 are in possession of the suit land and in that view of the matter the trial Court rightly observed that the instant suit as framed is not maintainable for declaration simpliciter without any prayer for consequential relief as it has been found that the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit land and the cases relied on by Mr. Syed Ziaul Karim aptly supports the view. 

 Send down the records at once.

lawyer:
Mr. M H Khandker, Senior Advocate, Mr. Lutfar Rahman Mondal & Mr. A J Mohammad Ali, Advocates with him, instructed by Mr. Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellants. 
Mr. Golam Rabbani, Senior Advocate instructed by Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record-----For the Respondent.
parties:
Rahima Khatun (Mst) & others ----- Appellants
Vs.
Dally Rani Dasi ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff-respondent filed the suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the suit land against appellant No. 1 and the predecessor-in-interest of the other appellants. She produced evidence that one Giribala Baishnabi was the recorded tenant as' Dakhalkar' of the suit land situated within Rajshahi Municipality in CS record; Ext. 11. She constructed a house thereon which is standing till today. She gifted her interest in favour of her foster son Gopal Chandra Ghosh by a registered deed of gift (Ext. 5) on the 23rd Poush, 1326 BS corresponding to 6.6.1919. Gopal was recognised by the landlord as a tenant and he was given rent receipts Ext. 6.6 (a). Gopal sold the suit land to Brojendra Nath Goswami by a registered sale deed, Ext, 9 dated the 27th Ashar, 1337 BS corresponding to 12.7.30. Brojendra was also recognised by the landlord as a tenant and was granted rent receipts, Ext. 6 (b)-6 (h). Brojendra paid municipal taxes too vide receipts Exts. 2-2 (i). After the death of Brojendra his two sons Biswanath Goswami and Benoy Goswami inherited the disputed land. The plaintiff and her husband were disciples of Biswanath and Benoy who gifted the suit land to the plaintiff-respondent by a registered deed of gift, Ext. 1 dated 6.3.61 which was executed and registered by her husband PW 4 Shambhu Nath Das by virtue of a power of attorney Ext. 3 granted to him by Biswanath and Benoy. One Shyam Sundar Das was a monthly tenant in the suit premises under Brojendra. He used to run a biscuit factory in the eastern side and reside at the western side of the premises. He sold away the movables to PW 6 Probhash Chandra Pal on 19.11.58 and left for India. The plaintiff-respondent took possession of the suit property after the gift on 6.3.61 and the said PWs 4 and 6 used to run the biscuit factory. The defendant-appellants forcibly entered into the western part of the house on the 1st Sravan, 1369 BS corresponding to 17.7.62 and hence the suit filed in 1967. 

 7. The sole basis of Giribala's interest is an entry in the CS record, Ext. 11 showing Giribala as 'Dakhalkar'. No evidence of her title was granted to consider whether in such circumstances the subsequent deeds of transfer, namely, Exts. 5 and 6 have any basis and as to whether the finding of fact arrived at by the first Appellate Court should have been interfered with by the High Court Division in second appeal. 

 8. Mr. MH Khandker, the learned Counsel for the defendant-appellants, submits that a CS khatian, or, in other words, a record of rights, is not a document of title. It does not create or extinguish title to land. At best, along with other evidence, it may support an evidence of title. He has cited the cases of Lal Miah Vs. Haji Md. Ibrahim Meah and others, 28 DLR (AD) 61, Pankajeni Debi Vs. Sudhir Dutta, 60 CWN 793 and Kazi Md. Hossain Vs. Sree Ram Banda, 70 CWN 1066 in support of his submission. He further submits that the word ' Dakhalkar in the CS khatian Ext. 11 merely shows that Giribala was a tenant-at-will and that she had no transferable and heritable right. Her alleged gift to her foster son Gopal by Ext. 5 and Gopal's subsequent sale to Biswanath Ext. 9 had conveyed no interest to the donee and transferee. Consequently the plaintiff-respondent obtained nothing from Biswanath and Benoy by way of gift, and she is bereft of any title to the suit land. Mr. Khandker has relied upon the case of Bipradas Pal Choudhury Vs. Azam Ostagar, 22 CWN CXVI (Notes) and submit that section 105 of the Bengal Tenancy Act does not apply to non-agricultural lands situated in mofussil municipality. Giribala could have a transferable and heritable right in the suit land only if there was a registered lease in her favour in terms of section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. Mr. Khandaker submits that the Judge of the High Court Division did not consider this aspect of the case. Hence an interference with the finding of fact of the first Appellate Court was not warranted under the circumstances. 

 9. Mr. Golam Rabbani, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent on, the other hand, does not dispute the proposition that a record of rights is not a document of title. He, however, contends that from the surrounding circumstances, a case of permanent tenancy has been made out. 

 10. Some findings of the Trial Court, we find, remain unrevised by the first Appellate Court, namely, that Giribala constructed a house on the suit land, that there is no evidence that Shantikana demolished the same and constructed a new one and that she lived therein and later inducted her own tenant. The unrevised finding of the Trial Court establishes the fact that after Giribala's possession of the suit land Gopal possessed the same from 6.6.1919, the date of gift Ext. 5, upto 12.7.1930, the date of sale to Brojendra Ext. 9. During these long years Gopal paid rent to the landlord which was accepted . There is no evidence that the landlord took any step to evict Gopal. Thereafter Brojendra obtained possession by purchase from Gopal on 12.7.30, paid rent to the landlord and also paid municipal taxes. He was succeeded by his two sons Biswanath and Benoy who possessed the same through tenant Shyamsundar Das. Then they gifted the suit land to the plaintiff-respondent on 6.3.61 Ext. 1. Brojendra and his two sons were in possession of the suit land for long 31 years and there is no evidence that the landlord sought to evict them in any way. The landlord allegedly settled the suit land to. Shantikana in 1939 by a dubious transaction of granting a Patta, Ext. F which itself does not create any permanent tenancy in her favour, the transaction not being in conformity with section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. Considering the long history of Giribala and her successors possession for nearly 50 years, construction of structures of considerable duration, not objected to by the landlord, evidence of transfers, alienation and succession from time to time, recognition of transfers by landlord by granting dakhilas and absence of any attempt by the landlord to take possession, the entry in the record of rights as 'Dakhalkar' fades into insignificance. These are matters which cannot be ignored in determining the character of Giribala's possession. All these facts in their totality have crowned Giribala and her successors with the status of permanent tenants. It is difficult under the circumstances to limit Giribala and her successors possession as being one of tenants-at-will or as one from year to year. 

 11. Ordinarily, the word "Dakhalkar' in the record of rights is no doubt indicative of a mere tenant-at-will without any transferable or heritable interest, but the word cannot be limited to a mere tenant-at-will under all circumstances. Merely because the word 'Dakhalkar' has been used Giribala's fate cannot be sealed. The subsequent history and attendant circumstances as above are relevant facts to be taken into consideration in determining the character of her possession. In the case of Prodyut Sen Gupta Vs. Nagendra Kumar Chowdhury, 52 CWN 72 it has been rightly observed as follows : 

 "In view of the finding of the Courts below that the tenancy has become a non-agricultural one, we are of opinion that it cannot be said that the record does not recognise the tenancy, merely because the word 'dakhalkar' has been used." 

 15. Hence the use of the word 'Dakhalkar' in the CS record Ext. 11 is not conclusive. The subsequent history of possession of the suit land and other attendant circumstances admit of an inference that the tenancy was a permanent tenure and not a tenant-at-will. Consequently the High Court Division was justified in interfering with the finding, which is a mixed finding of fact and law, arrived at by the lower Appellate Court.
