Md Haroon-ar Rashid Advocate------For Petitioner.
No one appears------For Opposite Parties.
parties:
Hasna Banu  ------ Petitioner
Vs
Bangladesh and others  ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. Plaint case, in short, is that one Tamej Sheikh was owner in possession of 3 decimals of land including the suit land, which was accordingly record in his name in CS Khatian No. 315. Tamej Sheikh transferred said land to Nandalal Das and Bateswar Das, sons of Mohan Das and delivered possession. SA record of rights was separately prepared in their names. By a registered deed of sale dated 24-12-69 Nandalal Das then transferred the suit land to Md Chan Miah. Md Chan Miah by registered sale deed dated 22-12-76 transferred said land to Alimul Hyder and handed over possession. When Alimul Hyder was thus owner in possession, he by two separate deeds of sale dated 27-6-81 and 15-11-82 transferred the suit land to the plaintiff and delivered her possession. The plaintiff got her name mutated and possessed on payments of rents. 

 4. The suit land was then recorded first in the name of Chan Miah in RS Khatian and then as khas in the name of the government. Defendant No. 2 Additional Divisional Commissioner (Revenue) served a notice dated 30-12-90 upon the husband of the plaintiff asking him to vacate the land by 30-1-91 otherwise he would be evicted therefrom by removal of unauthorised structures. Such notice cast a doubt over the title of the plaintiff who was accordingly, constrained to institute the suit. 

 5. Defendant No. 2 alone contested the suit by filing a written statement. His case, in short, is that the suit land was within Ramchandrapur hat of the erstwhile 'Zaminder.' With the wholesale acquisition of land receiving interest under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the suit land vested in the government. RS record of rights accordingly recorded the suit land as khas of the government. The suit land was situated at the periphery of Ramchandrapur Bazaar. By purchase from persons who had no title the plaintiff acquired no right title or interest in the suit land. Husband of the plaintiff got the suit land mutated in collusion with corrupt 'Tahshilder' and such mutation had no legal effect. 

 10. Mr Md Haroon-ar Rashid, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the plaintiff proved her title and possession in the suit land by both oral and documentary evidence while the defendant failed to prove that the suit land vested in the government and the trial Court correctly decreed the suit but the appellate Court set aside said decree without considering the evidence on record. 

 12. The plaint case is that the suit land originally belonged to one Tamej Sheikh and CS record of rights was accordingly, prepared in his name. CS Khatian No. 315, Exhibit 1 recorded the suit land comprising of CS plot No. 828 as 'Nal'. Nature of tenancy was recorded as 'Borga Korfa' under land receiver Durga Sundari Basu and others. The appellant Court took the view that such tenancy held as 'Barga Korfa' had no 'raiyati' right, had no right to transfer before the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 came into force. He however, did not mention any law or authority in support of his view. 

 15. When the nature of tenancy was recorded as 'Barga Korfa' the intention was very clear that it was not a simple interest of 'Barga' as we popularly understand. Such tenancy was definitely heritable and transferable. 

 16. But in the absence of any material on record the appellate Court held that such tenancy 

 17. It must also be noted that the land was recorded as a 'Nal' land. Immediate superior rent receiver was Durga Sundari Basu and others, not Ramchandrapur Zamindars. 

 19. Plaintiff adduced original title deeds of Chand Miah and Alimul Hyder, Exhibits 3 and 4. She also adduced SA Khatian No. 787 which recorded the suit land in SA plot No. 2859 as 'Chandina' in the names of Nandalal and Bateswar, Exhibit 2. 

 22. Recording of the suit land as 'Chandina' in SA record of rights might have created all problems for the appellate Court. Such record was prepared sometime in 1964. With the wholesale acquisition of rent receiving interest, all land "in a hat or bazaar" vested in the government with effect from 2 April, 1956. But under sub-section 3 of section 44  of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 such land would stand finally acquired and vested in the government with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of a notification in the official Gazette declaring that the Compensation Assessment-roll was finally published. 

 23. During the CS survey, the land was recorded as 'Nal'. With the passage of time when the bazaar in question expanded up to near the suit land, the recorded tenant might have made shops thereon for some quick bucks. With further extension of the bazaar, the shops might be now in the periphery of Ramchandrapur bazaar as claimed by defendant No.2. Land in the periphery cannot be deemed to be 'in the hat or bazaar' within the meaning of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Such land was therefore never intended by the legislature to vest in the government under section 20(2a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The defendant therefore, failed to produce any notification of final Compensation Assessment-roll vesting the suit land in the government. 

 26. Send down the record at once.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Syed A.B. Mahmudul Huq

lawyer:
Syed Emran Hossain, Advocate—For the Petitioner. [WIP No. 515/2017] 
Abdul Halim Mondal, Advocate—For the Petitioner. [WP No. 5531 of 2017] 
Shaheen Akhter, Advocate—For the Respondent No. 2. [WP No. 5531 of 2017]
parties:
Bangladesh Financial Association of Seventh Day Advertises ------ Petitioner [WP No. 515/2017]
vs
Judge (Joint District Judge) Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka and 182 others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The petitioners in the aforesaid writ petitions are either plaintiffs or defendants in Land Survey Tribunal cases filed by them or their opponents before the Land Survey Tribunals concerned as established by the Government throughout the country under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter called "the said Act") in order to determine the correctness of record-of-rights finally published through revision of the same under section 144 of the said Act. Being aggrieved either by orders passed by such Tribunals or judgments and decrees passed by them, the petitioners approached this Court and obtained the instant Rules calling in question the said orders, judgment and decrees. 

 7. Learned advocates in the instant writ petitions have argued, at length, various issues regarding the evidences on record and tried to make reference to different evidences from the lower Court records of the cases concerned, as have already been sent to this Court. However, this Court is of the view that disposing of such issues by this Court under writ jurisdiction will encompass re-examination and re-assessment of evidences, as adduced by the parties before the Tribunals, which is not permitted under writ jurisdiction. 

 8. As against this aspect, we have examined the relevant provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, in particular Chapter-XVIIA of the same as inserted vide section 2 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2004 (Act No. 09 of 2004). For the purpose of the revision of the record-of-rights in respect of the Lands in Bangladesh, as provided by section 144 of the said Act, the government has in the meantime promulgated Tenancy Rules, 1955 specifying the stages of works to be conducted by the concerned Revenue officials and Land Field Officers. In such exercise of different functions at different stages, when a draft record of right is published under Rule 29 of the said Tenancy Rules by the concerned Revenue Officer, the aggrieved person has the right to file objection against the same under Rule 30 of the said Rules. After disposal of such objection upon hearing the parties, the aggrieved person will have the right to prefer appeal under Rule 31 of the said Rules to the Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer or additional designation of Assistant Settlement Officer. Once such appeals are disposed of, the final record-of-rights in respect of the concerned land are prepared, if such orders of the Appellate Authority are not interfered with in the meantime on some limited grounds including fraud under Rules 42 and 42A of the said Rules. The matter does not end there, even after final publication of record-of-rights, the aggrieved party has been given an opportunity to challenge any entry in the said final record-of-rights by filing a suit before the Land Survey Tribunals concerned as established by the government in exercise of its power under section 145A of the said Act specifying the territorial limits and jurisdiction of such Tribunals. Such Tribunals have been empowered by the said provision only to entertain suits challenging the entry in the finally published record-of-rights as stated above. Such Tribunals have also been empowered by the said provision to declare the concerned record-of-rights to be incorrect and further to direct the concerned office to correct such record-of-rights in accordance with its decision and may also pass such other orders as may be necessary. 

 9. Obviously, because of such scheme as provided by the parliament through the aforesaid insertion of the Chapter XVIIA in the said Act and the Rules made there-under, thousands of citizens and persons approached such Tribunals with numerous suits challenging the entries in the finally published record-of-rights. Consequently, such Tribunals comprising of Joint District Judges have been flooded with various number of cases. Since the Tribunals have been given the powers to dispose of such cases in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, so far as the same is not inconsistent with the provisions of the said Act, in respect of certain matters mentioned tinder section 145B of the said Act, thereby making the Tribunal a quasi-civil court having limited powers of the Civil Court, the same have disposed of, or are in the process of disposing of, the said numerous number of suits. In such process, the litigants before the Tribunals have every reason to become aggrieved either against any order passed by the Tribunals in interlocutory matters or against judgment and decrees passed by them after conclusion of hearing. In such circumstances, it appears, the said huge number of litigant persons found themselves in a very helpless position to challenge or assail such orders, judgments and decrees passed by the said Tribunals in view of the admitted position that the government has not yet established any Land Survey Appellate Tribunal for giving redresses to the said aggrieved litigants in appeals to be filed by them against the said orders, judgment and decrees. 

 13. Nevertheless, even after publication of the said gazette, this Court issued the said Suo Motu Rule on 3-3-2015, being Suo Muto Rule No. 3 of 2015, and, according to the information given by the learned advocate concerned, the said Rule has been made absolute on 25-7-2019 with the direction upon the government to establish as many Land Survey Appellate Tribunals as may be required to hear appeals arising out of judgments, decrees or orders of the Land Survey Tribunals in Bangladesh. There is nothing on record as well as in the submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the government has taken any steps as of today for establishing such Appellate Tribunals which may function properly. Therefore, huge number of litigants, who are aggrieved by different orders, judgments and decrees passed by the Land Survey Tribunals, are now moving from one bench to another bench of the High Court Division with writ petitions to get redress. However, as stated above, in order to give such redress, we are required to reassess or reexamine the evidences adduced by the parties before the Tribunals concerned, which is not possible under writ jurisdiction. Though the statute, in particular section 145B of the said Act, provides that the government 'may' establish Land Survey Appellate Tribunals to hear the appeals arising out of the judgment and decree or order of the Land Survey Tribunals, with the establishment of Land Survey Tribunals in the meantime, this Court is of the view that, this 'may' as used in the said provision must be read as 'shall'. Otherwise, the entire purpose of the provisions under Chapter XVIIA of the said Act will become useless. 

 16. Let the Lower Courts' Records, which have already been sent and tagged with the concerned writ petitions, be sent down to the concerned Tribunals.

full_judgment:
6. Heard the submissions of the learned DAG and considered the materials on record. It is the admitted position that the accused-petitioner filed the said Power of Attorney before the Assistant Commissioner, Land, Narayanganj in a mutation proceeding for correction of record of rights in their favour. It has been decided by our Apex Court that the Revenue Officer acting in mutation case under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 ("the said Act") is not a court as he just does an inquiry in the said proceeding. In Shahera Khatun's case cited above, the Appellate Division distinguished between two proceedings, namely the proceeding under section 143 (maintenance of record of rights) and the proceedings under section 144 (revision of the record of rights) of the said Act and held that a Revenue Officer acting in mutation cases under section 143 of the said Act is not a Court, although the same officer acting in a proceeding under section 144 of the said Act is a court in view of Rule 39 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. Therefore, filing of forged documents before the Revenue Officer acting under section 143 in mutation proceeding, as in the present case, does not invoke the bar under section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and in such a case the court can take cognizance on the Petition of Complaint filed by a private person. 

 Let the lower court records be sent down immediately.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Attorney-General, instructed by B Hossain, Advocate-on-Record -----For the Appellants.
Abdur Rob Chowdhury, Senior Advocate (with MA Samad, Senior Advocate), instructed by Md. Zahirul Islam, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Bangladesh and others -----Appellant
Vs.
Mir Md. Imam Hossain ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: The question arose that in this appeal is whether in presence of an alternative remedy, the High Court Division is justified in invoking its writ jurisdiction to interfere with the order of Revenue/Settlement Officer who had directed to change the record of rights prepared in respect of the disputed property in question and declared the same as abandoned property. 

 2. The Writ petitioner, Arifabad Co-operative Housing Society Limited, claimed to have purchased the disputed property from Roshan Ally, MH Hirji, Nasiruddin Hirji, Boustan Hijri and Najli Hirji by registered deed dated 15th December, 1980 and thereafter, it mutated its name in the record of rights. The society thereupon made 140 housing plots and allotted those plots in favour of the members of the said society; most of whom thereupon constructed residential houses with prior permission of the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha (RAJUK). The writ respondent No.4, a Revenue Officers, subsequently by order dated 28th October, 1996 directed for recording the said land along with other lands as abandoned property in Miscellaneous Case No. 2103 of 1994. The writ petitioners then sought for judicial review of the said order in the High Court Division. The Secretary, Ministry of Lands, contested the writ petition and claimed that the Revenue Officer legally changed the record in accordance with law since the recorded tenant Gulshan Roushan Ally left this country in 1971 and his whereabouts had not been traced out on the date of promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 and that the property became abandoned property. 

 There is no dispute that the property in dispute was recorded in the names of the writ petitioner's predecessors' and after purchase, it mutated its name in the record of rights, paid rent to the Government, allotted plots to its members and some of the allotees had constructed residential houses with prior approval of RAJUK. Subsequently at the instance of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, Miscellaneous Case No. 2103 of 1995 was started as per Rule 42(Ka) of the Tenancy Rules 1959 on the plea that Plot Nos. 1685,20707 of Khatian No. 1560 was recorded in the name of some individuals. The Revenue Officer, thereupon, after service of notice directed for recording 48.26 acres of land of RS Plot Nos. 4233, 4234, 4235 and 4236 along with 29 other plots as abandoned property in the name of the Government. 

 3. Article 2(1) of PO 16 of 1972 defines 'abandoned property' means 'any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts is not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property including such property mentioned in clauses I and II". Admittedly the disputed property was not enlisted as abandoned property within the meaning of Article 2(1) PO 16 of 1972. It is only on 20th October, 1996, at the instance of the Deputy Commissioner, a Revenue Officer directed for recording the disputed property as abandoned property in Miscellaneous Case No. 2103 of 1995.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 132 of 2005
lawyer:
Omar Faruq, Deputy Attorney General, instructed by B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record.  ----- For the Petitioners. 
Amir Hossain, Advocate-on-Record. ------ For the Respondents
parties:
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Represented by the Deputy Commissioner and others, Rangpur ----- Petitioners.
VS
Khariat Hossain and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
3. The respondents 1 and 2 filled (filed) the above suit on the averments that Bimalendu Roy, Tarini Prasad and two others took pattan of the suit land and C.S. Record was prepared in their names and subsequently Tarini Prasad and the two others surrendered the property in favour of the original landlord who then took the same to his Khas possession; Abdul Aziz, the father of the plaintiffs, then took pattan of the suit land by registered kabaliat in the year 1943 and went into possession of the same on payment of rent to the landlord and S.A. record was duly prepared in the name of Abdul Aziz; subsequently on 13.10.82 the land was transferred to the plaintiffs by a deed of haba-bill-ewaj; and the plaintiffs, continued to possess the suit land on payment of rent to the government; then Abdul Hamid and others, with malafide motive, filed a false petition to enlist the suit land as Shariat and at their instance the defendant No.1, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Rangpur, by order dated 13.03.84 passed in Misc. Case (Shariat No. 9 of 1983-84) cancelled the record of rights and declared the suit land as government khas land and directed the defendant No.2, the Thana Upazilla Revenue Officer, to take over the possession of the suit land and then the plaintiffs filed the instant suit challenging the above order dated 13.03.84. The defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land being a beel is the khas land of the government and the claim of the plaintiffs is vague and based on fabricated papers and further since the kabuliyt was for one year only there is no legal basis of the claim of the plaintiffs after the expiry of one year. The trial court, after hearing, decreed the suit. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed appeal which, after hearing, was allowed and the suit was dismissed. On revision the High Court Division made the Rule absolute. 

 4. The learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in setting aside the findings of the appellate court without properly discussing and controverting the findings of the lower appellate court which are based on sound reasons upon consideration of materials on records and the suit land being beef and khas land of the Government and the papers of the plaintiffs being fabricated and the plaintiffs having failed to establish their right title and possession in the suit land and the kabuliyat being made for only one year, the claim of the plaintiffs has no legal force as the period of kabuliyat expired. 

 5. As it appears the High Court Division made the rule absolute holding that there is no dispute as to the fact that the suit land was taken settlement by the father of the plaintiffs from the original landlord upon execution of a registered kabuliyat in the year 1943 and the language and terms of the kabuliyat indicate that the same is not such an agreement which will terminate automatically at the end of one year term as specified therein; the kabuliyat described the suit land as cultivable land and the conditions contained therein show the that the suit land is to be used for the purpose of cultivation and so it is difficult to accept the submission that the suit land could subsequently be properly described as beel; nine defence witnesses though deposed to the effect that the suit land is used for the purpose of fishery but the above evidence should not be allowed to outweigh the evidence contain in the registered kabuliyat which described the land as cultivable land, more so, when the trial court came to a specific finding that the evidence of defence witnesses was not believable; and since the witnesses physically appeared before the trial court the learned Assistant Judge was in a better position to assess the veracity of their evidence and also the evidentiary value of the deposition of those witnesses, in Rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rules which was added by Gazette Notification on the 7th of April, 1967, an additional power was given to the Revenue Officer to deal with cases involving fraud which was not covered within section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and so the submission of the learned advocate of the petitioner that the Revenue Officer does not have the authority to cancel the record of rights under this provision of law has basis; in the facts and circumstances of the instant case there does not appear to be any incidence of fraud as quite clearly the plaintiffs predecessor went into possession of the suit land on the strength of a registered document and he continued to remain in possession until coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and also thereafter and moreover it is also evident from Exhibit-3 that the government has accepted the predecessor of the plaintiffs as tenant and received rent from him from 1956 up to 1981 and therefore, it cannot be said that the predecessor of the plaintiffs was in illegal possession; Abdul Aziz, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, continued to be in possession of the suit land by way of holding over as tenant and became a tenant under the Government on the coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and hence there was no illegality or irregularity in the record of rights; the suit land was described in the kabuliyat as cultivable land and the kabuliyat was granted for the purpose of cultivation and hence in the absence of any local verification to show that the nature of the suit land changed subsequently it must be presumed that the suit land remained as it was at the time of kabuliyat i.e. cultivable land and; S.A. record was created from earlier records based on "Table Surver" as distinguished from local or filed survey, and therefore S.A. Record does not necessarily reflect the true nature of the land and moreover it is apparent from the records that upon inquiry, the Magistrate found the suit land to be used for purposes of cultivation and is in possession of the plaintiffs. 

 6. We are of the view that High Court Division after due consideration of the evidence and materials on record and answering the relevant issues arrived at a correct decision and there is no cogent reason to interfere with the said decision.
case_type_name: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal

lawyer:
JN Deb, Advocate------For the Petitioner. 
ABM Mostafa Kamal, Advocate------For Respondents No.4. 
Abul Hossain Azadi, Assistant Attorney-General------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Abdul Moin  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land, Secretariat Building & ors  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. It is stated in the writ petition that the petitioner's father acquired the property in question measuring 3.33 acres of land in Khatian No. 2 under Sylhet Municipality by purchase on 12th Chaitra, 1354 BS by a registered Kabala. But since the respondent No.4. Lacca Tura Tea Estate illegally took over possession and managed to record the same in its name in the record of rights, father of the petitioner filed Title Suit No. 371 of 1963 in the First Court of Sadar Munsif, Sylhet against the Ministry of Land and Lacca Tura Tea Estate and others for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in respect of the said land along with other lands. The said suit was decreed in part declaring title only in favour of the father of the petitioner in respect of the second schedule land by judgment and decree dated 27-2-1973 against which the respondent Nos.l and 4, namely, the Ministry of Land and Lacca Tura Tea Estate, preferred Title Appeal No. 100 of 1973 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet. Similarly, the father of the petitioner preferred cross appeal, Title Appeal No. 76 of 1973, as the trial Court failed to pass a decree for recovery of khas possession regarding the second schedule land and also for not making the commission Report, Map, etc part of the decree. Title Appeal No. 100 of 1973 filed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 4 was dismissed and Title Appeal No. 76 of 1973 was allowed by judgment and decree dated 8-9-1983. During pendency of the aforesaid appeal petitioner's father died and accordingly, his three brothers and mother impleaded themselves as appellants. Thereafter, the petitioner and his co-owners filed Title Execution Case No.5 of 1984 and ultimately, obtained possession of the land on 8-3-1984 through Court by executing the decree. After conclusion of the said execution case the mother of the petitioner died leaving behind the petitioner and his three brothers and of them, two died unmarried and the third died leaving behind one daughter and the said daughter transferred-her share in favour of the petitioner and delivered possession thereof. The petitioner thus became the sole owner in possession of the suit land. The heirs of the respondent No.4 in Title Appeal No. 76 of 1973 however, preferred two revisional applications being Civil Revision Nos.161 and 162 of 1984 before the High Court Division. Ultimately, the Rules in the aforesaid two revisional applications were discharged by the judgment and order dated 3-9-1987. The said heirs then filed two Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 245 and 246 of 1988 before the Appellate Division which were also dismissed by judgment and order dated 27-1-1991. 

 3. Accordingly, the petitioner filed Mutation Case No. 107/83-84 before the Revenue Deputy Collector Sylhet under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for correction of record of rights in his favour in pursuance of the aforesaid judgment and decrees passed by the highest Court of the country. But the Revenue Deputy Collector stayed the matter. Hence the petitioner preferred Mutation Appeal No. 95 of 1990 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet, who heard and allowed the said appeal with direction to record the name of the petitioner. The petitioner thereafter filed Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1991 before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Sadar, Sylhet for correction of the record of rights. The Assistant Commissioner (Land) thereafter by order dated 23-1-1994 approved mutation in favour of the petitioner and consequently, a separate khatian was opened in the name of the petitioner. 

 4. The respondent No. 4 Lacca Tura Tea Estate, thereupon, preferred Mutation Appeal No. 22 of 1994 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet against the order passed by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) asserting that the land in question was a vested property and, as such, it took settlement of the same from the Government and it was therefore rightly recorded in its name in the record of right. The petitioner having received notices of the said mutation appeal, contested the same submitting all papers, namely, the judgments and decrees passed by the Civil Courts including the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court declaring title of the petitioner thereto and giving possession. But the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) by the impugned order dated 3-6-1998. Annexure-I, forwarded the case record to the Ministry of Land without giving any decision either allowing or rejecting the mutation. Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) while forwarding the record to the Ministry observed the Lacca Tura Tea Estate was the owner and possessor of the land in question on the basis of settlement by the Government and there was no scope of mutation in favour of the petitioner. He also mentioned in the aforesaid order that there were two title suits pending in respect of the land in question by two other private individuals and without disposal of the said suits and without the results of the said suits being submitted to the Ministry there was no scope to pass any mutation order. 

 7. It is noted from the record that the petitioner in order to establish his right, title and interest in the land in question and for recovery of khas possession thereof filed a civil suit being Title Suit No. 371 of 1963 and obtained the decree in his favour which was finally affirmed by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. The dispute with regard to the title and possession of the land in question between the parties, namely, the Government of Bangladesh, Lacca Tura Tea Estate and the petitioner should therefore be taken to have been finally resolved. The petitioner therefore started a Mutation case under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for mutation of his name by removing the name of the Government and/or Lacca Tura Tea Estate in the record of right on the basis of the aforesaid decrees. The petitioner eventually obtained necessary Mutation order on 23-1-199.4 in his favour by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) in Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1991 and in pursuance thereto a separate khatian was opened in his name. The respondent No.4 Lacca Tura Tea Estate thereupon filed a Mutation Appeal No. 22 of 1984 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) whereupon the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) dragged on with the matter for 4 years and then without deciding the matter himself forwarded the case record regarding the mutation to the Ministry of Land by the impugned order dated 3-6-1998 with the observation as stated above. 

 8. Since the petitioner sought correction of the record of right by mutating his name in respect of the land in question on the strength of the final judgment and decree of the highest Civil Courts of the country he rightly approached the Revenue Deputy Collector by filing an application under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 54 reads as under: 

 "The Revenue-officer shall make such alteration in the records-of-rights or the Compensation Assessment Roll as may be necessary to give effect to any directions issued by the Commissioner or other officer under section 49 or an order made by a Special Judge under section 51 or section 53 or under sub-section" (4) of section 52 or to any final order or decree of a Civil Court of the High Court Division passed in any suit, appeal or proceeding declaring tide to and, or possession of any land." 

 9. When the matter was subsequently brought before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) he was required in law to decide the matter either giving a decision instead of forwarding the same to the Ministry of Land by giving unwarranted and illegal observations. Since the question of title and possession have been settled by the highest Court of the country the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) had, in fact, no option in law but to mutate the name of the petitioner by correcting the record of right: The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) not only acted without jurisdiction in sending the matter to the Ministry of Land without deciding the matter himself with untenable observations but also did so in colourable exercise of his official power. The impugned order dated 3-6-1998 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Sylhet is therefore declared to have been passed without any lawful authority.

lawyer:
Md. Moksudur Rahman, Deputy Attorney- General instructed by B. Hossain, Advocate-on- Records ------ For the Appellant in all the appeals.

parties:
The Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property (L & B), Tangail ------ Appellant
Vs.
Bholanath Guha & ors------Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Respondent No. 1 filed Miscellaneous Case Nos. 1002 to 1005 of 1969, in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Tangail, for correction of rights under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The case of respondent No. 1 was that the case land originally-belonged to Anath Bandhu Guna who died leaving four sons, namely, Akhil Sandhu Guha, Amar Bandhu Guha, Anil Bandhu Guha and Aghar Bandhu Guha as heirs and while the said heirs were owning and possessing the, land they, settled the same with respondent, No. 1 in 1353 B.S. by granting Pattannamas and realising rent by granting dakhilas. Further case of the plaintiff respondent was that the revisional record-of-right was wrongly prepared in the name of the said four sons of Anath Sandhu Guha overlooking the possession of the plaintiff on the basis of the settlement from the owners. The present appellant was made opposite, party No. 7 in the aforesaid Miscellaneous cases, and he contested the cases by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that the documents relied upon by the plaintiff were not genuine; that after the death, of Anath Bandhu Guha the land belonged to his four sons who left for India long before, and the case land vested ill the Custodian of Enemy Property. The learned Munsif allowed the Miscellaneous Cases and directed the correction of the Khatians, holding, inter alia, that the pattannamas Exts. 1 to 1 (b) and the Dakhilas Exts. 2 to 2(g) are genuine and that respondent had been in possession of the properties. On appeal by the present-appellant the learned Subordinate Judge, Tangail, set aside the judgment of the learned Munsif on the finding that the materials produced by the plaintiff were not sufficient for corning to the finding on the case land, He further held that complicated question of title was involved in the matter and that the question of possession was not a material issue in the present case. 

 3. The respondent then filed revisional applications before the High Court Division challenging the aforesaid judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge and obtained Rules. A Single Judge of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order reversed the decisions of the lower Appellate Court and restored those of the trial Court, holding, inter alia, that section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, is meant for, rectification of mistake in the entry of record-of-right and that the incidental reference to the plaintiff's title did not convert the proceeding into a title suit. The learned Judge further held that there was no, complicated question of title involved in the instant cases. 

 4. Leave was granted to consider as to whether the rectification of record-of-rights as contemplated under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, would be allowed in a case, where the plaintiff's possession in the land in question is based Oil, unregistered Pattannamas and Dhakhilas claimed by the plaintiff to have been granted by owners thereof. 

 6. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents, however, argues that lower appellate Court misconceived the scope of section 143A in holding that possession is not a material question in deciding an application under section 143A. He further contends that the lower appellate Court overlooked the reliefs sought for in the application which were not for declaration of title on the basis of Pattannamas and rent receipts but were applications for correction of the error in the records-of-rights due to the non-consideration of the fact of plaintiff's possession in the case land. The learned Counsel submits that the learned Munsif on consideration of evidence and report of the local investigation by Circle Officer (Dev) found plaintiff in possession and he also found prima facie title in favour of the plaintiff on the basis of Pattannamas and rent receipts and the High Court Division rightly restored the decision of the trial Court setting aside those of the lower Appellate Court. 

 (1) Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission of entry in the record-of-rights prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV may, not-withstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, file an application along with necessary requisites, for the purpose of correcting mistakes in such record-of-rights in the civil court which would have jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession of the land to which such entry relates or in respect of which such omission was made. 

 10. An application under section 143A is not a suit for declaration of title but is a proceeding for rectification of mistakes in the records of right prepared on the basis of possession in the land in question. The scheme of the section show that possession is the material question. This was a special provision and this section was inserted after section 143 by E.P. Ordinance VIII of 1967. It was, however, omitted after a few years by Ordinance No. LXIV of 1975. 

 11. The lower appellate Court apparently misconceived the scope of an application under section 143A and the High Court Division rightly observed that with the scope of section 143A, there is hardly any ground for the appellant to challenge the title of the plaintiff. The learned Judge found that the appellant, Custodian of Enemy Property, had no document in his possession to claim the property as enemy property except the record of right containing the disputed entry. Before the High Court Division no one appeared on behalf of the present appellant. The learned Judge of the High Court Division having found the plaintiff's prima facie title and clear possession of the case land, rightly reversed the decision of the lower appellate Court and restored that of the trial Court No illegality could be pointed out calling for an interference\ with the impugned decision.

Mr. Justice Chowdhury A.T. M. Masud
Mr. Justice Syed Md. Mohsen Ali

lawyer: Md. Khurshid Alam Khan, Senior Advocate—For the Petitioners.
parties:
Hazrat Ali and others ---------- Petitioners
VS
Suraiya Begum Choudhury (Dhali) and others --------- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short. are that the opposite party Nos. 1-12, as plaintiff, filed Other Class Suit No. 49 of 1982 in the court of Sub-ordinate Judge. (now Joint District Judge) 1st Court, Tangail praying for simple declaration stating that the suit property originally belonged to Mashaullah and Nabiullah in equal share. When they were in possession and enjoyment of 9.47 acres land in Shadhanpur Mouza under Khatian No. 99, Plot No. 3082 including 7.78 acres of land in equal share, took loan of Taka 200 from the predecessor of the plaintiffs Munshi Samiruddin. Said loan of Taka 200 stood at Taka 800 including interest accrued thereon. For recovery of the said money Munshi Samiruddin filed Mortgage Suit No. 319 of 1930 in the court of Munsif, Tangail against Mashaullah and heirs of Nabiullah and got a decree on 21-6-1930 (decree signed on 30-6-1930). The judgment debtors failed to pay the decretal amount within the time mentioned in the order, but humbly prayed for releasing a portion of the mortgaged property in their favour leaving the rest in favour of decree holders. Prayer was considered by the decree holder and released 5.30 acres of land in favour of the judgment debtors under khatian No. 99. On that understanding Samiruddin and others got a preliminary decree in respect of 4.17 acres of land in Suit Plot No. 3082 and subsequently, the decree was made final. Thereafter, they got dakhila by dint of Pattan from Promath Nath Chowdhury. Jamiruddin and others possessed the suit land as bargadar. After it came under the Jamindary court of wards one Amena Begum Chowdhury got a dakhila. That a partition suit was filed being Partition Suit No. 88 of 1953 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Mymensingh for partition of the property including a portion of the suit land which was disposed of by amicable settlement. Mamtaz Begum Chowdhury got the suit land in her share and transferred the same to her son Nurul Haider Chowdhury by a registered heba deed dated 1 1-7-- 1964. After the death of Nurul Haider Chowdhury the plaintiffs possessed the suit land, but in the last R.O.R. survey the suit land wrongly recorded in the name of defendant Nos. 1-14, 16.19 and 20-23. The defendants had no title and possession in the suit land. When the plaintiffs went to pay rents in the month of Poush, 1388 13S in the local Tahshil Office have come to know about wrong record of right, hence, the present suit for declaration of title in the suit land. 

 4. The suit Plot No. 3082 wrongly recorded in the name of Hudu Sheikh in ROR No. 204. On 7-6-1973, 0.33 acre of land sold by Felu Sheikh to Ahsanuddin, Kasimuddin, Idris Ali and Foyezuddin. Joyen Sheikh on 30-9-1946 sold 01 61/, sataks of land to Daroga Ali Sheikh and Jamat Ali Sheikh. Felu Sheikh on 30-9-1943 sold a portion of the land to Daroga Ali and others. Daroga Ali sold 0.141/, sataks of land on 8-2-1953 to Akkel Ali Sheikh. Moyenuddin and Hazrat Ali, on 23-1-1931 sold 0.33 acre of land to Khoyaz Ali and Hatem Ali. Moyezuddin again sold 0.11 acres of land on 3-10-1974 to Khoyaz Ali and Hatetn Ali. Moyezuddin and Hazrat Ali sold their purchased land including some other land on 29-12-1964 to Fazar Ali and Foyezuddin. Sabjan Bewa on 3-4-1925 sold some land to Farazuddin and Foyezuddin. Plaintiffs have had no title and possession in the suit land. The suit land meaning 4.17 acres are in possession of the petitioners A. Baset, Imam Ali and Hazrat Ali and some other persons. Claim of the plaintiffs are false, vague and based on some forged papers and hence, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 12. He submits that the petitioners by several registered deeds dated 30-9-1943, 7-6-1943, 29-12-1964, 3-4-1973 and 24-3-1976 made inter transfers between the co-sharers who have been possessing the same with the petitioners on payment of rents to the government. Since the plaintiffs are not in possession simple suit for declaration is not maintainable without consequential relief. He submits that the trial court while dismissing the suit discussed all the evidences both oral 'and documentary and held that the plaintiffs could not able to prove their title and possession in the suit property on the basis of the documents Exhibits- 1-8, but on appeal the appellate court while setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court, most unfortunately misconceived and misconstrued the law in this regard and found possession of the plaintiffs in the suit property which is absolutely contrary to the evidences on record. The appellate court also failed to give any conclusive findings how the plaintiffs acquired title in the suit property on the basis of decree passed in Mortgaged Suit No. 319 of 1930 and decree passed in Partition Suit No. 88 of 1953, as such, committed an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 14. Heard the learned Advocates for the petitioners. have gone through the revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, plaint in suit along with amendments thereto, written statement, additional written statement, evidences both oral and documentary available in lower court records and impugned judgment and decree of both the courts below. 

 15. Admittedly that the property belonged to Mashaullah and Nabiullah as raiyat in possession under zaminder, accordingly. CS Khatian No. 99 stand recorded in their names in equal share, wherein, it was noted that they are in possession of the suit property along with other plots since 1314 BS The plaintiffs filed the, suit for declaration of title claiming that ROR Khatian No. 203 wrongly recorded in the name of defendants who raised claim of title in the suit property. The plaintiffs in their plaint at the 1st instance at paragraph 03 claimed that Mashaullah and Nabiullah failed to pay rents to the zaminder, consequently, for arrear rents zaminder by initiating legal proceeding purchased the property in execution of the decree. Thereafter, predecessor of plaintiffs named Jahanara Begum and others took settlement of the suit property in the year 1944 and continued in possession on payment of rents to the zaminder obtaining dakhilas and acquired an indefeasible title in the .property. Subsequently, the government acquired the property and placed the same under Court of wards. Their predecessor paid rents to the government through court of wards and obtained dakhila, thereafter, they filed Partition Suit No. 88 of 1953 which was decreed on compromise and the suit property along with other non-suited property fell in the share of Momtaz Begum Chowdhury. Subsequently, Momtaz Begum Chowdhury by a registered deed of Heba-bil-ewaz dated 11-7-1964 transferred the property to her son Nurul Haider Chowdhury, predecessor of the present plaintiffs. 

 17. The plaintiffs claimed that their predecessor obtained settlement of the property from zaminder by two settlement dakhilas in the year 1944 and paid rents to the zaminder, subsequently to the government through court of wards. In support of their such contention the plaintiffs submitted DCR in the name of Momtaz Begum and defendants Hafizuddin and others. Rent receipts dated 23-12-1957. 20-5-1969, 27-8-1967, 7-9-1959, 7-2-1959 and 22-11-1957 in the name of Momtaz Begum Chowdhury and rent receipt dated 1-4-1986 in the name of defendants Hafizuddin and others (Exhibit-'2 series'). Nothing has come to this court from plaintiffs side how all those rent receipts were issued by the government in the name of Momtaz Begum Chowdhury without recording her name in record of right. The rent receipts filed in the name of Momtaz Begum Chowdhury show nothing for which plot of land and khatian rents were paid and all those rent receipts written with pencil and description of joma bondi and quantum of land defers from each others. Exhibits- `2Cha' and '2 Chha' show that plaintiffs paid rent to the government in the name of defendants Hafizuddin and others. In Partition Suit No. 88 of 1953 present defendants or their predecessors were not made party as defendant. In the decree of said partition suit under schedule 43 property under Plot No. 3082 measuring 4.17 acres under khatian No. 99 has been included but mouza has been mentioned as Jahanchala and Plot No. 3082 has been interpolated by over writing figure 8 in red ink. From CS Khatian No. 99 we find that Plot No. 3082 contain 7.78 acres, meaning thereby, for the rest quantum of land predecessor of the defendants were co-sharer, but they were not made party, as such, the decree so have been obtained by the predecessor of the plaintiffs Momtaz Begum Chowdhury including the property, is not at all binding upon the present petitioners. They also could not show on the basis of compromise decree Momtaz Begum Chowdhury got possession of the suit plot through court. 

 18. By a registered deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz Momtaz Begum Chowdhury gifted the suit property along with other non-suited property to her son Md. Nurul Haider Chowdhury on 11-7-1964, but Nurul Haider Chowdhury did not take any step for recording his name in the khatian. After a long time, present plaintiffs filed the suit claiming title in the property on the basis of two documents one is decree passed in Mortgage Suit No. 319 of 1930 which was not executed by the decree holder and another a compromise decree passed in Partition Suit No. 88 of 1953 wherein present petitioners; predecessor were not made party. Though in the schedule a plot has been included showing the same under mouza Jahanchala, but the suit property is under mouza Sandhanpur, as admitted by both the parties. Rent receiving interest of the property in question was acquired by the government and with the acquisition of rent receiving interest from zaminder, predecessor of the present defendants as riayat in possession were recognized by the government as direct tenant and prepared ROR Khatian No. 203 in their names by modifying record of right under section 46 of the EBSAT Act 1950, as appearing from the ROR khatian (Exhibits-'5-A', 'F-1' and 'F-2') filed by the defendants. Section 46 (i) of the SAT Act, clearly provides that; 

 "After the Compensation Assessment-roll or Compensation Assessment-rolls in respect of all estates, tenures, and interest of rent-receivers in holdings or tenancies comprised within a district, part of a district or local area, in respect of which a record-of-rights has been prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV, has or have been published, such record-of-rights shall be modified by eliminating therefrom the entire chain of interest of rent-receivers and showing therein only the tenants who will come directly under the Government as a result of the acquisition of such interests; and one or more numbers to be borne on the Revenue-roll of the district shall be assigned by the Collector in respect of the areas to which such record-of-rights relates in accordance with such rules as the Government may make in this behalf; and the record-of-rights so modified shall be reprinted." 

 19. As per provisions in section 46, had the predecessor of the plaintiffs in possession of the suit plot by way of settlement from the then zaminder, the government would have modified the ROR khatian in the name of predecessors of the plaintiffs, Momtaz Begum Chowdhury instead of recording the name of the predecessor of defendants. By recording the name of defendants predecessor by modification under section 46 of the SAT Act, it proves that they were in possession as tenant under the zaminder. Consequently, the government by recording their names in ROR khatian recognized them as direct tenant under the government and as tenant accepted rents from them. Therefore, it cannot be said that ROR khatian wrongly recorded in the name of the defendants. 

 20. It is true that mere recording of name of some persons in the khatian does not ipso facto establish title without basis for recording such khatian. In the present case, admittedly, predecessor of the defendants Mashaullah and Nabiullah were tenant under zaminder and CS record stand recorded in their names. The plaintiff claimed that by the decree in Mortgage Suit No. 319 of 1930 and decree in partition suit title of the predecessor of defendants Mashaullah and Nabiullah ceased, but the said decree in mortgage suit though obtained, was not put in execution, consequently predecessor of the defendants Mashaullah and heirs of Nabiullah remained in possession of the property. Subsequent, settlement as claimed by plaintiffs in the year 1944 by two documents (Exhibits '6' and '6A') show that both the documents written by same persons with same pen and ink one showing settlement of 4.17 acres from Plot No. 3082 in the name of Amena Begum Chowdhury and others and another one for 4.71 acres seems to be interpolated in the name of Amena Begum Chowdhury and others. Exhibit-'6' pattan nama discloses the fact that the property in question was sold in auction in Execution Case No. 9-1800/2936 and taken possession by zaminder, but the case of the plaintiffs is otherwise which contradicts their chain of acquisition of title in the property and in both the alleged settlement dakhila several words have been interpolated. If the property acquired by zaminder in execution of a decree the story made in the plaint that the predecessor of the plaintiff got the property on the basis of a decree passed in Mortgage Suit No. 319 of 1930 contradicts with their settlement which were not filed in earlier Partition Suit No. 88 of 1953. Had the predecessor of the plaintiffs obtained settlement from zaminder and continued in possession of the same ROR khatian ought to have been modified in their names recognizing them as direct tenant under the government, but all those documents though filed by the plaintiffs in suit could not connect with the chain of title and the statements made in the plaint. 

 21. I have gone through the judgment of the trial court and find that the trial court discussed all the evidences both oral and documentary and rightly held that because of non-execution of the decree passed in mortgage suit and not making the predecessor of the defendants as party to the Partition Suit No. 88 of 1953 and not showing any document of compromise between the predecessor of the defendants and the plaintiffs sharing the quantum of land between them and absence of rent receipts showing payment of rents to the zaminder after obtaining settlement no title established in favour of the plaintiffs. Moreover, from the decree passed in Partition Suit No. 88 of 1953, it appears that the predecessor of the plaintiffs had vast property in the area and after SAT Act came into force their predecessor ought to have furnished a statement of landed property to the Government, but no such statement showing entire property owned by the predecessor of the plaintiffs was filed before the court. Rent receipts showing payment of rents in the name of Momtaz Begum Chowdhury upto 1969 do not support that she paid rent for the suit property in her name in the absence of any record of right. On the other hand, ROR khatian stand recorded in the names of Hafizuddin and others, predecessor of the defendants. 

 Communicate a copy of this judgment to the court concerned and send down the lower court records at once.

parties:
Md. Younus Mia being dead his heirs: Sohel Ahmed and others
Vs.
Illias Ali Chowdhury being dead his Heirs: Mubin Chowdhury
full_judgment:
6. Irfan Ali Chowdhury once mortgaged the suit land with Town Bank, Sylhet and the bank filed certificate case for mortgage money and he amicably paid the dues and the property was released from mortgage. At the initial stage of settlement and survey operation the suit land was recorded in Irfan Ali Chowdhury's name, but defendant No.2 subsequently fraudulently got it recorded in the name of Krishna Singha, son of Amu Singha beyond his knowledge. The original plaintiff then filed objection case No.33 of 1961 and order was passed on contest for recording the plaintiffs name. But defendant No.1 then got the name of the plaintiff changed and caused preparation of record of right in his own name beyond knowledge of the plaintiff. 

 9. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement stating, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to Amu Singha in fate right who took settlement from the original plaintiff by executing kabuliyat dated Ashar 1344 B.S. While Amu Singha was living therein, he died leaving his son Krishna Singha, who died unmarried leaving his only nephew (sister's son) defendant No.2 as his only heir. Accordingly, defendant No.2 held and possessed the suit land. During settlement and survey operation the suit land was recorded in the name of Krishna Singha noting the name of the original plaintiff as landlord. The plaintiff in collusion with the Objection Officer changed the record-of—right in his name. Defendant No.2 then filed appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was allowed on contest on 09.09.1961. The further case of defendant No.1 is that defendant No.2 was possessing the suit land partly as homestead and partly as chara bari (abandoned homestead) and then he transferred part of the suit land as noted in schedule II of the written statement by kabala dated 07.08.1965 to defendant No.1 and delivered possession. Defendant No.1 has been possessing part of the suit land purchased by him as stated above by constructing but and planting trees. The plaintiff is cunning and he took defendant No.2 in his confidence with high hopes that he would buy the land at a high price. Defendant No.2 having decided to sell part of the suit land to defendant No.1 began to kill time and refused presentation of kabala for registration and defendant No.1 then presented the kabala dated 07.08.1965 for registration before the Sub-registrar. Defendant No.2 did not appear at the instance of the plaintiff. So defendant No.1 had to file appeal before the District Registrar and the kabala was registered on contest on 02.02.1966. The plaintiff and defendant No.2 are in collusion and under influence of the plaintiff, defendant No.2 is remaining silent. 

 10. After hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record the Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit. Then the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No.239 of 1997, which was dismissed on contest. 

 II. That the Courts below came to the relevant findings upon consideration of the evidence on record and the High Court Division committed error of law in setting aside those findings on the ground of non-consideration of material evidence without mentioning which of the material evidence on record was not considered by the courts below." 

 13. Mr. Abdul Quayum, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He further submitted that both the trial Court and the appellate Court concurrently found that the plaintiffs-respondents could not prove by oral and documentary evidence surrender and possession in favour of the original plaintiff followed by dispossession, and thus the High Court Division committed error of law in reversing the concurrent finding of fact without adverting to oral and documentary evidence. He further submitted that the Courts below found that the record of right is correct and based on evidence and as such, the High Court Division could only reverse such finding by adverting to evidence on record, which it did not do. 

 14. Mr. Qumrul Hoque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No.8 made submission in support of the impugned judgement-and order of the High Court Division. He also submitted that neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court took into consideration the contents of Exhibit- `Ga'(sale deed in favour of defendant No.1-predecessor of the appellants) which shows that Gopendra Singha was in possession of the suit land on payment of rent to the original owner Irfan Ali Chowdhury. Subsequently, he claimed the property by inheritance from Krishna Singha, and thus the story of inheritance by Gopendra Singha from Krishna Singha is falsified. Hence, the High Court Division was correct in reversing the decision of the Courts below, even though their findings were concurrent. He further submitted that the wife of Amu Singha surrendered the land to the plaintiff. He further submitted that the Courts below failed to appreciate Exhibits 2 and 3 and did not consider the evidence of P.Ws 1 to 5, who unequivocally deposed that dispossession took place on Chaitra, 1373 BS after defendant No.2 executed the deed on 07.08.1965 in favour of defendant No.1 and wrongly held that the plaintiff failed to prove his dispossession. The learned Advocate also submitted that the Courts below failed to consider material facts on record showing that defendant No.2 was not a tenant under the original plaintiff nor was he the heir of Amu Singha, and hence no title passed to defendant No.1. He further submitted that the High Court Division correctly found and observed that defendant No. 2 illegally dispossessed the plaintiff in Chaitra, 1373 BS and defendant No.1 did not produce any rent receipt or any other papers to show that Krishna Singha was a tenant of the plaintiff. Moreover, Gopendra Singha did not come to support the claim of defendant No. 1. He lastly submitted that the original plaintiff was in possession of the suit land through tenants W.C. Keymer and his wife Rosemary by registered lease deed dated 1944. They handed back possession of the property to the original plaintiff after two years of the tenancy. 

 15. Mr. Mohammad Abdul Hai, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of respondent Nos. 1,2 and 5-7 also made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division. 

 16. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

 21. We note that the High Court Division mentioned that the trial Court after hearing the parties, without considering the evidence on record, wrongly and illegally dismissed the suit. However, we note from the impugned judgement that the High Court Division did not specifically refer to any of the evidence and materials on record to show which evidence the Courts below did not consider. The deed, by which Irfan Ali Chowdhury got the suit property is indeed very old. However, subsequent events and documents relating to those later events tend to indicate that Irfan Ali Chowdhury was no longer in possession of the suit land. On the contrary the evidence of the witnesses shows that defendant No.2 and his predecessors-in-interest were all along in possession of the suit land. We note that Krishna Singha, the predecessor of defendant No.1 got his name recorded in the record of rights as tenant, which the original plaintiff got corrected. But thereafter, Gopendra Singha (defendant No. 2 who sold the suit property to defendant No.1) filed an appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and got his name recorded in the record of rights. Khodeja Akhter Chowdhury who is the daughter of Irfan Ali Chowdhury deposing as P.W 1 could not controvert such claim. She admitted that her father's challenge against the record of rights was not fruitful. She also could not say whether her father took the matter further on appeal under section 53 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. We note that P.W 1 stated in her evidence that her father took possession of the suit land in 1342 BS (c.1935 AD), whereas PW4 stated that in 1950 Manipuri people lived on the suit land. Coincidentally, in Title Suit No.301 of 1965, Irfan Ali Chowdhury had claimed that possession of the suit land had been handed over to him in 1362 BS. (c.1955 AD). Moreover, we note that P.W1 stated in her deposition that 1362 BS was mistakenly written and that the correct date was 1342. This is clearly falsified by the evidence of P.W4. 

 26. In the facts of the instant case discussed above, we find that the High Court Division has reversed the concurrent finding of facts of the Courts below without specifically identifying any evidence which was misread or not considered by the trial Court or the appellate Court. The reference to non-consideration of the deed in favour of Irfan Ali Chowdhury dating to 1927 is of little consequence in view of the fact that admittedly the defendants' predecessors were the tenants in possession of the suit land from the original owners, having jote right by way of registered kabuliyat, and the record of rights was in their names as tenants. Irfan Ali Chowdhury purchased the land with the defendants' predecessor in possession as tenant. The finding of the trial Court and the appellate Court is that the plaintiffs could not prove that Irfan Ali Chowdhury ever went into possession of the suit land. 

 27. We find that the trial Court has given a very elaborate judgement discussing the evidence and materials on record, and came to a finding based on those evidence and materials. The High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction could only reverse those findings by specific reference to evidence and materials, which were not considered or were misread by the trial Court, which would have materially affected the decision had they been considered.

8. Finding himself in a predicament, the learned Counsel for the appellant relied upon Ext. D, an order of the Revenue Officer dated 25.3.53. By this order the defendants were shown in the Record-of-Rights to be "in forcible possession" of the land of the plaintiff. The learned Advocate for the appellant submitted that in view of the fact that Ext. D, the record of rights, was corrected on the plaintiff's own petition by directing that the disputed plots 1310, 1320, and 1342 be recorded in his name, and at column No. 23 the names of the defendants be recorded as in forcible possession from 1359 B.S. and as that order was passed on 25th March, 1959 corresponding to 11th Chaitra 1359 B.S. the learned Munsif for good reason observed that it could not be held that the plaintiff's bargudar left the suit village Inter than in Poush 1359 B.S. It is contended that, as the appellate court did not consider the material facts and circumstances on which the -trial court based its decision, the finding of fact as to the starting point of dispossession by the appellate court was not binding in second appeal. In support of this contention reliance is placed on A.H. Md. lsmail Vs. Sachidananda  Bhauacharjcc 40 C.W.N. 769. 

 9. Mr. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury learned advocate for the respondent, has pointed out that Ext. D was not mentioned in the written statement and that it was produced for the first time when evidence was about to be closed. He has submitted that the lower appellate court rightly held it to be a suspicious document the order dated 25th March, 1953. (Exhibit-D) was not a record of rights. It was an order passed by the Revenue Officer in an objection case filed by the plaintiff. The learned Counsel for the appellant also took exception to the following observation of the learned Subordinate Judge. This order was passed on the basis of the opinion of the revenue authority and the contesting defat did not take any step to prefer appeal disputing the fact that they came into possession of the suit land forcibly in 1359 B.S." It is contended that it was the plaintiff who should have preferred an appeal against the order dated 25th March,1953. As that order of the Revenue Officer did not support the defendants' case that the suitland was their ancestral lands but that they were merely "on forcible possession" therein, the learned Subordinate Judge, we find, rightly made the above remark. From that it can not be said that the onus was wrongly placed on the defendant.

full_judgment:
2. Respondent No.1 filed Miscellaneous Case No.123 of 1973 in the court of Munsif, Sherpur for correction of record of right under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It relates to land measuring 1.12 acres out of 2.00 acres of C.S. Khatian 1465 corresponding to R.O.R. Khatian No. 1760 and 13 decimals of land of C.S. Khatian No.1669 corresponding to R.O.R. Khatian No.2190 under Mouza Sherpur, District Mymensingh now Jamalpur. 

 "143A. Special provisions for correcting mistakes in the record-of-rights:(1) Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission of entry in the record-of-rights prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV may, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, file an application along with necessary requisites, for the purpose of correcting mistakes in such record-of-rights in the Civil Court which would have jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession of the land to which such entry relates or in respect of which such omission was made." For the purpose of this appeal, the other sub-sections need not be quoted. 

 5. There cannot be any doubt that the grant of any relief under the provisions of this section would depend on its existence at the time the relief is being sought and granted. It appears that the aforesaid Ordinance omitting the section from the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force in January, 1976. The judgment of the trial court was delivered on March 31, 1977. In so far as the judgment resulted in the dismissal of the miscellaneous case, be such dismissal on any ground whatsoever, it is not hit by the omission of section 143A from the statute concerned. But point is when did the proceeding, namely, miscellaneous case under section 143A was started. As appears from the record, it started in 1973 when section 143A was not omitted from the Act.

Abdul Quayum, Senior Advocate with JN Deb, Advocate instructed by AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on-record—For the Petitioners.

Jamira Khatun and others ------ Petitioners 
VS. 
Md Fazlul Karim and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
3. The defendant No. 1 Nazibulla h contested the suit by filing written statement denying the claims of the plaintiffs stating, inter alia, that the suit land along with other lands belonged to Taluk No.1079 Bakor Mohomad and Niskor Benombary (numberless) Taluk Niamat Ali Shah and Liakat Ali Shah and the disputed land was not part of Taluk No. 1102/30 Abdul Talik; that without local investigation the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any relief, that the plaintiffs, the pro-forma defendants or their predecessor have/-had no right title and possession in the suit land, the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants in collusion with each other instituted the suit, that the kabala in the name of the wife Abdul Khalid dated 12th Baishakh 1326 BS as it mentioned in the plaint do not attract the suit land. Moreover, since the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants had got no right, title and possession over the suit land and the suit is not at all maintainable in its present form inasmuch as the suit land belonged to Abdul Monaf in his Maliki right under his khas possession and while the said Abdul Manaf owned and possessed the land in Maliki right by executing a kabaliyat dated 4-4-1948 they took settlement of 3 kadar 3 powa land from the said Abdul Monaf with a rent of Taka 16 per year and thereafter by taking possession of the suit land has been enjoyment and possessing the same by using it as his family graveyard, as well as in some part of the suit land he has been growing bamboos and trees; that his son, one daughter and one nephew were buried in the said graveyard, but the plaintiffs or their predecessor did never possess the suit land; that though he has been possessing the suit land in the last settlement survey it was recorded in the name of his landlord Abdul Monaf and as such for correction of record he filed Miscellaneous Case No. 139 off 1969 in the First Court of Munsif, Sylhet Sadar under Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was decreed in his favour and accordingly the record was corrected and the judgment passed in that suit cannot be declared or set aside since the plaintiffs were aware of the judgment of the case dated 5-8-1970, moreover, the suit is barred by limitation; that subsequently by two amendment petitions the said Nazibullah amended his written statement twice, by the first amendment the quantum of his alleged settlement with him by Abdul Monaf was increased upto 4 kedar 2 powa, and by the second one the statement regarding burial of the family members of the plaintiff with his permission in the suit land had been struck off. After hearing, the Assistant Judge by his judgment and decree dated 19-10-1999 dismissed the suit with the finding that the suit though is maintainable but barred by limitation with the finding that the suit land belonging to Abdul Taluk as reported by the Advocate Commissioner's report is not reliable, and the defendant has been enjoying and possessing the suit land. On appeal the said judgment was affirmed by the appellate Court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 17-7-2000 agreeing with the findings of the Trial Court. 

 4. Mr. Abdul Quayum, learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioners submits that the High Court Division while making the Rule absolute did not reverse all the findings and decisions of the Court below; that though the plaintiffs claimed the suit land measuring 0.14 acres as land of 1102/30 Abdul Taluk; but the PW 1 (plaintiff No. 2) who deposed for all the plaintiffs admitted in chief examination that "নাঃ সম্পতি এই তিন পোয়া আমাদেও পূর্ববর্তী আং করিম এর স্বত্ব দখলীয় ছিল" and also in cross examination admitted that "আমরা আব্দুল তালুকের ২২ শং সম্পতি পাব" and he contesting defendant filed the khatian No. 424/5 of Dag No. 1860 (Exhibit-Ga) in the name of plaintiffs for an area of 0.22 acres of Abdul Taluk, All of which clearly proved that the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest over the suit land; that the trial Court while considering the local investigation report specifically stated that without finding or placing a fixed point by the Commissioner the whole work became unwise and accordingly ignored the report as not reliable and also considers the suit Khatian in the name of the defendant as belonging to Baker Mahamud Taluk and Khatian No. 424/5 (Exhibit-Ga) in the name of the plaintiffs as belonging to Abdul Taluk and asserted that the plaintiffs did not raise any question regarding the entries in the Khatian and as such, held the suit land as belonging to Baker Mahmud Taluk that in the suit graveyard there is no burials of any relation of the plaintiffs, rather on the other hand, the brother of the defendant No.1 and son, daughter and a nephew of defendant No. 1 also buried in the suit graveyard which has not been denied by the plaintiffs by cross examining the said defendant No. 1, rather the PW 1 in his cross examination admitted that neither his parents nor his relations were buried in the suit graveyard; that the defendant No.1 on mutating his name in view of judgment and decree as passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 132 of 1969 of the First Court of Sadar, Munsif, Sylhet has been paying rent but on the other hand the plaintiffs are not paying any rent concerning Dag No. 1859 which clearly proves the possession of the defendant No. 1; that the suit is bad for defect of party in view of the fact of non-impleading the heirs of Abdul Monaf in whose name the record of rights were prepared and subsequently corrected by the defendant No. 1 vide judgment and decree dated 5-8-1970 as passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 132 of 1969 and in case of setting aside of the said decree as passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 132 of 1969 the record of rights would stand in the name of Abdul Monaf and a decree for declaration of title cannot be given without impleading the heirs of Abdul Monaf as defendant; that the judgment and decree in Miscellaneous Case No. 132 of 1969 was passed on 5-8-1970 and the plaintiffs brought the suit on 19-9-1985 and stated that the plaintiffs came to know about the wrong record of rights in the first part of Srabon 1392 BS; but, could not prove the date by any witnesses and as such, the present suit was hopelessly barred by limitation; that all the 3 PW's are related with each other and in view of the fact and circumstances of the case in absence of any neutral witnesses the plaintiffs cannot get the relief; that the plaintiffs suit as framed is not maintainable inasmuch as the plaintiffs claimed declaration of title for themselves along with pro-forma defendant Nos. 2-9 which is not permissible in law; that there was a suit being Title Suit No. 293 of 1965 in which there was local investigation covering the present suit land and the report dated 5-11-1969 has been filed by the defendant No. 1 in the present suit and the same was marked as Exhibit-'kha' and in that report the suit land has been held as land of Baker Mahamud Taluk and the land of the defendant No. 1 

 5. It appears from the record that admittedly the suit land is graveyard and the contesting defendant admitted that some family members of the plaintiffs were buried in that graveyard. It appears that in the suit the pertinent question is that the suit land relates to which Taluk. It appears from the report of an advocate commissioner that the suit land belonged to Abdul Taluk as is claimed by the plaintiffs. But the said report was not properly considered by the trial Court with the plea that the investigation was not started from any fixed point, but in arriving into such decision the learned Judge has considered his earlier order of the Court whereby the report was accepted by the order No. 41 dated 02-08-1989 passed by the Assistant Judge and admittedly against that order the defendant moved the Court but was unsuccessful. It appears that the trial Court considered the commissioner's report with a negative approach and the appellate Court do not at all bother to see that report. That in respect of the question of limitation, the High Court Division held that previously there was no cause of action for the plaintiffs to file any suit since they were not disturbed by anybody and the decision of the Miscellaneous Case No 132 of 1969 was not binding upon them since they were not a party in that case. 

 6. It is apparent that the defendant did not take settlement of any land relating to the Taluk named as Abdul Taluk, rather he may have taken settlement of land relating to other Taluk which is adjacent to the land of Abdul Taluk. Therefore the claim of the defendant has not been established and the Courts below without properly appreciating of that exhibit illegally decided the fate of the suit. It appears that the so-called record of right in the name of Abdul Monaf and subsequently corrected in the name of the contesting defendant by filing a suit under section 143 A of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not at all relevant to the suit land and the plaintiff is not bound by the decree of the suit. 

 8. The High Court Division held that on misreading of evidence and on non-consideration of the evidences on record the Courts below found that the defendant has been enjoying and possessing the suit land, this sort of finding is nothing but illegal occasioning failure of justice. On the contrary, the plaintiffs have been able to prove their right, title and possession over the suit land.

Syed Mojizur Rahman for AH Md Shahadat Ali Khan, Advocate------For the Petitioner.
