parties:
Abdur Rahim Chowkrder @ Abdur Rahman Sheikh since deceased ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Raji Haider and others ------ .Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
8. In 1394 BS, the suit land was given to defendant No. 1 for 'Borga' cultivation. When defendant No. 1 refused to give 'Borga' share to the plaintiffs, they started CR Case being No. 17 of 1988 in the local Upazila Magistrate Court. During the prosecution of the case defendant No. 1 declared that he had title and possession in the suit land, which was recorded in the record of rights in the name of his father Hashem Ali. The plaintiffs also came to know that Hashem Ali obtained an ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 49 of 1957 and got the record corrected in his name on the basis of the decree. 

 10. Defendant No. 1 alone contested the suit by filing a written statement. His case in short, is that his father Hashem Ali Sheikh got the suit land by way of 'Pattan'. When he was thus owner in possession of the suit land, the suit land was wrongly recorded in the names of original owners in the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Hashem Ali was then constrained to institute Title Suit No. 49 of 1957 against original tenants including those the plaintiffs claimed to have acquired title for declaration of title practically for correction of the record of rights and got a decree on 28-10-1957. On the basis of the decree, Hashem Ali made an application being Miscellaneous Case No. 4222/60-61 under section 54 for correction of the record and got an order on 28-3-1961. Then, the record was finally corrected in Mutation Case No. 9P/87-88 and the suit land was recorded in his name. Hashem Ali possessed 5.02 acres including the suit land until his death and after him defendant No. 1 continued possessing said land as his sole heir for more than 12 years by making a dwelling and living therein; and also by cultivation. 

 14. Trial Court on the evidence on record decreed the suit as prayed for. On appeal therefrom at the instance of defendant No.1, the appeal was dismissed and decree of the trial Court affirmed by the impugned judgment and decree. Hence this Rule. Mr Syed Mofizur Rahman, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the suit as framed in the manner and form was not maintainable and also barred by limitation. 

 15. In the absence of any declaration sought for against the decree dated 28-10-1957 passed in Title Suit No. 49 of 1957 and order dated 28-3-1961 passed in Case No. 4222/60-61 for correction of the record of rights, he submits, the plaintiffs are not entitled to any decree. 

 16. He submits that in view of the fact that the record of rights under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was wrongly prepared in the names of previous tenants, which was ultimately corrected and mutated in the name of Hashem Ali, father of defendant No.1 by order dated 14-1-1988 passed in case No. 9P/87-88 on the basis of actual physical possession, both the Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit without taking into consideration of long possession of defendant No. 1 in the suit land, which occasioned failure of justice. 

 22. The issue facing me is whether or not the appellate judgment and decree affirming those of the trial Court decreeing the suit in its entirety are well founded on the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence, oral and documentary, on record and in law. 

 23. I have perused the entire record. 

 35. Here why Ishaque Ali purchased the land in the name of defendant No.2 Ramendra Nath who belonged to a different community has not been explained. PW 1 Raji Haider claimed that defendant No. 2 was their 'Karma chari' At, the time of transaction, he was a mere boy of about nine years only. No other witness was examined to prove that defendant No.2 was a 'Karmachari'. Further, in presence of 10 plaintiffs, who are direct descendants of Ishaque Ali, he cannot be believed to have purchased the land in the name of defendant No. 2. Moreover, during his lifetime, there is no evidence on record that Ishaque Ali ever demanded return of the land from defendant No.2. 

 In the circumstances and on such evidence on record, concurrence by the appellate Court of the view of the trial Court on the 'Benami' transaction must be held to be not based on any accepted principles of law relating to 'Benami' transaction and cannot be accepted. 

 44. On the other hand, defendant No.2 deposed as DW 1 that his father took 'Pattan' of the suit land along with other land from recorded tenants Indobhushan, Nani Bala, Rebuti Ranjan, Subhasini and Sarala Bala long ago. He could not say how his father took 'Pattan'. His father used to possess the land on the basis of 'Pattan'. His father obtained a decree in Title Suit No. 47 of 1957 in respect of the suit land. In 1968, his father died leaving him as one son and one daughter. He started cultivating the suit land since the death of his father and living in the huts raised. He got the land mutated on the basis of the decree. He paid 'Chowkidari' tax. 

 52. The above oral evidence of the parties on possession if compared with the evidence of the defendant No. 1 becomes overwhelming and weightier. The trial Court also could not but accept the possession of defendant No.1. Similarly, findings of the Courts below that defendant No. 1 possessed the suit land on behalf of the plaintiffs as 'Borgadar' and defendant No.2 was a 'Benamdar' of Ishaque Ali, predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs in respect of two 'Kabalas' dated 18-12-1972 and 1-4-1974 Exhibits 1(c) and 1(d) are all arbitrary as not based on the evidence on record. 

 59. For foregoing reasons, the plaintiffs must be held to have failed to prove title and/or possession in the suit land. Finding on possession, however concurrent by the Courts below, being not based on the evidence oral and documentary and law, cannot be binding in revision. The case is very old. So, I had to take pain to find afresh the issues the parties are found to be in variance on the basis of the evidence on record and law. 

 Send down the record at once.

caseno:
Second Appeal No. 439 of 1974
First Appeal Tender  No. 3 of 1974.
lawyer:
Abdus Salam, Advocate ------ For Appellant.

parties:
Jafar Ali ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Khagendra Chandra Dutta And Others ------ Respondent.
full_judgment:
2. The disputed plot No. 1025 measuring an area of 1.25 acres of appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 36 originally belonged to Bhuk-ailas Raj State and after acquisition it was recorded in the Khas Khatian of the Government as bhiti land. 

 3. Plaintiff's case is that the suit land was settled to the plaintiff after due enquiry and he was possessing the same. Some people instigated the Hindus of the locality to file an objection case before the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Comilla challenging the legality of the lease on the ground that the suit land was recorded in the C.S. Khatian as a cremation ground. It was asserted that after lapse of time the suit land changed its character and during the last revisional operation the same was recorded as bhiti land. 

 4. The case of the defendant is that in the recent settlement operation the suit land was recorded in the khas khatian of the Government as a bhiti land with a note in the remark column, “সাধারণের ব্যবহার্য” but through mistake the word “শ্বশান” was not recorded. 

 6. Mr. Abdus Salam, the learned Advocate for the appellant, has contended that as in the recent settlement operation the suit land was recorded as “সাধারণের ব্যবহার্য” bhiti land the court of appeal ought to have held that the present record of right would prevail over the C.S. record. In support of his contention Mr. Salam has cited Bhupendra Krishna Chose V. Abdur Rahman reported in 51 C.L.J 18 where it has been held that in a conflict between the old record of rights, and a recent record of rights, the recent record is to be presumed to be correct unless it is proved by evidence to be incorrect and the burden of proof to show that it is incorrect is upon the party challenging it. In Abhiram Bedanta V. Chintamani Bedamia reported in 100 I.C. 1927 (701), cited by Mr. Satan it has been held that when there are two records of rights prepared at different times, entries in both of them will be presumed to be correct entries of facts existing at the time the entries were made and that there is nothing in the law which would entitle a party to say that the entry in the sub-sequent record is rebutted by the entry in the previous record. 

 "(1) For those unoccupied lands in which the public have rights and which therefore cannot be leased, e.g., roads, halots, drinking water tanks, embankments, wells, etc., 

 9. In the present case the land was recorded in the C.S. record as well as S.A. Khatian as “সাধারণের ব্যবহার্য”As the public had rights in the disputed land the settlement made in favour of the plaintiff was not legally done, and by the impugned orders such settlement was correctly cancelled by the revenue authorities.

lawyer:

full_judgment:
2. The facts, in short, are that the predecessor-in interest of the respondent Nos. l to 8 instituted of Title Suit No.120 of 1992 in the Third Court of the then Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on 27.06.1992 for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the suit property after removing all structures from the suit property stating, inter-alia, that Abdul Kader was the C.S. recorded tenant of the suit property. Abdul Kader sold the suit property to Sarat Chandra Ghose Ukil by a registered deed No.351 on 12.01.1921. Sarat Chandra Vs. Oulshan Benum & Ors (Md. Abdul Malin Jill Ghose Ukil gave a registered Borga kabuliyat for 6 years on 19.05.1924 to Sk. Ahsanullah alias Munshi and Sk. Mohammad son of Sk. Ahsanullah. After 6 years, Sarat Chandra Ghose Ukil took back the possession of the suit property to his own possession and made a will of .70 acres on 24th Ashar, 1335 B.S. (1928 A.D.) in favour of Premthosh Ghose and Bimala Chandra Ghose who filed the probate Case No.7 of 1934 and Probate was granted on 19.07.1935. Premtosh Ghose and Bimala Charan Ghose sold .70 acre by a registered deed being No.4030 on 24.09.1946 to one Sk. Hossainuddin son of late Kamatullah. Sk. Hossainuddin died leaving Samiroddin and others as his heirs. Samiruddin and others sold two Pakhi on 12.09.1955 to plaintiff's name and bename and possession was handed over. Plaintiff was possessing the suit land since then. But the defendant Nos.1 to 8 dispossessed the plaintiffs by force on 09.01.1992 and illegally entered into the suit land and constructed some kucha houses on the suit land. Plaintiff A.N.M. Obaidul Islam made a waqf of the land comprising of S.A. khatian No.197 and S.A. plot No.298/303 and. he worked as MutwIli of the of the said waqf Estate. Remaining .35 acre was recorded in the name of plaintiff Obaidul Islam. Subsequently the suit property was recorded under R.S. plot Nos.1207, 1208, 1209 and 1210 of H.S. Khatian No.202. Upon application of the plaintiff R.S. plot No.1210 was separated from the R.S. Khatian and .33 acre was recorded in the plot Nos.1207, 1208, 1204. Other one bigha was purchased in the benami of his wife Gulshan Begum and recorded in her name after keeping .7 acre out of .35 acre in his name donated in favour of his wife, 4 sons and 3 daughters. The same was decreed on 06.08.1992 in Title12(Md. Abdul Matin.J) M/s. N.F.M. Universium Est Suit No.303 of 1990. In the above way plaintiff was in possession of the suit property and for the dispossession, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit. 

 3. The petitioner as defendant No.14 contested the suit filing the written statement. The case of the defendant petitioner, inter-alia, is that one Abdul Kader was the C.S. recorded tenant and he made a gift in favour of his 3(three) sons namely, (1) Sheikh Elahi Bux, (2) Sheikh Abdul Karim and (3) Sheikh Abdul Nabi on 31.05.1917. Subsequently on 16.04.1943, Sheikh Elahi Bux and Sheikh Karim got the suit land in their favour by an amicable partition/family arrangement. Sheikh Elahi Bun died leaving two sons namely (1) Syed Hossain and (2) Siddique Hossain. Syed Hossain died leaving one son namely Arzu Mia. Arzu Mia died leaving his widow Tahera Khatun as his legal heir. Siddique Hossain son of Sheikh Elahi. Bux died leaving his wife Aziza Begum, one son Sirajul Islam and daughter Tahera Begum. Sheikh Abdul Karim son of Abdul Kader died leaving his only son Mia Hossain and Mia Hossain died leaving wife Sonaban Bibi and 3 sons (I) Abdul Mutalib, (2) Abdus Shahid and (3) Abdul Hamid. Subsequently on 04.07.1995, all the heirs of Sheikh Elahi Bux and Sheikh Abdul Karim sold 4.50 acres out of 5.68 acres to the defendant petitioner and mutated his name and paid rents to the Government. Defendant No.14 petitioner is in possession of the suit property. In the above facts and circumstances the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 5. We have heard Mr. Rafique-ul Huq, learned Counsel and Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner and perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and other papers on record. 

 "We find that the suit land was already recorded in the names of original plaintiff Obaidul Islam and his wife Gulshan Begum during survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in plot Nos.298/302 and 298/303 appertaining to S.A. Khatian Nos.196 and 197. Such record of rights published sometime in 1964. On the basis of such record of right the plaintiff possessed the suit land exclusively on payment of rents on proper receipt exhibit 8 series. Similarly under the R.S. survey the suit land was again recorded in the names of Obaidul Islam and his wife Gulshan Begum in R.S. plot Nos.1207, 1208, and 1209 appertaining to R.S. Khatian-Nos.202 and 225 and R.S. record of rights was published in 1980." 

 In view of the undisputed record of rights and payment of rent by the plaintiffs and oral and documentary evidence the High Court Division rightly found the plaintiffs in exclusive and specific possession of the suit land.

full_judgment:
2. The facts involved in the case, in short, are that the suit land originally belonged to Dhan Bibi and Toyab Mia from whom Julfikar Ali and Majar Ali took jote settlement by executing a registered Kabuliyat dated 15 Sravan, 1283 B.S. concerning an area of 1 hal, 2 kedars and 2 jasti at a rental of TK. 4.50 per year and for arrear rents the landlord filed rent suit No. 132 of 1935 and got decree and while said Majar Ali was in possession transferred the suit land in favour of Masaddar Ali 35 years back and handed over title deeds and possession thereof and the said Masaddar Ali possessed the suit land by planting trees and bamboos and died 24 years back leaving behind the plaintiffs as his heirs who recent in the year 1982 came to know about the wrong record of rights in the names of defendants and on approach by them; Majar Ali, the proforma defendant No. 25 executed a registered deed of relinquishment on 21.04.1982 in their favour. 

 3. The defendant Nos. 1 (ka), 1 (kha), 2(ka)-(cha), 3, 12 and 15 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter-alia, that Majar Ali after auction shifted to the other place and relinquished 6 kedars, 3 powas, 2 reks and 10 gondas of patit jungel in favour of Munir Miah, Chand Miah and others on executing a Sharanlipi dated 2nd Ashwin, 1362 B.S. and regarding his non-relinquishment though the same has been recorded in the name of Majar Ali, 1 the plaintiffs corrected the same in their favour by filing case before the Revenue Authority and accordingly, prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 4. Leave was granted to consider the submissions of Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel, for the appellant that the findings of the High Court Division are that the suit itself suffers from defect of patties for not substituting the heirs of the deceased proforma defendant who admitted the correctness of the plaintiff case in his written statement. The learned Counsel further submitted that the High Court Division has failed to appreciate. the evidentiary value of a Muktipotra if the said document is proved as a document regarding title and therefore, non-consideration I of so on a document while passing the judgment by the High Court Division results in erroneous decision and the lower appellate Court in its judgment fully considered the legal effect of 'Shoronlipi' and 'a rent receipt' as produced by the D.W.'s and came to a specific finding that such Shoronlipi and 'rent receipt' cannot be treated under the facts and circumstances of the present case document to be relied on or on the basis of which the title of the defendants as claimed could not be established but the High Court Division without applying it's judicial mind came to an erroneous finding. In addition, Mr. Islam submitted that in the absence of any legal infirmity in the findings of fact arrived at by the Court of Appeal, the High Court Division committed error in interfering with the decision of the Court of Appeal below. Mr. Islam also submitted that proforma defendant No. 25 having admitted the sale of the suit land in favour of the predecessor of the plaintiffs by a registered document and also admitting possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land for over twelve years, the High Court Division erred in law in interfering with the finding of facts of the Court of Appeal below that the plaintiffs filed the suit within the period of limitation after coming to know of the wrong recording of the suit land in the record of rights". 

 5. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants submitted that the findings of the High Court Division are that the suit itself suffers from defect of parties for not substituting the heirs of the deceased pro-forma defendant who admitted the correctness of the plaint case in his written statement. The learned Counsel further submitted that the High Court Division has failed to appreciate the evidentiary value of a Muktipotra if the said document is proved as a document regarding title and therefore, non-consideration of such a document while passing the judgment by the High Court Division results in erroneous decision and the lower appellate Court in its judgment fully considered the legal effect of 'Shoronlipi and 'a rent receipt' as produced by the D.W.'s and came to a specific finding that such 'Shoronlipi' and 'rent receipt' cannot be treated under the facts and circumstances of the present case, a document to be relied on or on the basis of which the title of the defendants as claimed could not be established but the High Court Division' without applying it's judicial mind came to an erroneous finding. In addition, Mr. Islam submitted that in the absence of any legal infirmity in the findings of fact arrived at by the Court of Appeal, the High Court Division committed error in interfering with the decision of the Court of Appeal below. Mr. Islam also submitted that proforma defendant No.25 having admitted the sale of the suit land in favour of the predecessor of the plaintiffs by a registered document and also admitting  possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land for over twelve years, the High Court' Division erred in law in interfering with the finding of facts of the Court of Appeal below that the plaintiffs filed the suit within   the period of limitation after coming to know of the wrong recording of the suit land in the record of rights. 

 6. Mr. M. A. Mannan, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents submitted that the heirs of defendant No.25 who died after filing written statement, being necessary parties in the suit having not been substituted, the suit is apparently bad for defect of party; that the plaintiffs failed to prove the alleged story of transfer of the suit land by defendant No.25 to Masaddar Ali, plaintiffs' predecessor either by executing any document or by adducing any evidence as payment of any consideration money, delivery of possession, and more particularly when P.W.1 in his deposition stated that except his oral statement there is no other material to show when and how the transfer took place, and in that view of the matter the claim of their acquisition of title relinquishment but that does not confer any title to the plaintiffs and the statement made in the said document is not sufficient to hold that the plaintiffs could establish their title to the suit land as the same is not a document of transfer; that the writ statement filed by the defendant No.25 was not proved by any body as such, the statement allegedly therein do not deserve to be considered by any Court of law but the Court of Appeal below acted illegally in taking into consideration said written statement. The learned Counsel further submitted that the Court of Appeal below erroneously held that by the unregistered 'Shoronlipi no title passed to the defendants, having failed to notice that the defendant No.25 was holding the jote right (tenancy right) only while superior interests remained with the defendants landlord and as such, relinquishment by 'Shoronlipi' and by endorsement in the back of the counterfoil of rent receipt was sufficient to pass title to the defendants who were landlords of defendant No. 25; that the defendants adduced documentary evidence in support of their possession in the suit land and they proved the factum of possession by adducing evidence in respect of manner of possession inasmuch as they in their written statement stated that they possess the suit land by growing winter vegetables and also paddy in some portion of the same and the witnesses of possession D.W.'s 3 and 4 unequivocally supported the defendant's possession in the suit land but the Court of Appeal below on a misreading of the evidence on record arrived at an erroneous findings of possessing in favour of the plaintiffs. The learned Counsel finally submitted that it is the case of the defendants that out of /14/ annas share of kabuliyat land, the defendant No.25 relinquished 6 kedars 3 powas 2 reks 10 gondas of land in favour of the landlord by executing 'Shoranlipi' and also by endorsement on the counterfoil of the rent receipt and defendant No. 25 retained 5 kedars 2 powas 1 jaista out of the kabuliyat   land and RW. 1 in his deposition did not deny the said assertion and this fact coupled with 'Shoronlipi proved the case of the defendant. 

 7. We have heard the learned Counsel of both sides. On perusal of the record it appears that it is the allegation of the plaintiffs that his father after his grandfather, Zulfiqur Ali became the owner and possessor of the suit land P.W.1, Md. Torun Mia deposed in support of his case. During cross-examination P.W.1 admitted that the rent suit against Zulfiqur Ali was filed. The predecessor of the plaintiffs lost his right in auction. It was further admitted that there was no registered deed of transfer   between the parties regarding the suit land. The plaintiffs claim by exhibit-1 is not satisfactorily proved. How the plaintiffs proved themselves to be the successor of the suit land, when the other heirs of Zulfiqur Ali has not been brought into record. Plaintiffs' father Masaddar Ali's purchase story could not be substantiated by producing documentary evidence. P.W.1 himself in cross-examination admitted that except his oral statement, there is no iota of evidence, to show what transfer took place. The plaintiffs further claimed that defendant No. 25 relinquished the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs by way of registered decd. P.W.2 Mukul Mia stated that the defendants are in possession of the suit land. He is also a solitary eye witness of exhibit-5. He seems to be unaware of the contents of the document. P.W.3, Abdur Noor, stated that he does not know in whose name the suit land has been recorded. P.W.4 also gave a contradictory statement regarding the mode of securing and acquiring title of the plaintiffs. It appears from the statement of P.W.'s that none could prove the title of the plaintiffs' predecessors over the suit land. 

 10. It appears that there is no finding regarding the document exhibited by the defendants particularly the 'Swaranlipi executed by the admitted tenant in favour of the admitted landlords and the alleged endorsement by the tenant on the counter-foil of the rent receipt issued by the admitted landlords regarding the relinquishment of their tenancy, these two vital documents were not at all considered though the defendants made specific assertion on the basis of such documents. In absence of any finding regarding these documents, it appears that the Court of Appeal below failed to decide whether the defendant End. No. 25, Syed Mazer Ali had got any right, title and interest in the suit land at the relevant time, in the absence of such right, title, he had no authority to issue any 'Muktipatra' in favour of anybody as alleged by the plaintiffs. Moreover, admittedly the defendant No. 25 had expired during pendency of the suit land and his successors ought to have been substituted in the suit, though no where in the record it is appeared that nobody claimed that the defendant No. 25 has no successor in the world. The Court of Appeal below also considered the written statement of the defendant No. 25 in arriving into his decision though its contention was not approved by anybody. 

 11. The High Court Division observed that the suit suffers from defect of parties and no contention of the defendant No. 25 in his written statement which was not proved by anybody, was illegally considered   beyond the scope of law; that the plaintiffs were known about their alleged wrong recording since long time but they did not file any suit within six years from date of their knowledge and hence the suit is barred by limitation. The High Court Division further observed that the suit was decreed on the basis of a document which cannot be treated as a deed of acquiring title by anybody. It appears from Section 100 of Sylhet Tenancy Act that the said provision is not at all relevant to the instant suit.

lawyer:
ASM Khalequzzaman, Advocate-on-Record------ For the Appellant (in CA No. 216 of 2000). Jainal Abedin, Deputy Attorney-General instructed by AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on Record------ For the Appellant (in CA No. 217 of 2000).

parties:
Abdul Aziz ------ Appellant
Vs.
Hindu Deity Luxmi Gobinda Jew and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Short facts are that the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 34 of 1970 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge(now Joint District Judge), Dhaka for declaration of title stating, infer alia, that the plaintiff is a Hindu Deity installed long ago in a temple situated in a portion of the suit land. The suit land was dedicated for establishment of the deity and also for performing the Sheba Puja and other religious ceremonies. The suit land was recorded as such in her name in the CS record of rights as debuttor properties. The plaintiff has thus been owner in peaceful possession of the suit land. During the survey operation under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, one Debendra Chandra Bhattacharjee was the Shebayet of the plaintiff and he was a simple man and completely under the influence of one Suresh Chandra Roy under whom he used to serve. Taking the advantage of such influence Suresh unduly gained over Debendra Chandra Bhattacharjee and fraudulently got the suit property recorded in his name as secular property. The said Debendra Chandra Bhattacharjee was turned out from the shebayetship and the present shebayet was appointed and he has regularly performing the sheba puja, etc of the deity. The said Suresh Chandra Roy left the then Pakistan and settled in India, Taking advantage of the wrong record of rights in the name of Suresh, respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were trying to declare the suit property as enemy property. The plaintiff has always been in peaceful possession of the suit property. The said wrong record of rights having created cloud over the title, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the present suit. 

 4. The case of defendant No. 2, is that the suit property became enemy property and, as such, vested in the defendant Government. The plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit property and, as such, it has no locus standi to bring the suit. The case of the defendant No.4, on the other hand, is that the suit is barred by limitation and the plaintiff has no locus standi to file the suit as he is neither the shebayet nor the suit property is a debuttor property, that the suit land and other lands of mouza Daulatpur and Kirtibashdi were taken in its possession by the Government under section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and were accordingly recorded in the newly prepared khatian No.1 as khas land and the said land was settled with him and one Shafiuddin Ahmed in Settlement Case Nos. 173 of 1966-67 and 176 of 1966-67 on 3-4-1967. 

 7. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division while exercising jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure exceeded his jurisdiction in setting aside the concurrent finding of the fact arrived at by the Courts below on proper appreciation of evidence on record and the next submission that the. Courts below upon considering the oral as well as documentary evidences found that the suit was not brought before Civil Court by the aggrieved persons against the order of Revenue Officer under section 92(4) of the SAT Act within the period of limitation and, as such, the suit is also barred by limitation and this finding having been based on proper appreciation of evidence on record the learned Single Judge erred in law in not holding that the suit is barred by limitation and the last submission that the Courts below after considering Exhibit found that the suit properties were not Debuttar at the relevant time and the High Court Division acted wrongly in revision in reopening the evidences and came to a wrong finding that the suit property was a debuttar property. 

 8. We have heard Mr ASM Khalequzzaman, the learned Advocate-on-Record for the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 216 of 2000 and Mr Jainal Abedin, the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 217 of 2000 and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected, papers. None appears for the respondents in both the appeals. 

 9. It is undisputed that the suit land was recorded in the CS Khatian Exhibits 1 and 1(a) as debuttar property in the name of the plaintiff deity Luxmi Gobinda Jew Bigraha but the SA Khatian in respect of the suit land was prepared in the name of Suresh Chandra Roy. The definite case of the plaintiff is that one Debendra Chandra Bhattachatjee was the shebayet of the deity and before him Sharat Chandra Bhattachatjee was the shebayet of the plaintiff deity. But the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of Suresh Chandra Roy who had no title and possession the rein, it appears that the High Court Division discussed the evidence of PW 1 Prafulla Chandra Bhattacharjee the present Shebayet and other plaintiffs witness. PW 1, Prafulla Chandra Bhattacharjee in his evidence stated that the deity was installed long ago. He further stated that before him, his father was the shebayet. He also stated that he himself cultivated a portion of the suit property and his bargadars cultivated the remaining portion. He also stated that he did not receive any notice for treating the suit property as enemy property. He further stated that the property has not been declared as abandoned property and the plaintiff was never dispossessed from the suit land. He further stated that his father Debendra Chandra Bhattachatjee and others did not file. Miscellaneous Appeal No. 395 of 1965 before the Commissioner of Dhaka Division, PW 2, Jogesh Chandra Dey aged about 70 years. PW 3 Md Ali. aged about 59 years and other PWs stated that the deity was installed in a portion of the suit land long ago and the shebayet of the deity possesses the suit land. 

 11. The High Court Division held that the suit land was recorded in the name of the deity Luxmi Gobinda Jew Bigraha in the CS Khatian as a rent free jote. It also appears that there is no evidence on record that the deity ever migrated to India at any point of time or that the deity was taken to India by the shebayet. It may be pointed out that the suit property was once treated as an abandoned property and subsequently as an enemy (now vested) property. The High Court Division held once the property became an abandoned property and vested in the Government the same cannot be treated as enemy property and, therefore, such action of the defendants in treating the suit property as enemy property is evidently illegal and without jurisdiction. 

 13. We have already pointed out that undisputedly the suit land was recorded in the name of the deity in the CS Khatian Exhibits 1 and 1(a). The CS Khatian has a presumption of correctness under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act but the SA Khatian has no such presumptive value, it is true that presumption of correctness of entry in the CS Khatian is rebuttable by adducing cogent and reliable evidence, in the instant case there is no attempt even to rebut the correctness of entry ill the CS Khatian prepared in the name of the deity. The High Court Division relying on the case of Sukumar Bose and others vs Abani Kumar Halder and others reported in 60 CWN 778 observed that in that case it was held that a debuttor property can never be turned into a secular property, in view of the proposition that once a property becomes a property of the deity which is immortal, it continues to be a property of the deity for all times to come. The dedication of the property to an idol may take place at the time of installation of the idol or may precede it or it may take place after the installation of the deity and after the dedication in all cases it remains the property of the idol and ceases to be the property of the donor. Even if a particular image may be destroyed, the deity whose visible form the image continues for ever and its property as debuttor property remains totally unaffected. 

 14. In view of our above discussion, that the CS Khatian Exhibits 1 and 1(a) were correctly prepared in the name of the plaintiff deity, the title of the suit land remained with the deity and the deity possessed through shebayet and preparation of the SA Khatian in the name of Suresh Chandra was apparently without any basis. The High Court Division it appears, on analysis of evidence on record, found possession of the plaintiffs shebayet in the suit land, Moreover, if according to defence case the property was once taken over as abandoned property, as claimed by the defendant, the same cannot be treated as enemy property again. 

 16. In the above facts and circumstances, we are of the view that the High Court Division, on correct assessment of the materials on record and the law relating to debuttor property, arrived at a correct decision and there is no cogent reason to interfere with the same.

full_judgment:
2. The petitioners Rai Saheb Abinash Chandra Bhattachaija and others preferred Six applications, being the Civil Revision Nos. 290 of I966. 291 of 1966, 292 of 1966, 993 of 1966, 294 of 1966 and 295 of 1966 before this Court under Section 115(1) or the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained 6(six) Rules thereupon impugning a judgment dated 31.12.1965 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court and Special Judge, Comilla in Special Appeal Nos. 30, 31, 33, 34, 35 and 36 of 1964 dismissing the Appeals on contest by the single Judgment that were filed under Section 51 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act,1950 stating in Civil Revision No.290 of 1966 that the land in question is a 13hiti. measuring, 24 feet X 18 feet, recorded in C.S. Plot No.1674 under the C.S. Khatian No.395 and the Petitioner took settlement of it under a registered Patta dated 30.11.1940 from the Ex.Landlord who was a Shebait of a Dehottar Estate, namely, The Sri Sri Gour Nityananda Mohapravu and Sri Sri Radha Govinda l3igraha with powers to make pucca and other constructions. 

 2(a). In the recent survey operation, the land has been recorded in the name of the Petitioner in plot No.3I28, under the Khatian No.527, in Mouza Brahmanbaria. Subsequently, a proceeding was started, being No.2734 of 1961 under Section 49 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for revision at the instance of the local Tahsildar on the grounds that the disputed land is a part of Taha-Bazar and khas land of the Ex-rent receiver: The petitioner contested the proceeding by submitting his written objections and stating, amongst other that the land in question was not the. Khas land of the Ex. land receiver. The Assistant Settlement Officer has allowed the objections of the Petitioner by his order dated 21.10.1961. But the Opposite Party preferred a Revisional application on the grounds that the disputed plot was within the ambit and periphery of the Ananda Bazar, whereupon the settlement officer directed a local enquiry by the Charge officer. Comilla and the charge officer submitted a report stating that the bulk area of Gagat Bazar would not be taken to be within the periphery of Fiat except two small plots. Viz 3725 and 3543, which might he kept under acquisition and the rest may by recorded in the names of the possessors:. The plot numbers 3170, 3167, 3157, 3156, 3145, 3144, 3232, 3134, 3139, 3136 and 3130 might be taken within the periphery of flat and recorded in the name of the Collector and the remaining plots might he recorded in the names of the .possessors and the Compensation Assessment Roll he corrected accordingly. 

 2(b). In Civil Revision No. 291 of 1966, the predecessors of the Petitioners Gopal Chandra Roy and another purchased a Exhibit land, measuring 16 X 13 cft, recorded in C.S. Plot No. 1675 under the khatian No. 34 (Plot No.3129under the P.R.R. Khatian No. 126/127) and constructed big structures about 20 years ago and the Petitioner paid rent to the Government and the Tahsildar  started the Miscellaneous Case No. 2717 of 1962 and the case was dismissed on 18.7.1962 holding the Petitioners are non-agricultural tenants. But a notice was served upon them acquiring the property against which the Petitioners tiled the Miscellaneous Case No. 12 of 1962 which was dismissed summarily on 14.1.1963. The Petitioners then preferred the Special Appeal No. 30 of 1964 in the Court of the Special Judge which was also dismissed on analogous hearing. 

 2(c). In Civil Revision No. 292 of 1966 the Petitioner Mathur Chandra Pal and another were non-agricultural tenant in a bhiti, measuring 19 1/2 X 13 cubic feet recorded in Plot No. 3121 under the P.R.R. Khatian No. 524 by taking its settlement from the Ex. landlord who was a Sebait of the Debottor Estate by Registered Patta dated 18.3.1940 at yearly rental and dwelling therein by making pucca constructions of a two storied building and during the S.A: operation, the said bhiti was recorded in the names of the Petitioners as tenants under P.R.R. Khatian No. 524. Upon an objection filed by the opposite party, under Section 49 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, a case being No.2731 of 1961 was started and the Assistant Settlement Officer by his order dated 21.10.1961 upheld the records. But the Settlement Officer served a notice upon the Petitioners under Section 49 and 50 of the Act on 18.8.1962 in a Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 1962 where the record was cancelled upon summary rejection of the Petitioner's objection and the learned Special Judge has also been pleased to dismiss the Special Appeal No. 70 of 1963 preferred by the Petitioners by his common judgment dated 31.12.1965. 

 others stated that they were non-agricultural tenants in a Bhiti, measuring 15 X 13 cubic feet in Part of C.S. Plot No. 1674 under the C.S. Khatian No. 369/395 under a registered Patta dated 25.5.1942 executed by the Ex-landlord i.e, the Sebait of the Debottar Estate at yearly rental and was living therein by making pucca constructions and it was recorded in the names of the Petitioners in Plot No. 3125 under the P.R.R.  2(e). In Civil Revision No.294 of 1966 the Petitioner Rebati Mohan Chowdhury stated  that he is a non-agricultural tenant in a Bhiti, measuring 23 X 20 cubic feet recorded in C.S. Plot No. 1674 under the C.S. Khatian No. 369/395 under a Patta from the Ex-landlord who was a Sebait of the Debottar Estate about 25 years age and was living by raising big structures and the P.R.R.  2(f). Plot No. 3122 under the P.R.R. Khatian No. 525 in her name and the Assistant Settlement Officer upheld the recording. but the Settlement Officer cancelled it in the Miscellaneous Case No.16 'of 1962, by an order dated 14.1.1963 and her Special Appeal No. 72 of 1963, renumbered as the Special Appeal No. 34 of 1964, was also dismissed by the Special Judge in a common judgment dated 31.12.1965. 

 5. From the Order Book it appears that on 14.1.1969 the Rules were discharged for non-prosecution without any order as to costs and records were dispatched on 26.3.1969. On 28.8.1970 Rules in Civil Revision Nos. 291, 292 and 293 were restored by vacating the order dated 14.1.1969. Reminder for lower Court's records was issued on 21.3.1972 and a Rule upon a 'restoration application for Civil Revision No. 294 of 1966 was issued in July, 1973, being the C.R. 840(R)/73 and on 20.5.1975, the C.R. 606(R)/73 was issued as to why the order dated 14.1.1969 should not be vacated. 

 On 18.3.1978 the C.R. 606(R)/75 was made absolute. On 25.11.1982 the heir of deceased Petitioner No.2 was substituted and the Order of abatement was set aside holding that the records need not be called for. On 8.12.1982 the Rules were heard in part and on 09.12.1982 an order was passed for issuance of urgent reminder for records. By Order dated 24.1.1983 it was found that no reminder was issued for the lower Court's records and an enquiry was ordered to be held into the matter by the Assistant Registrar also directing for issuance of a fresh reminder. On 25.1.1983 the 2nd reminder was issued and on 16.3.1983 the Deputy Registrar was directed to call for an explanation from the concerned officers why the lower Court's records of the Civil Revision Nos.290-295 of 1966 have not been transmitted as yet, inspite of several reminders. 

 On 10.5.1983, six files of lower Court's records have been received from the Subordinate Judge 3rd Court, Comilla and on examination found complete. 

 Plot No.1674 was recorded in the names of the persons who were ex-rent receivers and the rent-receiving interests have been acquired by the Province Of East Pakistan by the Notification dated 2nd April. 1956 and the property has vested in the province of East Pakistan free from encumbrances under Section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (2nd Amendment) Ordinance, 1960 (East Pakistan Ordinance No. XII of 1960). 

 In the C.S. Nos.395 and 369 one Radhika Mohan Chowdhury and others were the ex. Rent-receivers under Touzi No.203 in the Pargana "Shatrakhandai" of the Comilla Collectorate. There is no record in the office to show whether these ex. Rent-receivers were Sebait of any Debottar Estate. 

 The land stands recorded in Collector's Khatian No. 1 Under the provisions of the Ordinance No. XII of 1960, lands within the flat-I3atar are non-retainable properties by the Ex-rent receivers, cultivating raiyat or non-agricultural tenants. 

 It is not a fact that the P.R.R. Khatians in respect of alleged Plot numbers were opened in  the names of the Petitioners. One Khatians being No. 527 was opened in the names of the Petitioners in respect of some Plots and that was fraudulently recorded and it was subsequently cancelled by the Settlement Officer, Comilla in proceedings under Section 49 of the Act in the Miscellaneous Cases mentioned by the petitioners. The Rent-Roll, prepared in their names were also cancelled subsequently. No rent was realised from the Petitioners on the basis of that fictitious P.R.R. 

 The disputed lands are situated in a Bazar which is proved by some of the Dakhilas filed by the appellants themselves. Whether the disputed lands are Debottar lands or not should he decided by a competent Court. As the disputed lands are situated in a Bazar which is known as Ananda Bazar, the Settlement Officer is not wrong in allowing the assessment of compensation directing correction of records under Section 49 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 12. In the Counter Affidavits the Opposite Party stated that one Radhika Mohan Chowdhury and others were the ex. Rent-receivers of touzi No.203 under the Pargana 'Shatrakhandi' in the C.S. Plot No. 1674 under the C.S. Khatian No.395/369 and there is no record in the office of the Collactorate. Comilla to show whether these ex. Rent-receivers were Sebait or that the property was Debottar. Under the provisions of the Ordinance No. IX of 1960, the Sebait of the Debottar Property were to act as agent under the Provincial Government for management of such an estate and were liable to submit statements and accounts to the Collector or the District but no such Sebait as alleged in respect ()I' the properties involved ever approached the authority for appointment of agent. 

 13. On perusal of the records of the Courts below and the instant petitions, it appears that the alleged Pattas that were obtained by the Petitioners from the Sebaits of the Deities have neither been produced as exhibits nor furnished in support of their contentions. 

 15. The Petitioners next contended that the land in question is not situated within the periphery or a Bazar. In support of their contentions the Petitioners stated that a local enquiry was held on 18.7.1962 by one Mr. S. Ahmed. Charge Officer. Comilla who held that Ananda Bazar was more or less compact block intervened here and there by shops lying in the following  plots which might be taken to he within the periphery of Hat and recorded in the name of the Collector, viz. Plots No. 3170. 3167. 3157. 3156. 3144. 3132. 313-1. 3139. 3136 and 3130 and the Plots of the Petitioners were not included and they have been recorded in the names of the Petitioners. 

 In the Counter Affidavits, the Opposite Party has stated that the C.S. Plot No. 1674 has been classed as a Hat known as Ananda Bazar and during the S.A. operation, the C.S Plot No. 1674 has been split up in S.A. Plot Nos. 3119. 3120. 3121. 3122. 3123. 3124. 3125. 3126. 3127, 3128 and 3130 covered by Ananda Bazar within the Brahmanbaria Municipal Area. If the C.S. Plot No. 1674 has been split up in those S.A. plots and the C.S. Plot itself' was classed as Hat, namely. Ananda Bazar, it is really an exception that all the above plots have been acquired as Bazar except the Plots of the Petitioners which situate in between. The Petitioner Rai Shaheb himself stated that he is carrying on business in one part of the building and sub-let the other part to monthly tenants also for carrying on business. In the Affidavit-in-reply, the Petitioners stated nothing about this split up of the C.S. Plot No.1674 and acquisition or all other surroundings plots. If the C.S. Plot No. 1674 was recorded as a Hat. there is no reason why the splitting plots shall not be classed as Hat. 

 16. Admittedly, the S.A. record-of-rights have not been prepared in the names of the Petitioners. In paragraph 7 of the Counter-Affidavits, submitted in the C.R. No. 290 of 1966 the Opposite Party, Government stated that "it is not a fact that the P.R.R. Khatian No. 4527 with Plot No. 3129 was opened in his name. One Khatian No.527 was opened in his name with Plot No. 3128 which has been subsequently cancelled by the Settlement Officer. Comilla by a proceeding under Section 49 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in Miscellaneous Case No. 13 of 1962 by S.D.O. Comilla on 18.1.1963." 

 The Petitioners themselves stated in their applications that "they applied for certified copy of the said order which was not supplied to them by the Revenue Officer, but the same will be seen it' the records are called for." 

 The Records have been called liar and we do not find such a report in the records. 

 "49. The Commissioner or any officer Mg interior in rank lo that of a joint Deputy Commissioner of a district empowered in in this behalf of the Commissioner or a Settlement officer or empowered may on direct the revision of any Compensation Assessment-roll or any portion of such roll and assessment-roll or any portion of record-of-rights on the basis of which such roll has been prepared all any time during the preparation of such roll and may direct such revision on an application made within the three months from the date of final publication of such roll and may also of his own motion, direct such revision at any time before payment of compensation, but so as not to affect any order passed by the superior Revenue Authority wider Section 41 or Special Judge antler section 51 or under sub-section (4) of section 52 or under section 53: 

 This section authorities the commissioner or an) officer empowered by him to revise the compensation assessment-roll and the record-of-rights. Section 51 and 53 of the Act made Provisions for Appeal to the Special Judge providing also that the decision of the Special judge on such an Appeal shall notwithstanding anything contained in Section 52 he final. 

 Section 19 On the other hand, provides for preparation of record-of-rights, its draft publication disposal of objections relating to any entry or omission. 

 23. Considering the facts and circumstances of the Rules and materials on record and legal position. I find no merit in these Rules. 

 The impugned Judgment and Order dated 31.12.1965 passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Juke. 3rd Court, Comilla and the Special Judge dismissing the Special Appeal Nos. 30. 31. 33. 34. 35 and 36 of 1964 under Section 51 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and affirming the order of summary dismissals dated 18.1.1963 passed in Miscellaneous Case Nos. 12. 13. 14. 16. 17 and 56 of 1962 is hereby upheld. Send down the Lower Court's Records at once.

full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff-respondents' case is that the suit land, schedule, "Kha" land, part of schedule "Ka" land, appertains to Taluk Fela Nyamat Fakhrunnessa Estate, a Waqf Estate, of which Jalaluddin Ahmed Miah was Mutwali. Jalaluddin settled with Syed Ahmed Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos. 4-11 schedule "KA" land in rayati right for 5 years by a registered kabuliyat dated 19.5.44, Ext.2 Jalaluddin then sold out his superior interest therein in favour of defendants No. 12, Mvi. Abu Taher Mia (respondent No. 15 herein) by a registered patta dated 8.8.52, Ext. 3, As cultivation was unprofitable, Syed Ahmed surrendered his tenancy in "Ka" schedule land by a deed of Istafanama dated 12.3.53 in favour of defendant No. 12, Ext.4, and made over possession to him. Defendant No. 12 and defendant No.13 (respondent No.16 herein) then became joint Mutwallis of Waqf Estate. They orally settled the suit `Kha' schedule land at a rental of Tk. 4.50 in rayati right in Falgoon, 1360 B.S. with the plaintiff, who has been possessing the same since then. The lease was affirmed by a Rafanama dated 3.9.68 Ext.1 between the plaintiff and the aforesaid joint Mutwallis. The plaintiff came to know that the aforesaid Syed Ahmed sold the `Kha' schedule land to Sekandar Miah, Predecessor of defendants Nos. 1-3 (present appellants) by a registered kabala dated 12.3.59 Ext. A. It is the plaintiff's case that Syed Ahmed had no saleable interest in `Kha' schdule land on 12.3.59. Kabala Ext. A was false, fraudulent and without consideration. The plaintiff also came to know that defendants Nos.1-3 filed a miscellaneous case in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Feni, under section 1/3A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act against defendants Nos.4-14 for correction of record of rights. They lost the case in the trial Court but won the appeal before the District Judge, Noakhali, in Title Appeal No. 217 of 1969. The plaintiff was not made a party in the said proceeding. The suit was for a declaration of title to the 'Kha' schedule land and also for a declaration that the judgment in the aforesaid title appeal was not binding on the plaintiff. The plaintiff also pleaded adverse possession in the plaint. 

 4. The suit was decreed by the trial Court. Some of its findings, not reversed by the lower appellate Court and so noticed by the High Court Division, are that there was no assertion by the contesting defendants that Syed Ahmed did not surrender the 'Ka' schedule lands in favour of Abu Taher or that they were in possession of any land of the tenancy of Syed Ahmed. The Istafanama Ext.4 dated 12.3.53 was, therefore, accepted to be a document acted upon. As the defendants Kabala Ext. A was executed on 12.3.59 i.e. 6 years of Ext. 4, Sekandar Miah got nothing by it. The defendants failed to produce any rent receipts of Syed Ahmed or Sekander Miah to show their possession after Ext. 4. On the country, the plaintiff proved his possession of the suit; and by production of rent receipts Ext.5. The trial Court thoroughly discussed the evidence of P.Ws. and D.Ws. and gave a positive finding that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land. It also held that the appellate judgment in the miscellaneous case for correction of record of right was not binding on the plaintiff, he being not a party to the same. 

 10. Apart from reiterating those submissions, Mr. M.A. Rouf, learned Counsel for the defendants-appellants, submits further that the High Court Division acted illegally by relying on the Rafanama, Ext. 1 in the absence of proof of previous approval by the Administrator of waqfs. He submits that by making the Administrator of Waqfs a party to the suit, the requirement of approval is not fulfilled. The lower appellate Court critically analysed the oral evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 and the recital of Rafanama, Ext.1 and his finding as to onus of proof, title and possession is final and conclusive and cannot be interfered with in second appeal. The plaintiff, not being a recorded tenant in the khatian, was not a necessary party in the miscellaneous case for correction of record of rights and, therefore, he was not competent to challenge the appellate judgment. Mr. Rouf finally submits that Syed Ahmed did not surrender his tenancy and the Kabala Ext. A was a bonafide transaction for valuable consideration and that the heirs of Sekandar Miah, the present appellants, are still in possession of "kha" Schedule land. Besides, the heirs of the original plaintiff Ali Azam transferred the suit land in favour of present respondents Nos. 1 and 2 during the tendency of the second appeal before the High Court Division, which fact has not been considered by the High Court Division. 

 12. It is clear that the lower appellate Court did not discuss the evidence on record with regard to possession and, therefore, its abrupt finding that the plaintiff had failed to prove his possession was rightly interfered with the trial Court's finding on possession was arrived at after full discussion of the evidence on record. We also find that the plaintiff was rightly entitled to a declaration that the appellate judgment in the proceeding for correction of record of rights was not binding on him as he was not a party thereto. It is to late in the day to claim that Syed Ahmed did not surrender the tenancy because die appellants did not join issue with the plaintiff on this score. No Court has ever found that Syed Ahmed had a saleable interest in the suit land on 12.3.59, that Ext. A was a genuine transaction for valuable consideration and Sekandar Miah or the contesting defendants were ever in possession of the suit land. The sale of the suit land by the heirs of the original plaintiff during the tendency of the second appeal will be governed by the doctrine of lis pendens and there is not much to it.

vs.

full_judgment:
2. Plaintiff-respondent filed Title Suit No. 95 of 1965 in the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for declaration that the assessment of rent under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in respect of the Schedule land is without jurisdiction and in violation of the agreement between plaintiff and defendant Government. Plaintiff also prayed for refund of Tk. 95,000/- paid by the plaintiff as arrear rents etc. It was averred by the plaintiff that the suit land was acquired by the Government under the provisions of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 in favour of the plaintiff to whom delivery of possession was made in terms of a bilateral agreement between the Government and plaintiff. Government received the full amount of compensation paid to the owner with capitalized value from the plaintiff. Since then plaintiff has been carrying on production of textiles in the mills established thereon. Plaintiff claimed that the aforesaid agreement contained no term for payment or assessment of rent for the suit land. In 1962 plaintiff, however, received a notice from the Revenue Circle Officer as per Memo. No. (1207-E 80/58 dated 28.11.60 issued by the Board of Revenue. The Revenue Officer was alleged to have illegally assessed rents under section 50 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which, according to the plaintiff, was illegal as the lands have been delivered to him rent free and were, therefore, not liable to any assessment of rent.Land was shown rent free in the khatian. Plaintiff objected to the impugned rent under section 19(I) of the aforesaid-Act Mitch was disallowed. Plaintiff preferred appeal to the Special Judge who remanded the same resulting in only a small reduction of rent. It was also alleged that the Revenue authority gave retrospective effect to the order of the Board of Revenue by assessing arrear rents. 

 5. On the dismissal of aforesaid appeal by the learned Judges of the High Court Division the Government moved this Court and obtained Special leave to consider whether, in view of the provisions of section 22 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the learned Judges of the High Court Division were wrong in holding that the lands in question were not liable to assessment of rent. 

 The undersigned is directed to say that lands acquired both under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the E.B. (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 for Companies firms and Industrial concerns had hitherto been made over to the requiring bodies under a deed of transfer al lowing them to hold such land free of rent after realizing capitalized value of Government revenue or rent. As there are to be no fee simple or rent free lands now after state acquisition the question of extinguishing the free holds created in the lands acquired in the past and settled with the requiring bodies as referred to above with capitalization of the land revenue or rent and making such lands assessable to fair and equitable rent was considered by Government in consultation with their Law Officers. It has been decided that in view of the provisions of section 22 of the E.B.S.A. and T. Act, 1950, all land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the E.B. (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 for Companies, Firm and Industrial concerns and made over to the requiring bodies to hold free of rent after realizing capitalized value of Government Revenue or rent should be assessed to fair and just rent as provided in Sections 23 and 26 of the E.B.S.A. and T. Act, 1950. Necessary action any please be taken accordingly needless to say such persons Companies or Firms will receive in lieu a compensation as payable for rent free lands. 

 13. Thus, it appears that the Government direction as contained in the aforesaid letter dated 28th November 1960 to pay rent in respect of the lands acquired for and delivered to the respondent Mills is in accordance with law and Government is entitled to payment of rents already made in pursuance of the letter and also all future payments of rent to be made according to direction therein. No declaration that the suit land is not liable to be assessed under any provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 as being illegal, without jurisdiction, null and indoor any declaration that the plaintiff is not liable for the period, 1363-1368 B.S. can, therefore, be given. In this connection it may, however, be mentioned that no prayer was made in the plaint for declaring the letter dated 28th November 1960 as illegal, without jurisdiction, null and void, but even if such prayer was made by the plaintiff respondent Mills, this could not, (or reasons stated above, be granted, because directions for payment of rent as made therein are intra vires the provisions of law. Government has no power to grant exemption from payment of rent in respect of lands mentioned in section 22 of the Act, and if such exemption is granted it will be beyond its jurisdiction and power.

lawyer:
Rahima Khatun, Deputy Attorney-General with Md Ruhul Amin, Assistant Attorney-General—For the Appellants. 
Md Kamruzzaman Mia with Jahirul Haque Kislu, Advocates—For the Respondents.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh and others ------- Appellants
vs
Md Delwar Hossain and others ---------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Bhishmadev Chakrabortty, J: The defendants have preferred this appeal challenging the judgment and decree of the Joint District Judge, Court No.3, Dhaka passed on 7-10-2018 in Title Suit No.395 of 2017 decreeing the suit. 

 2. The plaintiffs brought the suit stating, inter alia, that the suit land measuring an area of 0.25 acres out of 0.79 acres appertaining to CS khatian 265, SA khatian 236 plot 208 corresponding to RS khatian 1566 plot 90 originally belonged to Durga Charan Mondal and Deebanishi Mondal in equal shares. During possession and enjoyment Deebanishi died unmarried and consequently Durga Charan became the owner in possession of the total land. Durga Charan died leaving behind his wife Shreemoti Sarala Betoya and daughter Tufani Mondal. For legal necessity Sarala Betoya sold the land to Skeikh Naymuddin Bapari through a registered kabala dated 27-8-1917 and accordingly SA record his been prepared in his name. Naymuddin Baperi through another registered kabala dated 3-2-1941 sold it to Sheikh Naymuddin Nambari son of Sheikh Hanif and handed over possession thereof. Accordingly RS record has been prepared in the name of Nambari as per his share. Naymuddin Nambari died leaving behind his son Abdul Hamid, father of the plaintiffs. Hamid died on 21-5-2007 leaving behind the plaintiffs as heirs and successors. Due to the ailment before death, Abdul Hamid failed to take any information about the recent record of rights and consequently it has been recorded in the name of the Bhawal Court of Wards in City Jorip khatian 680 for 0.25 acres. The plaintiffs came to learn about the said wrong record of rights on 20-9-2017 and instituted the suit for declaration of title and that the City Survey khatian 680 so prepared is erroneous. 

 3. The plaintiffs filed the suit on 21-11-2017 and the notices were issued upon the defendants on that day and served subsequently but they did not appear to contest it. Thereafter, the Court fixed the date to 1-3-2022 and 18-3-2008 for ex-parte hearing. The plaintiff amended the plaint on 18-4-2018 and finally the Joint District Judge on 5-6-2018, 1-7-2018 and 2-8-2018 examined witnesses of the plaintiffs, exhibited documents and passed the ex-parte judgment on 7-10-2018 decreeing the suit, giving rise to this appeal by the Government. 

 4. Ms. Rahima Khatun, learned Deputy Attorney-General takes us through the materials on record. In course of argument she has filed an application for accepting the additional grounds. She relied on the grounds taken therein and submits that no notices were served upon the defendants. The plaintiffs without serving any notice upon them obtained the ex-parte decree by practising fraud and, as such, the same would be set-aside. She then submits that the Joint District Judge failed to consider that City Jorip plot 22545 has been created from CS plots 212 and 208, and CS plot 212 was in CS khatians 48, 51 and 54 which were recorded in the name of Kumar Gobinda Narayan Roy Chowdhury on behalf of the Court of Wards and thereby arrived at an erroneous decision in decreeing the suit. She further submits that in CS khatian the suit land was recorded as Government's property. The plaintiffs have claimed the land by way of purchase without producing the original deeds. Secondary evidence is to be proved by the production of original copy which is not done here and, as such, the Joint District Judge erred in law putting reliance on those. She further submits that the judgment is non speaking and that mere record of rights prepared earlier in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs does not create any right in their favour. She refers to the case of Laxmibai vs Keshrimal Jain, AIR (1995) 178; Bangladesh vs Abdul Wadud and others, 25 DLR (SC) 90 and Sova Rani Guha-alias Soya Rani Gupta vs Abdul Awal Mia and others, 1994 BLD (AD) 257 = 47 DLR (AD) 45 and submits that the plaintiffs are to prove that the summonses were served upon the defendants before fixing its date for ex-parte hearing. She finally submits that the Court did not frame issues before passing the decree as were required by the law. Under the aforesaid premises, the judgment and ex-parte decree passed by the learned Joint District Judge would be set-aside. 

 5. Mr Md Kamruzzaman Mia, learned Advocate for the respondents submits that although Order V, rule 19B of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) provides for simultaneous service of summons through post but the best service is through process server. Here the process server served summonses upon the appellants and declarations to that effect were made at the bottom of the processes which prove services as good. He then submits that under Order VIII, rule 1 (amended provision in 2012) of the Code, the defendants are to file written statement in a suit within 30 working days from the date of service of summonses and time so prescribed may be extended for 60 days under proviso to sub-rule l of rule 1 of Order VIII of the Code. If the defendants do not submit written statement as per law, the Court shall proceed with ex-parte hearing of the suit. The provisions of the aforesaid Rule and Order are mandatory. He then submits that in this suit the notices were served upon the defendants but they did not appear before the Court to file written statement and consequently the trial Court had no other alternative but to proceed with the suit for ex-parte disposal. Mr Mia further submits that issues are to be framed on pleadings and as per provisions of Order XIV, rule 1 sub-rule 4, issues are of two types-(i) issues of fact and (ii) issues of law. Since the defendants did not appear before the Court, therefore, the question of framing issues does not arise. He takes us through the impugned judgment and submits that although the trial Court did not discuss the evidence but it has considered the oral and documentary evidence of the plaintiffs and being satisfied passed the ex-parte judgment which is very well speaking. He finally submits that the plaintiffs by the documents and oral evidence succeeded in proving the chain of their claim. There could be no reason to record the names of the defendants in the City Survey khatian and, as such, they did not dare to come before the Court to oppose the claim of the plaintiffs. The judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, therefore, would be affirmed and the appeal be dismissed. 

 6. We have considered the submissions of both the sides and gone through the materials on record. In course of hearing, the appellants have filed an application in this Court for taking additional grounds. They have brought allegation and took grounds that the plaintiffs suppressed the summonses and by practicing fraud upon the Court obtained the ex-parte decree. On perusal of the record, we find that the summonses to be sent through process server and registered post with acknowledgement due were submitted in the Court at the time of filing of the suit and those were sent to the defendants on 21-11-2017. The Court found, as it appears in the order dated 4-2-2018, that the summonses were duly served upon the defendants and fixed its next date to 1-3-2018 for submitting written statement. The defendant did not appear and submit written statement on that day and consequently the Court fixed its next date to 18-3-2018 for submitting written statement failing which it would be disposed of ex-parte. The defendant neither appeared nor filed written statement on 18-3-2018 and the next date of the suit was fixed to 18-4-2018 for ex-parte hearing. On that day the plaintiff amended the plaint. Subsequently, on 5-6-2018, 1-7-2018 and 2-8-2018 the plaintiffs examined 2 (two) witnesses and finally the Court passed the ex-parte judgment on 7-10-2018. Where the defendants did not appear in the suit despite service of notices upon them, the Court cannot sit idle for indefinite period. It has to proceed with the ex-parte disposed of the suit with the time prescribed under Order VIII, rule 1 of the Code as amend in 2012. 

 7. On perusal of the processes lying with the record, we find that the process server made declarations in the prescribed column showing that the summonses were served on 15-1-2018 upon the appellants. The summonses contain the signatures and seals of defendant's office. Although, law provides for simultaneous service of summons under rule 19B of Order V of the Code but if any one of the mode of service is found to be satisfactory, the Court may accept the service as good. In the record, we do not find any acknowledgement due returned but in the case of Mrs. Shamsun Nahar Begum vs Salauddin Ahmed & others, 4 MLR (AD) 405 = 4 BLC (AD) 285 and Abdur Rob Mollah vs Shahabuddin Ahmed and others, 12 BLC (AD) 118 it has been held that if Acknowledgement Due is not returned within 30 days, the summons should be treated as served. Learned Deputy Attorney-General although took an additional ground of non service of summonses upon the appellants and submits that the plaintiffs by committing fraud upon the Court showed that summonses served and obtained the ex-parte decree but failed to show that those were not duly served. From the record, we find that those were duly served upon the defendants [reliance placed on in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Sunil Kumar Khan, 10 BLC (AD) 153]. 

 8. Now the question arises whether the ex-parte decree passed by the trial Court can be maintained due to its briefness. In the case of Alfu Miah and others vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others, 45 DLR (AD) 112 it has been held — 

 "The Court is not required to give an elaborate judgment. How far a judgment passed in an ex-parte proceeding is to comply with the provisions of Order XX, rule 4(1) of the Code will depend on facts of each case. A judgment in ex-parte cases shall however state specifically and explicitly which of the reliefs are granted and against which of the defendants. No ex-parte decree would be set-aside for its briefness when the defendant fails to bring home either of the two grounds on which such a decree can be set-aside." 

 11. Learned Deputy Attorney-General in her additional grounds asserted that City Survey plot 22545 has come from CS plots 212 and 208. But on perusal of the CS, RS and City Survey sketch maps (Exhibit 11 series), we find that in CS and RS map CS plot No. 212 is far away from CS plot 208. Although the Government claims that CS khatian of the suit land was recorded in the name of Kumar Gabindo Narayan Ray Chowdhury on behalf Court of Wards, but the plaintiffs claimed by way of gradual purchase from CS recorded tenant Durga Charan's heirs and the exhibited documents support it. On perusal of the evidence on record and the maps, we find nothing in favour of the Government except the City Jorip khatian recorded in their name but it has no foundation. The oral evidence of two plaintiffs' witnesses are corroborative and prove their possession over the suit land. We do not find any reason to send the case on remand to the trial Court giving an undue advantage to the appellants. Although this is an ex-parte decree but the plaintiffs successfully proved their title and possession over the suit land. The trial Court correctly decreed the suit. 

 12. Therefore, we find no merit in this appeal. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree passed by the Joint District Judge, Court No.3, Dhaka in Title Suit No.395 of 2017 is hereby affirmed. 

 Communicate the judgment and send down the lower Court records.

Khatian No.199, Jagmohan Namadash and Harimohan Namadash had one ana share each. Said Jagamohan Namodash died leaving 2 sons Motiram and Sutiram who inherited 7.08 

 acres of land in the suit schedule property. Sutiram died leaving 2 sons Jogesh and Umesh, predecessor of defendant Nos.1 and 2-4 respectively. MotiraM died leaving 2 daughters plaintiff No.1 Sumitra and Niroda, mother of defendant Nos.5 and 6. The Plaintiff No.1 inherited 1.891/2 acres of land with limited right. Umesh transferred 1.89 acres of larid from his share to Sudangsho, Rakhal, Probat and others. Umesh died leaving defendant Nos.2-4. Who left the country giving their share to defendant No.1 and since then defendant No.1 is in possession of that share also. S.A. record correctly prepared in the name of the father of this defendant. As Motiram used to live in his father-in-law's house, Jagomohan did not give any property to Motiram. Plaintiff No.1 has been living in the village Gujiram within Thana Trishal. It has been further contended that original deed of gift was in the custody of defendant No.1. The defendant No.1 came to Mymensingh for filing written statement and stayed at Usha Boarding aild for safety kept the original deed of gift in Custody of the Manager of Usha Boarding.  8. Mr. S. N. Goswami, the learned Advocate on the other hand by filing affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of the opposite party No.2 oppose the Rule and submits that the Court of appeal below after considering and assessing the evidence on record independently, rightly and Judiciously reserved the judgment and decree of the trial Court in compliance with Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate also submits that the

 9. Heard the learned Advocates, perused the revisional application, counter affidavit, judgments of both the Courts below, lower Court's record and the provisions of law. 

 It is apparent that the findings of the trial Court is based on assumption without any plausible reason. On the other hand the e appeal Court below after assessing the evidence on record independently arrived at a finding with cogent reasons. 

 15. It is apparent from the evidence on record that the alleged deed of gift dated 16.01.1917 was not marked and exhibited in the suit. Further more, the learned Subordinate Judge, as a last Court of fact recorded his suspicion relating to existence of the original deed of gift and even after assessing photocopy of the said deed of gift arrived at a finding that the photocopy is manufactured for the purpose of the suit. If the deed of gift is not proved, then question of ROR in the name of the predecessor of the defendant does not arise. On perusal of both the judgment passed by the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below it appears that the Court of appeal below after assessing the evidence on record independently reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court in compliance of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code 

 " It is well settled Principle of law that the High Court in its revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 cannot interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the Court below and re-appreciate the evidence and interfere with the finding unless it is found that the findings recorded by the lower Court are perverse or there has been non-application of mind.
