13. It also appears that the pre-emptor appellant claimed that though he separated the “Jama” of the land in question but such separation has not been made following the procedures as detailed in section 117(1)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (SAT Act). On examination of section 117 of the SAT Act it appears that the same has laid down the procedure for subdivision of joint tenancy stating ‘No mutation can be made or no Jama/holding can be separated without subdivision of the holding and the revenue officer cannot initiate the procedure of such subdivision without an application of the person who wants his holding to be separated’. Thus there is no other way by which mutation or separation of the “Jama” can be made without subdivision of holding under section 117 of the SAT Act. In the present case the appellant admitted that he applied to the Assistant Commissioner (Land) for separation of “Jama” of his exchanged land and the concerned officer subdivided/separated the holding following the prescribed procedures of law. Once the Jama is separated, at the risk and benefit of a person, he cannot now say that the separation was not done following the procedure laid down in section 117(1)(c) of the SAT Act. In this respect the principle is he who takes advantage of his own act/action cannot subsequently claim that such act/action was not done in accordance with law as he is estopped from claiming so under section 115 of the Evidence Act. Moreover, the appellant cannot take the plea of non-service of notice upon the other party once he has taken benefit of such mutation or separation of “Jama”.Such plea, if any, can be taken only by the party affected by it or to whose disadvantage the same has been obtained and upon whom the notice was required to be served. But not the person at whose prayer separation has been made and who takes the benefit of such separation. Apart from this aspect it appears from the contention of the pre-emptee respondent that the property was mutated in the name of Rowshan Jahan Malek and then it has been again mutated in the name of the pre-emptor vide Mutation Case No. 32/1987-88 (Exhibit “Ka”) which has been proved by the Kanungo of the land office of Manikganj Sadar(OPW 2) on the basis of SA record after the pre-emptor exchanged the same and got possession along with the houses situated thereon and as such the pre-emptee contended that the pre-emptor thus falls within the purview of section 24(11)(a) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949(NAT Act). 

 14. In the present case, admittedly the pre-emptor became a co-sharer in the case land not by purchase but by exchange. So his existing interest in the case jote has accrued otherwise than by purchase and as such he falls within the prohibition of section 24(11)(a) of the NAT Act wherein it has been provided that: “Nothing in this section shall apply to (a) a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose existing interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase.” Meaning it has protected such transfer if the existing interest of such co-sharer claimant accrues otherwise than by purchase. This provision clearly enumerates the cases and classes of transfer which are not affected by this section 24 and on which no right of pre-emption arises under this Act. Again this Division in the case of SM Bashiruddin Vs. Z. Islam Chowdhury (35 DLR (AD) 230) protected a transfer to a co- sharer in the tenancy from pre-emption holding that “Transfer of a portion of share of the non agricultural land to a stranger opens right of pre-emption to one or more co-sharer tenants of such land but when a portion or share of such land is transferred to a co-sharer in the tenancy, this is protected.” 

 15. However, in respect of the terms “Co-sharer in land” and “Co-sharer in holding” it is necessary to mention that under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act (NAT Act) the legislature used the term ‘land‘ saying ‘one or more co-sharer tenants of such “land” may within 4 (four) months apply to the Court for pre-emption’. Whereas under section 96 of the SAT Act the term “holding” has been used saying ‘a co-sharer tenant in the holding by inheritance may apply for pre-emption’. The distinctive feature in these two provisions of law is clearly in respect of the term ‘co-sharer tenant of such land’ in one and ‘co-sharer tenant in holding’ in the other. 

 The term ‘holding’ has been defined in section 2(13) of the SAT Act in following terms: “holding means a parcel or parcels of land or an undivided share thereof, held by a raiyat or an under-raiyot and forming the subject of a separate tenancy”. 

 16. Whereas the term ‘non-agricultural land’ has been defined in section 2(4) of the NAT Act, in general terms saying “Non-agricultural land means land which is used for the purpose not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for purpose not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purpose or not,” but it does not include homestead/land as described in clauses, a, b and c of the said provision. But, the term ‘non-agricultural land’, as has been used in section 24 of the NAT Act, has not been interpreted elsewhere. In section 24(1) of the NAT Act the term “Non Agricultural land” has been used, not “Non Agricultural Tenancy”. This has been done by the legislature intentionally only to keep the number of pre-emptors limited to the co-sharers in the land, so that the land on pre-emption may not become unfit for use. 

 The legislature has consciously used the distinctive term “non agricultural land” not “tenancy”. A Non Agricultural tenancy may be owned and possessed separately by different owners by constructing their respective houses registering as separate holdings under the Municipal/Pourashouva Act but “Jama” of the tenancy, as khatian, remaining undivided with liability of paying rents jointly. That means there remains nothing common amongst the co-sharer tenants excepting their joint liability of paying rents, and thereby they cease to be co-sharers for all practical purpose thereby debarring all other co-sharers from pre-empting the transfer to a stranger. By using the expression “Non Agricultural land” the legislature has recognized the same as an entity or unit separate from “Non Agricultural tenancy”. 

 Thus, it is clear that the right of pre-emption under section 24 of the NAT Act has been provided only to the co-sharer tenants in the land. But in the present case “Jama” of the case land being separated by Rowshan Jahan Malek, earlier to her exchange with the pre-emptor and then the pre-emptor himself again having separated his “jama” after the exchange, he or his predecessor is no more a co-sharer in the land and as such though he may be a co-sharer in the tenancy, the right of pre-emption did not accrue to him and as such his application for pre-emption cannot succeed. Again in the case of Aminullah vs. Serajul Huq and others, reported in 65 DLR (AD) 82 it has been held: “the word ‘one or more co-sharer tenants of such land’ occurring in section 24 of the Act means a co-sharer in the ‘plot not the ‘holding’ as mentioned in section 96 of the Act” 

 17. On the other hand, though the term “khatian” has not been defined in the statute but it generally means a document prepared by the government which contains ‘complete information regarding the land or property’. In the “Glossary of Certain Settlement and Vernacular Terms” in common use in the sub-continent and well known in the Bengal Tenancy Act, the word ‘khatian’ has been described as under: 

 21. Now, it is necessary to see who is a “co-sharer tenant of land” and what has been meant by “co-sharer tenant in the holding”. Generally co-sharer means joint owners (in Bengali what is called “শরিক বা শরিক প্রজা”).When the term is used in respect of property it means-‘a person who shares his right, title and interest with some other person(s) in a holding or plot or in an undivided share thereof. Land in connection with section 24 of the NAT Act, appears to be a plot or a parcel of plots owned by two or more co-sharers jointly. So, in order to exercise the right of pre-emption under the aforesaid Act, the person so claiming must be a co-sharer in an undivided plot or parcel thereof. Side by side it is also to be seen whether such co-sharership comes to an end, if so, how? In 54 DLR 181 case it has been observed that ‘the word land as used in section 24 of NAT Act should not mean the quantum of land in one plot only. As the word co-sharer always implies the existence of more than one person jointly owning, similarly, such joint ownership may be in respect of land in one plot or in several plots. The land is always recorded under a holding for the purpose of revenue record and payment of rents. This holding may be joint or of several persons. The holding of any land could only be sub divided and rents distributed in accordance with the procedure spelt out under section 117 of the SAT Act which will affect the land appertaining to such holding. A holding is popularly known as “Khatian” comprising of such land. The concept of co-sharer cannot be conceived independent of any holding or tenancy. If the holding is recorded in the name of more than one person then each of such person or their successors in interests becomes co-sharers to each other in such land. Such co-sharer will be deemed to continue as such co-owner in both holding as well as in land so long the holding will continue to be joint. Contrary to such proposition, that sub-division of such holding will not affect the land in any way is fallacious in as much as sub-division of the holding and creation of new plot in subsequent survey or by mutation by the acts of parties, the previous co-sharer in the holding and/or the land cannot be deemed to still continue as such co-sharer’. 

 24. The learned Advocate for the pre-emptor appellant contended that the principles laid down in the 54 DLR 181 and 55 DLR 214caseshave been overruled by the case reported in 62 DLR (AD) 250. On perusal of all the decisions it appears that in 54 DLR 181case pre-emption was sought for where the land was partitioned earlier by final decree passed in a partition suit which terminated the co-ownership in such land till subdivision of rents takes place. And the principle laid down in the 55 DLR 214 case relates to separation of jama or sub-division of a holding or tenancy made under section 117(1)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and on such separation the co-sharership in such land came to an end. Whereas the moot question in 62 DLR (AD) 250case was whether a final decree in a partition suit or a registered partition deed puts an end to the co-sharership in the land so partitioned or such co-sharership continues till separation of the Jama. This Division in the aforesaid case held that “a final decree in a partition suit or a registered deed of partition puts an end to co-sharership extinguishing his right of pre-emption.” In the said case no question as to whether co-sharership in a land comes to an end by mere separation of the Jama/mutation without a decree in partition suit or by a registered partition deed was raised. So, the case reported in 62 DLR (AD) 250has not overruled the principle laid down in the case reported in 54 DLR. Rather that has dealt with only to the extent that a decree in partition suit or a registered partition deed is enough to separate the co-sharership in the land. But the principle laid down in the 55 DLR 114case has not been overruled apparently by the aforesaid decision of 62 DLR. In the case of Alfazuddin Ahmed Vs. Abdur Rahman 55 DLR (AD) 108, this Division held that ‘…………… because of the decree in the partition suit as there has been ceasing of the co-sharership of the parties and that the pre-emptors got the Jama of the khatian split up in respect of their land and got a separate khatian/Jama opened in their names before the transfer in question to the pre-emptee and consequent thereupon they ceased to be the co-sharers in the case khatian.’ From the above finding it can be easily concluded that by partition decree or partition deed co-sharership ceases but the finality of such ceasing occurs by splitting up of the Jama/khatian. Accordingly, it cannot be said that co-sharership does not cease by mere separation of the Jama/khatian by mutation, which in the present case has already been done firstly by Rowshan Jahan Malek, the predecessor of the pre-emptor appellant and subsequently by the pre-emptor-appellant himself. Thus the pre-emptor appellant having got the already separated property by exchange cannot be said to be a co-sharer in the property in question. Moreover, the facts of the present case being quite distinguishable from those of the 62 DLR (AD) 250case, the pre-emptor cannot take advantage of the said decision.

4. In the writ petition, it was stated, inter alia, that Moqbul Ahmed, predecessor-in-interest of writ-petitioner No.1 filed an application before the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Tejgaon. Circle, (writ-respondent No.5) for mutating his name in respect of 5.17 acres of land of S.A. plot Nos.1353, 1354, 1355, 1356, 1357, 1358, and 1365 of Mouza Tejkunipara within Police Station-Tejgaon, Dhaka on the basis of decree obtained in Title Suit No. 280 of 1970 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka; the application was allowed, but instead of 5.17 acres; 8.70 acres of land of S.A. khatian No.605 was mutated including the land of plot Nos.1370, 1377, 1383, 1384 and 1385 in respect of which Moqbul Ahmed had no claim. Writ-respondent No.6 (there are two respondent No.6, so, in order to clear the confusion they are described by name as well), Abdus Sattar Chowdhury, filed an appeal against the said order of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Tejgaon, before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka, (writ-respondent No.4), being Miscellaneous Appeal No.11 of 1990, who by his order dated 08.03.1994 allowed the appeal and sent Case No.19 of 1987 back on remand to the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Tejgaon Circle, Dhaka for reconsideration and decision. The predecessor-in-interest of petitioner No.1, late Moqbul Ahmed, moved the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka Division, Dhaka against the said order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) vide Miscellaneous Appeal No.62 of 1994 in which the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) dated 08.03.1994 was confirmed by order dated 05.11.1994. Writ-respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar Chowdhury, filed Miscellaneous Case No.355 of 1968 in the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka under section 143A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (the Act) impleading Peerzada Abul Quashem. Md. Hasnain Siddiqui and Satinath Bandapaddhaya as opposite parties for correction of record in respect of the same plots of land as mentioned hereinbefore. This was a fraudulent Endeavour behind the back of said Moqbul Ahmed and others. The miscellaneous case was twice rejected, but somehow Abdus Sattar Chowdhury managed to have the case decided in his favour beyond the knowledge of Moqbul Ahmed and others. Moqbul Ahmed filed an appeal before the Land Appeal Board against the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka, being No. 3-85/94(Appeal)- Dhaka; on hearing the appeal, the Chairman of the Land Appeal Board, Mr. Md. Enamul Huq, by order dated the 29th day of August, 1995 allowed the same and restored the order of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) dated 08.10.1989. Against the said order of the Chairman, Land Appeal Board, writ-respondent No. 6, Abdus Sattar Chowdhury, filed a review application before the Land Appeal Board which was registered as Case No. 3-108/95(Review)-Dhaka. The case was disposed of by the Full Board of the Land Appeal Board (hereinafter referred to as the Full Board) comprising of the Chairman and two other members by order dated the 9th day of December, 2003; the Full Board set aside the order dated 08.10.19879 passed by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) in Case No.19 of 1987 and at the same time, maintained the mutation of 7 S.A. plots being Nos. 1353, 1354, 1355, 1356, 1357, 1358 and 1365 measuring an area of 5.17 acres in the name of Moqbul Ahmed (the father of writ-petitioner No.1) and also maintained the mutation of 12 S.A. plots being Nos.1353, 1354, 1355, 1356, 1357, 1358, 1365, 1370, 1377, 1383, 1384 and 1385 in the name of Abdus Sattar. And thus, the Full Board modified the order dated 29.08.1995 passed by the: Chairman, Land Appeal Board in Case No.3-85/94(Appeal)-Dhaka; hence the writ-petitioners filed the writ petition. 

 5. Md. Mintu Chowdhury, leave petitioner, got himself added in the writ petition as respondent No.6 (as stated in the leave petition as well as in the impugned judgment and order) and contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia, that it was not correct that Moqbul Ahmed, predecessor-in-interest of writ-petitioner No.1 filed application  before the Assistant Commissioner(Land), Tejgaon Circle, Dhaka for mutating his name in respect of 5.17 acres of land of S.A. plot Nos.1353, 1354, 1355, 11356, 1357, 1358 and 1365 of Mouza Tejkunipara on the basis of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 280 of 1970. The aforesaid application was filed by Moqbul Ahmed for mutation of his name in respect of the concerned R.S. record of the said moan on the basis of the decree passed in the said title suit. the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Tejgaon Circle, Dhaka allowed the mutation illegally in respect of S.A. record which is contrary to decree of Title Suit No. 280 of 1970. On the basis of the decree in respect of R. S. khatians and R.S. plots, there cannot be mutation in respect of S.A. khatian and S.A. plots unless and until the concerned decree in respect of R.S. record was amended according to law. Moreso, the writ-petitioners did not claim that the said R.S. plots arc the corresponding S.A. plots. So the order of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) was set aside by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka vide Order dated 08.03.1994 in Miscellaneous Appeal No.11 of 1990 which was subsequently affirmed by the Additional Divisional Commissioner by order dated 05.11.1994 and then, by the Full Board in Review Case No.3-85/94 vide Order dated 09.12.2003. The disputed and the important question of fact cannot be resolved in writ jurisdiction. It is not correct that filing of Miscellaneous Case No.355 of 1968 by writ-respondent No. 6, Abdus Sattar, was a fraudulent endeavor behind the back of Moqbul. Ahmed and others and he managed to have the case decided in his favour. Miscellaneous Case No.355 of 1968 was filed in the then First Court of Munsif, Dhaka under section 143(sic, it should be 143A) of the Act for correction of record. After due service of notices of the miscellaneous case on the opposite parties, the same was decided in favour of Abdus Sattar. There was nothing for Moqbul Ahmed "to be constrained" with the result of Miscellaneous Case No. 355 of 1968 as he instituted Title Suit 280 of 1970 for correction of R.S. record and not S.A. record and obtained the decree in his favour in respect of 7 R.S. plots being Nos.1353, 1354, 1355, 1356, 1357, 1358 I and 1365 measuring 5.17 acres. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) rightly decided Miscellaneous Appeal No.64 of 1994 which was confirmed   by the Additional Divisional: Commissioner by Order dated 05.11.1994 and the Full Board as mentioned hereinbefore. The Land Appeal Board, on an erroneous view of the facts and law, affirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) dated 05.10.1989 and as such, the Full Board, on review, rectified the mistake in Review Case No.3-108/95(Review-Dhaka) by order dated 09.12.2003. Since the decree passed in Title Suit No.280 of 1970 is on the basis of A.S. record, as prayed for in the plaint of the suit, the Full Board had to sustain mutation of the aforesaid 7 R.S. plots measuring 5.17 acres in the name of Moqbul Ahmed. Simultaneously the Full Board had no other alternative but to sustain mutation in the name of Abdus Sattar Chowdhury in respect of 12 S.A. plots measuring 8.70 acres of land on the basis of the "judgment and decree" passed by the learned Munsif, First Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 355 of 1968 filed by him and that position was ultimately upheld by the Full Board in the review case. Unless and until the decree of Title Suit No. 280 of 1970 is amended by the proper Court in proper forum, no other Court or authority would be able to change it or give contrary decision in that respect. The Full Board rightly sustained mutation in the name of Abdus Sattar Chowdhury in respect of 12 S.A. plots as mentioned earlier as well as the mutation in respect of R.S. plots measuring 5.17 acres of land in the name of Moqbul Ahmed on the basis of decree of the civil Court. The order of the Full Board dated 09.12.2003 is not inconsistent and contradictory as alleged. The sustenance of mutation in the name of writ-respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar, in respect of 12 S.A. plots measuring 8.17 acres of land is correct and that has nothing to do with the mutation of 7 R.S. plots measuring 5.17 acres of land in the name of Moqbul Ahmed. The writ-petitioners never claimed that these are corresponding plots and as such, they are not entitled to get any relief in the writ petition on such controversial and disputed facts. It is not correct that the Full Board "has suffered from confusion in respect of R.S. plots, and S.A. plots." The order of the Full Board in Review Case No. 3-108/95(Review-Dhaka) being perfect and legal, does not warrant any interference. The writ-petitioners are to the satisfied with the decree of the civil Court passed in Title Suit No.280 of 1970 and therefore, they had nothing to be aggrieved unless and until the said decree is amended and corrected in an appropriate forum. 

 6. The writ-petitioners filed an affidavit-in-reply to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by added respondent No.6, Md. Mintu Chowdhury (leave petitioner herein) stating, inter alia, that it is false to say that the respondent is the absolute owner of the property in question on the basis of oral gift dated 14.03.2002 and possession of the said property was handed over to him. At no point of time, the father of added respondent No.6 was in possession of the property and as such, the question handing over the possession of the same to him does not arise. The land of C.S. plot No.560/609 covering an area of 37.66 acres of land appertaining to C.S. khatian No.211 of mouza Tejkunipara, District-Dhaka originally belonged to Satinath Bandapaddya alias Sagor Babu; for arrear of rents the said land was put to auction sale and one Promode Bala Devi purchased the same who, while in possession transferred 5.58 acres of land to Jinnatun Nessa and Kashem Ali by registered sale deed dated 16.05.1941 and delivered possession thereof to them. Jinnatun Nessa died leaving behind son Kashem Ali and daughter-Joynab Bibi and they, by two kabalas dated 25.07.1958 and 09.08.1958 respectively, transferred their shares to Syed Ahmed, Moqbul Ahmed and Khurshid Jahan (the predecessors of the writ-petitioners), but due to mistake, the said lands along with other lands were recorded in S.A. khatian in the name of Satinath Bandopaddya. The predecessors of the writ-petitioners filed Miscellaneous Case No.110 of 1969 for correction of the record. Respondent, No. 6, Abdus Sattar Chowdhury, claiming himself to be the owner of 8.70 acres of land of the aforesaid C.S. plot Nos.560/669 on the basis of Amalnama dated the 18th Sraban, 1350 B.S., alleged to have been executed by Satinath Bandapaddya filed Miscellaneous Case No.355 of 1968 impleading Peerzada Abdul Kashem and Mohammad Hossain Siddiqui as opposite party Nos.1 and 2 for correction of the record of right alleging that the same was wrongly prepared in their names. By order No.1, the Circle Officer (Revenue) was asked to enquire into the matter and submit report within 15 days. The predecessors of the writ-petitioners on coming to know about the said miscellaneous case filed an application for addition of party which was kept with the record. Satinath Bandopaddya was added in the miscellaneous case as opposite party No.3 by order dated 16.08.1969. Meanwhile Circle Officer Revenue, after holding local enquiry, submitted his report on 07.07.1969. The miscellaneous case was taken up for ex-parte hearing and Abdus Sattar i.e. writ-respondent No. 6 was examined and the Court, on the basis of the finding of the inquiry report, held that the miscellaneous case was not maintainable and accordingly, dismissed the said case by order dated 01.08.1970. The predecessors of the writ-petitioners did not proceed with Miscellaneous Case No. 110 of 1969 on the expectation that in view of the report of the Circle Officer (Revenue), Tejgaon, Dhaka, the khatian in respect of the property in question would the corrected. But subsequently, respondent No. 6, Abdus Sattar, managed to obtain an order of restoration of the said miscellaneous case and got the same heard ex-parte on 02.09.1970. The predecessors of the writ-petitioners on coming to know about the aforesaid ex-parte order which created cloud over their right, title and interest in respect of the said land, filed Title Suit No.280 of 1970 in the First Court of Subordinate. Judge, Dhaka impleading respondent No. 6, Abdus Sattar as defendant No.1, alleging practicing of fraud upon the Court in obtaining the said ex-parte order. In the plaint, it was stated that cause of action of the suit arose on the date when the plaintiffs 1 came to know about the order directing the entry of the name of defendant No. 1 in the khatian. As the Circle Officer (Revenue), Dhaka in his report dated 07.07.1969 identified the plots as R.S. plots, the predecessors of the writ-petitioners also described the suit land with 1 reference to R.S. khatian and R.S. plot. In spite of service of notices of the suit upon the defendants including respondent; No.6, Abdus Sattar, none appeared and consequently, the suit was decreed ex-parte declaring the right, title, interest of the predecessor of the writ-petitioners in respect of 5.58 acres of land of C.S. plot Nos.560/669. Thereafter, the predecessors of the writ-petitioners by filing Miscellaneous Case No. 9 of 1977-78 mutated their names in S.A. plot Nos. 1353, 1354, 1355, 1356, 1357, 1358 and 1365 and have been in possession thereof on payment of taxes regularly to the Government. Subsequently, Moqbul Ahmed, Syed Ahmed and Khurshid Jahan, while in possession, sold 5(five) acres of land to different persons including writ-petitioner Nos.2 and 3 and they have been in possession thereof by mutating their names and paying rents. The purchasers also constructed residential building on their purchased land. Thereafter, in 1987, respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar, filed application before the Circle Officer (Revenue), Tejgaon, Dhaka impleading Peerzada Abul Hashem and Hasan Siddiqui as opposite parties for correction of records as per court's judgment. Upon such application, Miscellaneous Case No.19 of 1987 was started which was disposed of ex-parte on 09.01.1988 by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) cancelling the order passed in Mutation Case Nos.12277/79-80, 12278/79-80, 12279/79-80, 12280/79-80, 12290/79-80, 12291/79-80, 12292/79-80, 12298/79-80, 4996/80-81, 8846/80-81, 8478/80-81, 9224/80-81, 2414/80-81, 2539/82, 2538/83, 4606/83, 11501/84, 706/86, 707/86, 6681/84, 6688/84, 7988/82, 10352/82, 11032/82, 3228/82 and 9/77-78. Subsequently the writ-petitioners and others who are purchasers from Moqbul Ahmed and others filed application for reviewing the order dated 09.01.1988 passed by the Assistant Commissioner (Land). Subsequent to the decision of the Full Board, respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar, again filed an application for mutation of his name. The application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No.42 of 2006. Writ-petitioner No.2 and 37 others who are purchasers from Syed Ahmed, Moqbul Ahmed and Khurshid Jahan got themselves added in the said miscellaneous case as opposite parties. The Assistant Commissioner (Land) after considering every aspects of the case and report of the Kanongo to the effect that respondent No.6 had no manner of possession and the opposite parties of the said miscellaneous case are in possession dismissed the miscellaneous case by order dated 19.10.2006. 

 7. Two supplementary affidavits were filed on behalf of added respondent No.6, Md. Mintu Chowdhury (leave petitioner): the first one in November, 2009 (date is not available from the record) and the second one on the 18th day of May, 2010. 

 8. In the first supplementary affidavit, it was stated, inter alia, that his father being the legal owner and in possession of the property in question filed Miscellaneous Case No.355 of 1968 (name of the Court not mentioned) during his life time against Peerzada Abul Kashem and Mahmood Hossain Siddique for correction of the record of rights wrongly prepared in their names, but on the basis of a misleading and wrong report, the miscellaneous case was dismissed ex-parte by order dated 01.08.2007. Subsequently, an application was filed by his father(Abdus Sattar) under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) for vacating the order dated 01.08.1970 passed ex-parte, but the application was rejected as not being maintainable vide order dated 27.08.1970. On another application filed by the father of the respondent under Order XLVII, rule 1 read with section 114 of the Code for reviewing the order dated 01.08.1970, the miscellaneous case was restored vacating the said order of dismissal by order dated 22.08.1970 (correct dated is 29.8.1970) fixing 02.09.1970 for hearing the case on which date after examining the father of the respondent (Abdus Sattar Chowdhury) and considering the exhibits filed on his behalf the names of the opposite parties of the said miscellaneous case were deleted from the case khatian and name of writ-respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar, was incorporated' which is apparent from annexure-'F-I' to- the affidavit-in-reply. The writ-petitioners while admitting identification of the concerned khatians and plots as R.S. one and in the report of Circle Officer (Revenue), Dhaka, the khatians and plots being identified as R.S. those facts cannot be resolved in writ jurisdiction. By annexure-'I' to the affidavit-in-reply, the writ-petitioners want to introduce new facts with a designed motive to create confusion and to make complication as if they had been seeking relief in a Court of appeal or revision and as such, the same did not deserve any consideration. The subject matter of a decree passed in a title suit (Title Suit No.280 of 1970 filed by the predecessors of the writ-petitioners) cannot be amended or corrected in a writ jurisdiction by passing the statutory provision of law. So, the Rule was liable to be discharged. 

 10. A Division Bench of the High Court Division hearing the writ petition by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute declaring the impugned order dated 09.12.2003 passed by the Full Board to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and directed respondent No.1 (the land Appeal Board) to cancel the same and writ-respondent No.5, Assistant Commissioner (Land), Tejgaon Circle, Dhaka to restore the S.A. records in the name of the writ-petitioners to the extent of 5.17 acres as it originally stood; hence this petition for leave to appeal. 

 11. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioners, has tried to assail the impugned judgment and order on the submission that the High Court Division instead of considering the propriety and legality of the order passed by the Full Board in the review case, misdirected itself in observing "we have already seen that the predecessors of the petitioners acquired title in the case property on the basis of the decree dated 29.12.1970 passed in Title Suit No.280 of 1970 against respondent No.6 and others" without considering that the judgment and decree was passed in the said suit on the basis of R.S. record and that runs counter to the claim of the writ-petitioners. He has further submitted that the High Court Division while exercising writ jurisdiction misdirected itself in finding fault with the order dated 02.09.1970 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 355 of 1968 as if it were deciding an appeal ignoring that alternative relief provided by the statute was neither availed by the predecessors-in-interest of the writ-petitioners nor by themselves for the last about 40 years and this caused miscarriage of justice in passing the impugned judgment and order. Mr. Mahbubey Alam has further submitted that the Full Board having found error on the face of the record to the effect that in the order dated 29.08.1995 passed by the Chairman in Appeal No. 3-85/94(Appeal)-Dhaka, it was observed “২৬। এই মামলার বাদী ২৮০/৭০ নং মামলা দায়ের করিয়া পূর্ববর্তী ডিক্রি রদের ডিক্রী লাভ করেন।” which is contrary to record inasmuch as the plaintiffs of that suit did not seek any such relief in the suit and as such, the Full Board rightly allowed the review application, the High Court Division erred in law in interfering with the order of the Full Board. He has lastly submitted that the High Court Division misdirected itself in making the Rule absolute on new grounds without considering that all 3(three) grounds taken in the writ petition, in fact, run counter to the claim of the writ-petitioners and thus exceeded its jurisdiction in passing the impugned judgment and order interfering with the order passed by the Full Board and as such, the same calls for interference by this Division. 

 13. From the impugned judgment and order, it appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute relying on the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 280 of 1970 wherein it was declared that the plaintiffs are the owners of the suit land. From the plaint of Title Suit No. 280 of 1970 which was annexed to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the added respondent as annexure-'I', it appears that the predecessors of the writ-petitioners filed the suit for declaration that they are the exclusive owners in possession of the suit land and that none of the defendants has any right, title or interest therein; in the suit, respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar Chowdhury, father of the leave petitioner was impleaded as defendant No.1 , but he did not contest the suit. The High Court Division came to the finding that on the basis of the decree passed in the said suit, the predecessors of the writ-petitioners got their names mutated by filing Miscellaneous Case No.9 of 1977-78 and S.A. khatian No.605/1 was prepared in their names and they had been paying rents regularly to the Government and after 17 years there from writ-respondent No.6 filed Miscellaneous Case No.19 of 1987 for mutating his name and correction of the S.A. record on the basis of the order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 355 of 1968 and on such application, the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Tejgaon Circle by order dated 09.01.1988 cancelled the mutated S.A. khatian in the name of the predecessor of petitioner No.1 and several others in respect of plot Nos.1353, 1354, 1355, 1356, 1357, 1358 and 1385 covering an area of 5.17 acres of land on the finding that he acquired title on the basis of the order passed in the said miscellaneous case (355 of 1968), though Maqbul Ahmed and others, the predecessors of the writ-petitioners, were not made parties in the miscellaneous case. 

 14. The star document of added respondent No. 6 relying on which the Assistant Commissioner (Land) cancelled the mutated khatian in the name of the predecessor of writ-petitioner No. 1 and others and the Full Board allowed the review application is the order passed in Miscellaneous Case No.355 of 1968. The High Court Division did not put any reliance upon the order passed in the said miscellaneous case on the view that the same was allowed ex-parte without serving   any notice upon the opposite parties though the same was earlier dismissed ex-parte on 01.08.1970. The High Court Division further noticed that the said miscellaneous case was restored on 29.08.1970 on the basis of an application filed on 27.08.1970 under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code, that is, just after two days of the filing of the application without serving any notice upon the opposite parties after an application filed under section 151 of the Code for vacating the order dated 01.08.1970 was rejected on 27.08.1970. In this regard, the High Court Division considered sub-section 13 of section 143A of the Act (since repealed) which provided that for the purpose of review, the relevant provisions of the Code, that is, Order XLVII thereof shall be made applicable for the purpose of filing an application for review and rule 4(2) of Order XLVII provides that no application for review shall be granted unless notice of the application has been served upon the opposite party. The High Court Division observed that the miscellaneous case was allowed ex-parte on 02.09.1970 without serving any notice upon the opposite parties and that again just after 3(three) days of the date of restoration of the case where order was passed to delete the names of the opposite parties from S.A. khatian and to incorporate the name of writ-respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar Chowdhury. In this regard, the High Court Division further noticed that in the said miscellaneous case, Moqbul Ahmed, Syed Ahmed and Most. Khurshid Jahan Akhter, the predecessors-in-interest of the writ-petitioners, were not made parties and the same was filed against Peerzada Abul Kashem and Mohammad Hasnain Siddiqui; Maqbul Ahmed, Syed Ahmed and Most. Khurshid Jahan Akhter filed an application in the miscellaneous case on 02.08.1969 under Order, rule 10 of the Code for adding them as opposite parties, the application was kept with the record. The High Court Division further found that 7(seven) plots in question were ROR plot being Nos.1353, 1354, 1355, 1356, 1357, 1365, 1384 and 1385 and those related to S.A. record and not R.S. record. The High Court Division further observed that in 1969, there was no existence of R.S. record and the Assistant Commissioner (Land) committed a bonafide mistake stating R.S. plots in place of S.A. plots inasmuch as R.S. khatian was finally published under section 144(7) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the District of Dhaka in Of 1985 or thereabout. The High Court Division further noticed that from annexure-G to the affidavit-in-reply, it was evident that the names of predecessors of the petitioners, Maqbul Ahmed, Syed Ahmed and Most. Khurshid Jahan Akhter, wife of Maqbul Ahmed, were mutated in Miscellaneous Case No.9 of 1977-78 and accordingly, mutated S.A. khatian No. 605/1 in respect of plot Nos.1353, 1354, 1355, 1356, 1357, 1358 was recorded correctly in their names in respect of an area of 5.17 acres only and from annexure-'G-1' to the affidavit-in-reply, it appeared that subsequently, R.S. khatian No.76 of mouza Tejgaon Shilpa elaka, previously Tejkunipara, P.S.-Tejgaon, previously Keranigonj was finally published under section 144(7) of the Act in the names of the aforesaid persons correctly and till date respondent No.6 did not take any step in respect of the said finally published R.S. khatian in the name of the petitioners' predecessors; since the later record of right, i.e. R.S. record was finally published in the names of the predecessors of the writ-petitioners, such entry in the record of rights shall be presumed to be correct unless it is proved by evidence to be incorrect and the R.S. record of rights shall prevail over the S.A. record. 

 16. The High Court Division further held that the Full Board exceeded its jurisdiction in allowing the review application inasmuch as it failed to point out discovery of new and important matter or evidence which after the exercise of due diligence was not within the knowledge of respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar Chowdhury or could not be adduced by him at the time when the order was passed by the Chairman, Land Appeal Board, without strict proof of such allegations as provided in Order XLVII, rule 4(2) of the Code. Mr. Mahbubey Alam found it difficult to assail this view of the High Court Division with reference to the Rules, 1990 or the Code. Mr. Mahbubey Alam could not also assail the finding of the High Court Division that the R.S. record was finally published under section 144(7) of the Act in the District of Dhaka in 1985 and thereabout and in 1969, there was no existence of R.S. record, so it is of no use to argue that since the predecessor of the writ-petitioners filed Title Suit No.280 of 1970 in respect of R.S. khatian and R.S. plots, the High Court Division was not justified in deciding the propriety of the order of the Full Board relying on the decree passed in the said title suit. In this regard, we like to observe that in a proceeding under section 143A of the Act (since repealed), title is not decided and the decree passed in a suit for title shall always prevail upon the order passed in such a proceeding, so the High Court Division committed no illegality in relying upon the decree passed in Title Suit No. 280 of 1970 in preference to the order passed in Miscellaneous Case No.355 of 1968 in interfering with the order passed by the Full Board. 

 18. A reading of section 6 of the Ordinance shows that by this section the Land Appeal Board has been vested with the power of review of its order if an application is filed for such review within the time prescribed therein. Of the Rules as quoted hereinbefore, rule 5 shows that in the application for review, the applicant shall have to state the law and the facts which were not considered in the order sought to be reviewed and shall also have to pin point the subjects of review (বিষয়সমূহ) of the order of the Land Appeal Board. From rule 5, it further appears that while considering the application foe review the Full Board must see that the applicant fulfilled the conditions as mandated therein and if not the application would deserve no consideration on merit. The application for review was not annexed either to the writ petition or to the affidavit-in-opposition and the supplementary affidavits-in-opposition, so we could not see the contents thereof. But from the order of the Full Board, it is apparent that neither any fact nor any law was stated or pointed out which was not considered by the Land Appeal Board while passing the order sought to be reviewed nor the subject matter for review was formulated or specified. Rule 5 of the Rules, 1990 is quite in conformity   with Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code. As per rule of Order XLVII of the Code, review of a decree or an order can be allowed only when the person who seeks review of such decree or order can make out a case of discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed or order made or on account of some mistake or error apparent   on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reasons. But in the instant case, respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar Chowdhury, failed to make any such case. And the Full Board also did not give or any such finding. 

 19. From the order of the Full Board, it appears that it reviewed the order of the Chairman, Land Appeal Board, in a casual manner without pointing out or giving any finding as to any law or fact which was not considered by him in passing the order dated 29.08.1995 or error apparent on the face of the record committed by the Chairman of the Board in passing the said order sought to be reviewed as provided in Order XLVII, rule 1(1) of the 7 Code. As pointed out by the learned Judges; respondent No.6, Abdus Sattar Chowdhury, failed to make out any case of discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the order was passed by the Chairman, Land Appeal Board and the Full Board did not also give any finding to that effect.

full_judgment:
The plaintiffs case is that their predecessors-in-interest Akbar Ali, Gullya Haji Azizur Rahman (plaintiff No. 10) and others got the suit land by amicable arrangement among the co-sharers and the suit land along with other lands were recorded in their names in the R. S. Khatian. Plaintiff Nos. 11 and 12 purchased some parts of the suit land from plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and 9. The plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land but the defendants collusively recorded their names as well as the name of the government during the last survey operation and hence the suit. 

 3. Mr. B. K. Das, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioners submits that the High Court Division misread the judgment of the lower appellate Court that it gave a finding that the lower appellate Court found that the presumption of R. S. record under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act been rebutted by subsequent entry in the M. R. R. Khatian standing in the name of the defendants. He submits that there is no such finding of the lower appellate Court. 

 5. Mr. B. K. Das relies upon the case of Meherjan Bibi Vs. Naimuddin Dhali, 33DLR 126. in which it has been held that in a case where the plaintiff relies upon the entry in the record of rights for the basis of his title it is not necessary for him to show the basis of his title as to the entry in the record of rights. 

 7. The lower appellate Court having dismissed the petitioners suit on a discussion of the evidence on record and the High Court Division having affirmed it correctly we find no ground for interference.
